title: Days 14 and 15: Shocks, Characteristics, and the Mathematics of Breaking Waves
text:
Thursday: Chapters 17–22

Chapter 17: The Method of Characteristics
The method of characteristics is the standard technique for solving first-order hyperbolic PDEs, and for understanding what “characteristic” meant in Days 11 and 12 it is the right place to start. The idea is to convert the PDE into a family of ODEs by changing to coordinates that travel with the signal rather than coordinates that stay fixed.
For a first-order PDE of the form
\[\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + c(u)\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 0,\]
the characteristics are curves \(x(t)\) satisfying \(dx/dt = c(u)\), i.e. curves that travel through the \((x,t)\) plane at the same speed as the local wave speed. Along any such curve,
\[\frac{du}{dt} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + \frac{dx}{dt}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + c(u)\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 0,\]
so \(u\) is constant along each characteristic. The PDE, which couples \(u\) at all points simultaneously, reduces to a family of decoupled statements: “on this curve, \(u\) does not change.” Solving the original PDE is then a matter of finding which characteristic passes through any given point \((x,t)\) and reading off its initial value.
The connection to Day 11 is immediate: mizer’s transport equation is exactly this, with \(x\) replaced by \(w\) (body mass), \(u\) replaced by \(n(w,t)\) (number density), and \(c\) replaced by \(g(w,t)\) (growth rate). The characteristic curves are the growth trajectories \(dw/dt = g(w,t)\). Day 12’s track_cohort() function is a numerical integrator for these characteristics. Day 11’s age-at-size derivation , \(\tau(w) = \int_{w_{min}}^w dw'/g(w')\) , is the closed-form solution for characteristics when \(g\) depends only on \(w\), not \(t\). Knowing this explicitly is more satisfying than having arrived at it by analogy.


Chapter 18: Gradient Catastrophe and Breaking Times
In the linear case \(c(u) = \text{const}\), all characteristics are parallel lines and nothing goes wrong. Chapter 18 is about what happens when \(c\) depends on \(u\): characteristics from different initial points can travel at different speeds and eventually intersect each other.
When two characteristics cross, the solution \(u\) at the crossing point would have to take two different values simultaneously , one inherited from each characteristic, which is impossible for a function. The solution breaks down in finite time. This is the gradient catastrophe: the spatial gradient \(\partial u/\partial x\) grows without bound, eventually becoming vertical, and at that moment the PDE solution in the classical sense ceases to exist.
The breaking time \(t_B\) is the time at which this first happens. For an initial profile \(u_0(x)\), the characteristics from \(x_0\) have speed \(c(u_0(x_0))\), so two characteristics from nearby points \(x_0\) and \(x_0 + \delta x_0\) will eventually meet if they are converging. Intersections first occur at:
\[t_B = \min_{x_0} \frac{-1}{c'(u_0(x_0))\, u_0'(x_0)},\]
where the minimum is taken over all \(x_0\) where the denominator is negative (i.e., where characteristics are converging). The breaking time is the reciprocal of the maximum rate at which initial data is being compressed.
For the mizer application, this is suggestive. The growth rate \(g(w,t)\) is not independent of \(n\) but depends on the prey field, which depends on \(n\) itself. This feedback means the “effective wave speed” for different size classes is not fixed, and there is in principle no reason characteristics cannot converge. Whether anything close to a gradient catastrophe actually occurs in the Anchovy simulation, and on what timescale, is not something the simulation has been checked for directly.


Chapter 19: Shock Waves
After the gradient catastrophe, the classical smooth solution no longer exists. Chapter 19 introduces the shock wave as the replacement: a propagating discontinuity in \(u\), where the solution jumps from one value to another at the shock location. Rather than requiring \(u\) to be smooth everywhere (which it can no longer be), the PDE is rewritten in integral (weak) form, which makes sense even across discontinuities.
The key result is the Rankine-Hugoniot condition, which determines the speed \(s\) at which a shock propagates:
\[s = \frac{[\phi(u)]}{[u]} = \frac{\phi(u_R) - \phi(u_L)}{u_R - u_L},\]
where \(\phi\) is the flux, and \(u_L\), \(u_R\) are the values of \(u\) immediately to the left and right of the shock. The shock is not free to move at any speed; it must move at exactly the rate that balances the flux on either side.
There is also the question of uniqueness. Weak solutions satisfying the Rankine-Hugoniot condition are not, in general, unique as multiple shock positions can satisfy the jump conditions. The Lax entropy condition selects the physically correct one: characteristics on both sides of the shock must run into the shock (not out of it). In other words, the shock is a sink for characteristics, not a source.


Chapter 20: Shock Waves: Traffic at a Red Light
Chapter 20 applies the shock theory to traffic flow. This is one of the canonical examples of conservation-law shocks because the initial and boundary conditions are physically clean and the result is intuitively verifiable.
The model treats traffic density \(u(x,t)\) as a continuum satisfying \(u_t+ \phi' u_x = 0\), where \(v\) is a speed-density relationship (cars slow down as the road gets crowded). The flux is \(\phi=uv\) .
The red-light problem: at \(t=0\) a line of stationary cars sits upstream of a red light at \(x=0\), with empty road downstream. When the light turns green, a rarefaction wave (covered in Chapter 22) propagates back through the queue, permitting cars to start moving. When a green light turns red, upstream traffic hits the stationary queue and the incoming flux exceeds the standing-traffic flux, characteristics from both sides converge, and a shock (the queue front) forms and moves backward at the Rankine-Hugoniot speed. The shock front is the queue growing, the rarefaction is the queue draining.
What the traffic example makes concrete is that both shocks and rarefactions are routine physical events in conservation-law systems, not pathological exceptions. Any time flux is non-monotone in the conserved quantity, you expect both to appear as different parts of the same initial condition evolve.


Chapter 21: The Viscosity Method
With multiple weak solutions available and the Lax entropy condition providing one selection criterion, Chapter 21 introduces a second, more analytical approach to the same question: vanishing viscosity, also called the viscosity method.
The idea is to regularise the equation by adding a small diffusion term:
\[u_t +c(u)u_x = ru_{xx},\]
and then take \(r \to 0^+\). The regularised equation has a unique smooth solution for each \(r > 0\), and as \(r\) shrinks these smooth solutions converge to a weak solution of the original equation. The solution they select is, under reasonable conditions.
The viscosity method matters beyond being an alternative derivation of the Rankine-Hugoniot condition. It gives a physical story for why that particular weak solution is the right one: it is the limit of physically-regularised systems (real fluids have viscosity; real traffic has reaction times and finite car lengths; real fish populations have diffusion in size-space). The sharp shock is an idealisation, but it is the limit of the physically realistic, smooth solutions.


Chapter 22: Rarefaction Waves
The last chapter of Thursday’s reading returns to the other half of the story. Where shocks arise from characteristics converging, rarefaction waves arise when they spread out. The initial data sends characteristics in diverging directions, leaving a region that no single characteristic reaches and the solution fills it with a fan of characteristics connecting the left and right states.
For the Burgers-like equation \(u_t + uu_x = 0\) with a step initial condition \(u_L < u_R\) at \(x=0\), the unique entropy solution is a centred rarefaction fan:
\[u(x,t) = \begin{cases} u_L & x/t < u_L \\ x/t & u_L \leq x/t \leq u_R \\ u_R & x/t > u_R \end{cases}\]
The solution in the fan region \(u = x/t\) is a similarity solution: it depends only on the ratio \(x/t\), not \(x\) and \(t\) separately. Physically, the fan is smooth (no gradient catastrophe), and each point within it has a unique \(u\) value determined by which characteristic passes through it.

title: Days 14 and 15: Shocks, Characteristics, and the Mathematics of Breaking Waves
text:
Friday: Exercises from Chapters 18–21
Friday was spent working through the exercises in chapters 18–21, rather than reading further ahead.It was partly independently and partly alongside Gustav (the project supervisor), which gave a useful chance to work through the trickier parts out loud. Chapters 17 through 22 cover material that is interconnected; the method of characteristics feeds into the gradient catastrophe, which motivates shocks, which require the Rankine-Hugoniot conditions and the entropy criterion, which the viscosity method justifies, and rarefaction waves complete the picture on the other side. Reading it all through on Thursday gave the shape of the argument; the exercises were the check on whether the pieces actually worked in hand.
The exercises in chapter 18 focused on computing breaking times for specific initial profiles. This turns out to be mostly calculus: finding \(c'(u_0)\,u_0'(x_0)\) and minimising \(-1/(c'\,u_0')\) over initial positions. The subtlety is in recognising which initial profiles will not break (those where characteristics everywhere diverge) versus those that will (characteristics converging somewhere), and not confusing the breaking time with the time of the catastrophe’s worst consequences.
The chapter 19 and 20 exercises were largely on applying the Rankine-Hugoniot condition to specific left and right states and tracking shock positions through time.
Chapter 21’s exercises on the viscosity method included verifying that the tanh shock profile satisfies the regularised ODE, and checking that the shock speed matches Rankine-Hugoniot. The algebra is not difficult once the structure is set up, but it is easy to get signs wrong without care.

title: Days 14 and 15: Shocks, Characteristics, and the Mathematics of Breaking Waves
text:
What’s Next

Back to the Simulation: Build the Wave Solution Step by Step
With the wave theory properly in place, the next priority is returning to the mizer simulation and working through the following sequence:

Validate the linear (density-independent) model. Confirm the steady state is a power law. Run time-dependent solutions starting from a Gaussian initial condition and verify the peak travels as a wave. Use a travelling-wave ansatz to reduce the PDE to an ODE, and cross-check against the Meiser vignette by setting diffusion to zero.
Switch mechanisms on one at a time:

Add reproduction: Perturbations should slow down as fish approach maturity.
Add the feedback loop (mature individuals seeding new recruits at the small-size end): The wave should return broadened at the lower end after a delay.
Add resource depletion: This is the mechanism required for persistent oscillatory waves. Without it, the wave should broaden and eventually settle back to steady state.

Isolate resource depletion. As a shorter intermediate test, skip the other mechanisms entirely and add only resource depletion. Measure how much it slows the Gaussian peak and check whether it alone can account for the observed ~3× generation-time oscillation period. Also check whether it is the resource depletion itself, or the resulting reduction in growth, that drives the slowdown.



Finding the Unstable Steady State: steadyNewton()
The dev version of mizer (3.1.0.9000, installable from GitHub) includes a new function steadyNewton() that solves the steady-state equation directly , without running the dynamics to equilibrium. This matters because the method does not depend on stability: it should be able to locate the unstable steady state that the periodic solutions oscillate around which is something ordinary time-integration would never converge to. The longer-term goal is to use this to answer the bifurcation question: at the transition from a stable to an unstable steady state, does productivity decrease?


Fishing: Window vs. Effort
The surprising result from Day 12, that a short fishing window (~5–6 months) barely affects fish density while a 10-year window at high effort crashes the population to zero, still deserves a proper follow-up. The intuition Gustav offered is that a constant flow from the resource is more efficient than alternating between years of underutilisation and overutilisation: during a long off-season the primary production is going to waste, and the resource can’t bank it. A short pulse avoids that waste and leaves the rest of the cycle to run undisturbed. Systematically comparing constant low-effort fishing with periodic high-effort short-window fishing, and checking whether the yield gap tracks the degree of primary-production underutilisation, would make this argument concrete.

title: Day 11: Generation Time, the Growth-Rate Proof, and Unwrapping Day 8’s Discontinuity
section: Closing the Loop on Day 8: Why Lambda = 2.05 “Broke” the Phase Plot
text:
Closing the Loop on Day 8: Why Lambda = 2.05 “Broke” the Phase Plot
Day 8’s phase-by-size-class plot (Arg() of the DFT coefficient at the dominant frequency, for each size bin) looked smooth at lambda = 2, but at lambda = 2.05 it showed sharp jumps across almost the full \(\pm\pi\) range at two size ranges. At the time this got filed as evidence of “a bifurcation point at lambda = 2,” treating the balanced food environment as a structurally special case.
That framing doesn’t hold up. Arg() only ever returns a value in \((-\pi, \pi]\), because a complex number’s angle is only defined modulo \(2\pi\). Whatever the true, unwrapped phase lag of the system is doing as size increases, the moment it crosses an odd multiple of \(\pi\), Arg() snaps it back into range producing an apparent jump of almost a full \(2\pi\) in the plot even though nothing physically discontinuous happened. If lambda = 2.05 makes that crossing happen (twice, within the size range tested) and lambda = 2 doesn’t, that alone is enough to produce exactly the pattern seen on Day 8, with no need for a bifurcation.


Code
library(mizer)
library(patchwork)
library(reshape2)
library(plotly)
library(dplyr)
library(mizerExperimental)
library(tidyverse)
library(glue)
library(ggplot2)

# Same single-species Anchovy setup as Day 8, wrapped in a function so it can
# be re-run cleanly for both lambda values without copy-pasting the pipeline.
run_anchovy <- function(lambda) {
  p <- list(
    dt = 0.001, dx = 0.1, w_min = 0.0003, w_max = 66.5,
    w_mat = 10, alpha = 0.1, gamma = 750, lambda = lambda, a0 = 100
  )
  kappa <- p$a0 * exp(-6.9 * (p$lambda - 1))
  no_w  <- round(log(p$w_max / p$w_min) / p$dx)

  params <- newSingleSpeciesParams(
    species_name = "Anchovy",
    w_min = p$w_min, w_max = p$w_max, w_mat = p$w_mat,
    no_w  = no_w,    lambda = p$lambda, kappa = kappa,
    alpha = p$alpha, gamma  = p$gamma,  ks    = 0
  )
  # getResourceRate() is the older name for this getter (mizer now suggests
  # resource_rate()) but it still works and is what was actually run today.
  r <- getResourceRate(params) * 0.001
  params <- setResource(params, resource_rate = r,
                        resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat")
  params@initial_n_pp[] <- params@cc_pp * 0.1

  # Spin up, then crash the large size class to kick the system off
  # equilibrium and let the food-limitation cycle from Day 7/8 develop.
  sim <- project(params, t_max = 10, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                 progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")

  idx  <- params@w >= 10 & params@w <= 100
  last <- dim(sim@n)[1]
  sim@n[last, , idx] <- sim@n[last, , idx] / 10^3

  sim     <- project(sim, t_max = 90, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                     progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
  sim_300 <- project(sim, t_max = 200, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                     progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
  sim_600 <- project(sim_300, t_max = 300, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                     progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
  list(params = params, sim_600 = sim_600)
}
# Note: this triggers a mizer warning about an "unrealistic erepro" value for
# Anchovy. That's expected for this toy single-species fit (it isn't tuned to
# match a real stock's reproductive biology) and isn't a sign of a bug.

# Reused from Day 8: power spectrum of a (mean-subtracted) signal, skipping
# the zero-frequency bin.
power_spectrum <- function(signal, dt) {
  signal <- signal - mean(signal)
  n      <- length(signal)
  freqs  <- (1:(n - 1)) / (n * dt)
  power  <- Mod(fft(signal))^2
  half   <- seq_len(floor((n - 1) / 2))
  data.frame(freq = freqs[half], period = 1 / freqs[half], power = power[half + 1])
}

# DFT coefficient at the dominant frequency, for every size bin at once.
# Mod() gives amplitude, Arg() gives the (wrapped) phase used throughout.
phase_by_size <- function(sim_600, params) {
  times  <- as.numeric(dimnames(sim_600@n)[[1]])
  bm     <- getBiomass(sim_600)[, "Anchovy"]
  ps     <- power_spectrum(bm[times > 300], 0.2)
  period_dom <- ps$period[which.max(ps$power)]
  omega  <- 2 * pi / period_dom

  post   <- times > 300
  t_vec  <- times[post] - times[post][1]
  n_post <- sim_600@n[post, "Anchovy", ]

  coeffs <- apply(n_post, 2, function(x) {
    signal <- x - mean(x)
    sum(signal * exp(-1i * omega * t_vec))
  })

  list(period_dom = period_dom,
       df = data.frame(w = params@w, amplitude = Mod(coeffs), phase = Arg(coeffs)))
}

run_2    <- run_anchovy(2)
run_2.05 <- run_anchovy(2.05)
res_2    <- phase_by_size(run_2$sim_600, run_2$params)
res_2.05 <- phase_by_size(run_2.05$sim_600, run_2.05$params)
df_2     <- res_2$df
df_2.05  <- res_2.05$df




Code
p1 <- ggplot(df_2, aes(x = w, y = phase)) +
  geom_line() + scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Size (g)", y = "Phase (radians)", title = "lambda = 2")

p2 <- ggplot(df_2.05, aes(x = w, y = phase)) +
  geom_line() + scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Size (g)", y = "Phase (radians)", title = "lambda = 2.05")

p1 + p2









What this shows: at lambda = 2, the phase stays inside \([-1.66, 2.68]\) radians across the whole size range, well within one branch of \((-\pi,\pi]\), so there’s nothing to wrap. At lambda = 2.05, phase spans \([-3.14, 3.13]\) radians, i.e. essentially the full circle, and there are two places where it jumps almost exactly \(2\pi\) between adjacent size bins: a jump of 6.16 radians around \(w \approx 0.0010\)–\(0.0011\) g, and a jump of 6.25 radians around \(w \approx 1.95\)–\(2.15\) g (both compared with a largest jump of only 0.31 radians anywhere in the lambda = 2 curve). \(2\pi \approx 6.28\), so these are indeed full wraps, not gradual structural changes.
(Day 8’s original eyeballed read placed the jump locations at roughly 0.003–0.01 g and ~1 g which is in the right ballpark but not exact, which is itself a small reminder that Day 8’s numbers were never claimed to be precise either.)
If this really were a dynamical bifurcation, it should leave a mark on the actual dynamics, not just on a quantity (\(\mathrm{Arg}\)) that is mathematically guaranteed to wrap. The size-time heatmap is a check on exactly that:


Code
times  <- as.numeric(dimnames(run_2.05$sim_600@n)[[1]])
t_win  <- times > 560 & times < 580   # ~4 cycles

bm_win <- sweep(run_2.05$sim_600@n[t_win, "Anchovy", ], 2, run_2.05$params@w^2, "*")
df_heat <- melt(bm_win)
names(df_heat) <- c("time", "w", "bm")
df_heat$time <- as.numeric(as.character(df_heat$time))
df_heat$w    <- as.numeric(as.character(df_heat$w))

ggplot(df_heat, aes(x = time, y = log10(w), fill = log10(pmax(bm, 1e-12)))) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "log10\nbiomass") +
  labs(x = "Time (years)", y = "log10(size [g])",
       title = "Size-time heatmap, lambda = 2.05")









What this shows: the heatmap at lambda = 2.05 looks like Day 8’s lambda = 2 heatmap ,with a slightly diagonal structure, everything brightening and dimming together. Nothing about the raw dynamics looks different near the two “jump” sizes. The only place the lambda = 2.05 case looks different from lambda = 2 is in the wrapped phase number, exactly what the wraparound explanation predicts and the bifurcation explanation doesn’t.

title: Day 11: Generation Time, the Growth-Rate Proof, and Unwrapping Day 8’s Discontinuity
section: How Long Does It Take to Grow Up? Calculating Generation Time
text:
How Long Does It Take to Grow Up? Calculating Generation Time
Day 8’s mechanistic story was that the oscillation period is set by how long it takes a recruit to grow up to maturity, supported indirectly by the period ~ w_mat^0.2 scaling law. The generation time itself had never actually been calculated. Today it was, using the steady-state growth rate from getEGrowth():


Code
params <- run_2$params
g  <- getEGrowth(params)["Anchovy", ]   # steady-state growth rate g(w)
w  <- params@w
dw <- params@dw

# age(w) = integral_{w_min}^{w} 1/g(w') dw', via the trapezoidal rule —
# i.e. cumulative time spent growing from w_min up to w.
integrand  <- 1 / g
age        <- c(0, cumsum((integrand[-1] + integrand[-length(integrand)]) / 2 * dw[-length(dw)]))
age_at_mat <- approx(x = w, y = age, xout = params@species_params$w_mat)$y

df_age <- data.frame(w = head(w, -1), age = head(age, -1))

ggplot(df_age, aes(x = w, y = age)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = params@species_params$w_mat, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = age_at_mat, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  annotate("point", x = params@species_params$w_mat, y = age_at_mat, colour = "red", size = 2) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "body mass (g)", y = "age (years)", title = "Age-at-size, Anchovy")









age_at_mat is exactly the generation time: how long, in years, a fish takes to grow from w_min to w_mat under the steady-state growth rate.
What this shows: at lambda = 2, age_at_mat = 3.50 years and the dominant FFT period (period_dom, same machinery as Day 8) = 8.33 years, giving a ratio of 2.38, not 3. Re-running the same calculation under the lambda = 2.05 parameters gives age_at_mat = 2.70 years against a period of 7.14 years giving a ratio of 2.65. So the period is consistently a small multiple of the generation time, somewhere around 2.4–2.7, in both cases closer to “two and a half generations” than to a clean “three generations.” The original ballpark guess was in the right neighbourhood, but the actual number ,once calculated rather than eyeballed, is a bit lower than that. The fact that it isn’t a clean integer (2, 3, or otherwise) in either case is itself worth sitting with rather than rounding away.

title: Day 11: Generation Time, the Growth-Rate Proof, and Unwrapping Day 8’s Discontinuity
section: The Phase-Growth-Rate Proof and Where It Breaks
text:
The Phase-Growth-Rate Proof and Where It Breaks
The rest of the day went into deriving, properly, how phase should depend on growth rate, rather than just asserting the relationship. The derivation has two pieces: where the phase physically comes from in mizer’s underlying equation, and what slope it should therefore have as a function of size. Each piece holds up on its own. What doesn’t hold up is the final prediction, once it’s actually checked against today’s numbers, and that failure turns out to be informative rather than just a dead end.

Where the phase physically comes from: mizer’s transport equation
Mizer’s size-spectrum dynamics are, at their core, a transport equation in \(w\):
\[\frac{\partial n(w,t)}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial}{\partial w}\big[g(w)\,n(w,t)\big] = -(\text{death terms}),\]
meaning biomass density is advected through size-space along characteristic curves defined by \(dw/dt = g(w)\). A characteristic starting at \(w_{min}\) at birth time \(t_{\text{birth}}\) reaches size \(w\) at time \(t_{\text{birth}} + \tau(w)\), where \(\tau\) solves \(d\tau/dw = 1/g(w)\) with \(\tau(w_{min})=0\). Separating variables,
\[\tau(w) = \int_{w_{min}}^{w} \frac{dw'}{g(w')} = a(w),\]
exactly the age-at-size integral calculated in the previous section. So a perturbation introduced at \(w_{min}\) at time \(t_{\text{birth}}\) is carried, to leading order, along this characteristic and peaks at size \(w\) at time
\[t_{\text{peak}}(w) = t_{\text{birth}} + a(w).\]


From peak time to phase, and the sign that connects it to Arg()
Model the (mean-subtracted) signal at size bin \(w\) as \(\text{signal}_w(t) = A(w)\cos(k t - \phi(w))\), with \(A(w)>0\) and \(k = 2\pi/{}\)period_dom the dominant angular frequency (the code’s omega). This cosine is at its maximum exactly when its argument is \(0 \bmod 2\pi\), i.e. when \(k t - \phi(w) = 0\). Solving for \(t\) defines \(t_{\text{peak}}(w) = \phi(w)/k\), i.e.
\[\phi(w) = k\, t_{\text{peak}}(w) = k\, t_{\text{birth}} + k\, a(w) \pmod {2\pi}.\]


The slope prediction
Differentiating \(\phi(w) = k\,t_{\text{birth}} + k\,a(w)\) with respect to \(w\) (product rule, with \(u(w)=k\) constant and \(v(w)=a(w)\), so \(u'(w)=0\)):
\[\frac{d\phi}{dw} = 0 \cdot a(w) + k\cdot\frac{da}{dw} = \frac{k}{g(w)},\]
using \(da/dw = 1/g(w)\) from the fundamental theorem of calculus applied to the age-at-size integral.
In plain language: picture each size class as a clock showing how long ago that fish was tiny. Bigger fish reflect what small fish were doing further in the past, and “phase” is just that time-lag written as an angle instead of a number of years. If growth is slow, a lot of lag builds up between one size and the next, so the angle should move a lot per step in size; if growth is fast, the angle barely moves. That same logic is what produces the wraparound in the section above: an angle that moves a lot eventually wraps around the circle.


Checking it against today’s numbers
The prediction is specific enough to test directly: Arg(coeffs) should fall steadily as size increases, and the total fall from \(w_{min}\) to \(w_{mat}\) should equal \(k \cdot a(w_{mat}) = 2\pi/2.38 \approx 2.64\) radians (using the lambda = 2 numbers from the previous section).
That is not what the lambda = 2 phase curve actually does. Reading the curve plotted earlier: phase starts at 0.98 radians at \(w_{min}\), rises to a peak of about 2.68 radians around \(w \approx 0.005\) g, and only then starts falling, reaching 1.40 radians by \(w \approx 9.8\) g (the nearest size bin to \(w_{mat} = 10\) g) before continuing down to \(-1.66\) at \(w_{max}\). The measured change from \(w_{min}\) to \(w_{mat}\) is \(0.98 - 1.40 = -0.42\) radians: the wrong sign (phase rose slightly overall, it didn’t fall) and less than a sixth of the predicted 2.64 radian drop.
Why the simple picture fails. The derivation assumes something that isn’t true, which is that growth rate is fixed. Neither holds.. Today’s derivation independently predicts what a non-feedback, one-way version of this system would look like, a phase that falls steadily and by a specific predictable amount, and the real curve does neither. Two independent checks (the heatmap’s structure; the wrong-signed, wrong-sized phase drop) land on the same conclusion.
The fixed-growth-rate assumption is also suspect on its own terms: the food supply driving growth oscillates along with everything else in this model, so \(g(w)\) measured at the unperturbed steady state is, at best, an average over a quantity that’s actually moving. Separating “the model is a feedback loop, not a delay line” from “the growth rate used was the wrong (time-averaged) one” isn’t possible from today’s numbers alone, both push in the direction of breaking the simple proof, and untangling them is the natural next step.
A side exploration today, looking for parameter settings closer to a pure sine wave (low harmonic content) rather than Day 8’s sharp-crash-long-plateau shape, was aimed at getting a cleaner signal to eventually retest this against a single-frequency, low-harmonic signal is a fairer test of a single-frequency theory than the one used above. Bumping the resource depletion rate from 0.001 to 0.01 (faster-replenishing resource pool) was the first thing tried:


Code
nice_biomass_plot <- function(sim, params, t){
  abm  <- melt(getBiomass(sim))
  abmr <- melt(getBiomass(sim, min_w = 0.01, max_w = 0.4))
  abmr$sp <- "small Anchovy"
  pbm <- sim@n_pp %*% (params@w_full * params@dw_full)
  pbm <- melt(pbm)
  names(pbm)[names(pbm) == "Var1"] <- "time"
  pbm$Var2 <- NULL
  pbm$sp <- "Plankton"
  bm <- rbind(pbm, abm, abmr)
  plot_ly(bm) %>%
    filter(time >= t) %>%
    add_lines(x = ~time, y = ~value, color = ~sp) %>%
    layout(yaxis = list(type = "log", exponentformat = "power",
                        title_text = "biomass (g/m^3)", range = c(-7, 2)),
           xaxis = list(title_text = "time (year)"))
}

p <- list(
  dt = 0.001, dx = 0.1, w_min = 0.0003, w_max = 66.5,
  w_mat = 10, alpha = 0.1, gamma = 750, lambda = 2.05, a0 = 100
)
kappa <- p$a0 * exp(-6.9 * (p$lambda - 1))
no_w  <- round(log(p$w_max / p$w_min) / p$dx)

params_fast <- newSingleSpeciesParams(
  species_name = "Anchovy",
  w_min = p$w_min, w_max = p$w_max, w_mat = p$w_mat,
  no_w  = no_w,    lambda = p$lambda, kappa = kappa,
  alpha = p$alpha, gamma  = p$gamma,  ks    = 0
)
r <- getResourceRate(params_fast) * 0.01   # faster turnover than Day 8's 0.001
params_fast <- setResource(params_fast, resource_rate = r,
                           resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat")
params_fast@initial_n_pp[] <- params_fast@cc_pp * 0.1

sim <- project(params_fast, t_max = 10, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
               progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
idx  <- params_fast@w >= 10 & params_fast@w <= 100
last <- dim(sim@n)[1]
sim@n[last, , idx] <- sim@n[last, , idx] / 10^3

sim     <- project(sim, t_max = 90, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                   progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
sim_300 <- project(sim, t_max = 200, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                   progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
sim_600_fast <- project(sim_300, t_max = 300, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                        progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")


This is set up and runs cleanly, but the comparison against the (now revised) proof hasn’t been done yet. That’s queued for tomorrow rather than claimed here.

title: Day 11: Generation Time, the Growth-Rate Proof, and Unwrapping Day 8’s Discontinuity
text:
What’s Next

Separate the two reasons the simple proof failed. Redo the phase-vs-growth-rate check using a growth rate that actually varies with time (not the fixed steady-state snapshot), to see how much of today’s mismatch that accounts for on its own and how much is left over that can only be explained by the feedback-loop structure itself.
Strogatz, Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos, Chapter 7 (limit cycles). Now that the oscillation looks like a genuine self-sustained cycle, it’s worth putting it on proper footing with the standard theory rather than reasoning about it ad hoc — and limit-cycle theory may have a cleaner way to handle phase in a feedback loop than the one-way delay-line model tried today.
Learn the discrete Fourier transform properly. So far fft() has been used as a black box. Understanding frequency bins, the Nyquist limit, and normalisation should put today’s phase argument on firmer ground.

title: Day 9: Confirming the Jam, Then Easing It
text:
Day 8 closed the loop on the oscillation mechanism: a synchronised, food-limited bottleneck at juvenile sizes, confirmed via FFT (one fundamental frequency, not a quasiperiodic mix), the w_mat scaling law (period ~ w_mat^0.2), and the phase/heatmap analysis (a standing wave, not a travelling cohort pulse). Discussing it with my supervisor, the consensus was that this is the traffic jam with recruits queuing against the food ceiling at small size.
That reframing raised the obvious next question: if it’s a traffic jam, can fishing act like ramp, thinning the queue at the bottleneck size enough to let the remaining fish through faster, and recovering some yield in the process? Today tested that directly, and ended up spending most of the day on a more basic question: is the jam itself too severe to be a realistic model in the first place?

title: Day 9: Confirming the Jam, Then Easing It
text:
New Diagnostic Tools
Before re-running the fisheries comparison, I added a couple of interactive diagnostics that make it much faster to see what’s happening across the whole size spectrum, not just at one size class at a time:


Code
library(mizer)
library(patchwork)
library(reshape2)
library(plotly)
library(dplyr)
library(mizerExperimental)
library(tidyverse) 
library(glue)
library(ggplot2)

nice_animation <- function(sim, t) {
  nf <- melt(sim@n)
  n_ppf <- melt(sim@n_pp)
  n_ppf$sp <- "Plankton"
  nf <- rbind(nf, n_ppf)

  plot_ly(nf) %>%
    filter(w > 10^-5) %>%
    filter(time >= t) %>%
    mutate(b = value * w^2) %>%
    add_lines(
      x = ~w, y = ~b,
      color = ~sp,
      frame = ~time,
      line = list(simplify = FALSE)
    ) %>%
    layout(xaxis = list(type = "log", exponentformat = "power",
                        title_text = "body mass (g)"),
           yaxis = list(type = "log", exponentformat = "power",
                        title_text = "biomass (g/m^3)",
                        range = c(-8, 0)))
}

nice_biomass_plot <- function(sim, t) {
  abm  <- melt(getBiomass(sim))
  abmr <- melt(getBiomass(sim, min_w = 0.01, max_w = 0.4))
  abmr$sp <- "small Anchovy"
  pbm <- sim@n_pp %*% (params@w_full * params@dw_full)
  pbm <- melt(pbm)
  names(pbm)[names(pbm) == "Var1"] <- "time"
  pbm$Var2 <- NULL
  pbm$sp <- "Plankton"
  bm <- rbind(pbm, abm, abmr)
  plot_ly(bm) %>%
    filter(time >= t) %>%
    add_lines(x = ~time, y = ~value, color = ~sp) %>%
    layout(yaxis = list(type = "log", exponentformat = "power",
                        title_text = "biomass (g/m^3)",
                        range = c(-7, 2)),
           xaxis = list(title_text = "time (year)"))
}


nice_animation plays the whole size spectrum (Anchovy + Plankton) forward through time, and nice_biomass_plot tracks total Anchovy biomass, small Anchovy biomass (0.01–0.4 g), and Plankton biomass on the same log-scale time series. Both make it much easier to see the bottleneck rather than infer it from a single summary statistic. Together with plotHover() on getBiomass() and the built-in getFlux(sim, power = 2), these became the standard diagnostic set for today.

title: Day 9: Confirming the Jam, Then Easing It
section: Setting Up: A Slightly Different Anchovy
text:
Setting Up: A Slightly Different Anchovy
The parameterisation was tweaked slightly from Day 8 with lambda being changed to 2.05 (the value that produced the sharp phase transitions in the Day 8 lambda sensitivity check), the resource depletion factor was loosened from 0.001 to 0.005 (less starvation than before), and the initial condition switched to a clean power law (0.001 * w^-1.8) instead of the old perturb-then-settle trick:


Code
p <- list(
  dt     = 0.001,
  dx     = 0.1,
  w_min  = 0.0003,
  w_max  = 66.5,
  w_mat  = 10,
  alpha  = 0.1,
  gamma  = 750,
  lambda = 2.05,
  a0     = 100
)

kappa <- p$a0 * exp(-6.9 * (p$lambda - 1))
no_w  <- round(log(p$w_max / p$w_min) / p$dx)

params <- newSingleSpeciesParams(
  species_name = "Anchovy",
  w_min  = p$w_min, w_max = p$w_max, w_mat = p$w_mat,
  no_w   = no_w,    lambda = p$lambda, kappa = kappa,
  alpha  = p$alpha, gamma  = p$gamma,  ks    = 0
)

r <- resource_rate(params)
r <- r * 0.005

params <- setResource(params, resource_rate = r, resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat")
params@initial_n[]    <- 0.001 * params@w^(-1.8)
params@initial_n_pp[] <- params@cc_pp

sim <- project(params, t_max = 10, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
               effort = 0, progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")

sim <- project(sim, t_max = 90, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
               effort = 0, progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")

sim_300 <- project(sim, t_max = 200, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                   effort = 0, progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")

sim_600 <- project(sim_300, t_max = 300, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                   effort = 0, progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")

plotHover(getBiomass(sim_600), tlim = c(550, 600))






Code
plotHover(getFlux(sim_600, power = 2), tlim = c(550, 600), log = "xy")






The FFT diagnostics from Day 8 were re-run on this version too, just to confirm the dominant period and feeding-level signature still look like the same family of dynamics before drawing conclusions from the fishing experiments:


Code
power_spectrum <- function(signal, dt) {
  signal <- signal - mean(signal)
  n      <- length(signal)
  freqs  <- (1:(n - 1)) / (n * dt)
  power  <- Mod(fft(signal))^2
  half   <- seq_len(floor((n - 1) / 2))
  data.frame(freq = freqs[half], period = 1 / freqs[half], power = power[half + 1])
}

dt    <- 0.2
bm    <- getBiomass(sim_600)[, "Anchovy"]
times <- as.numeric(names(bm))

ps_bm <- power_spectrum(bm[times > 300], dt)

plot_ly(ps_bm |> filter(period > 1, period < 50)) |>
  add_lines(x = ~period, y = ~power) |>
  layout(xaxis = list(title = "Period (years)"),
         yaxis = list(title = "Power", type = "log"),
         title = "Power spectrum — Anchovy biomass")

fl       <- getFeedingLevel(sim_600)
fl_times <- as.numeric(dimnames(fl)[[1]])
fl_small <- fl[, "Anchovy", 1]

ps_fl <- power_spectrum(fl_small[fl_times > 300], dt)

plot_ly(ps_fl |> filter(period > 1, period < 50)) |>
  add_lines(x = ~period, y = ~power) |>
  layout(xaxis = list(title = "Period (years)"),
         yaxis = list(title = "Power", type = "log"),
         title = "Power spectrum — feeding level (smallest size class)")

title: Day 9: Confirming the Jam, Then Easing It
text:
Confirmed: It’s Definitely a Bottleneck
getFlux(sim_600, power = 2) settles the question that’s been hanging since Day 8. This is unambiguously a bottleneck, not just a plausible interpretation of a standing wave. Watching flux directly on a log-log scale shows growth visibly stalling at juvenile sizes before the surviving fish push through into the adult range. There’s no more hedging needed here: it’s a traffic jam, and it’s visible in the flux itself, not just inferred from phase analysis.
But looking at the same diagnostics also raised a concern: the oscillation at large sizes is small, and the resulting yield numbers are correspondingly tiny. That’s the real tell that the current parameterisation is too extreme as the bottleneck is squeezing so hard that almost nothing of substance is reaching the sizes a fishery would care about, regardless of fishing strategy. A model where adult biomass barely oscillates isn’t just inconvenient for catching fish but it’s a sign the food-limitation effect is dialled up further than is biologically reasonable.
The plan: dial the resource depletion factor back further than today’s 0.005 (a smaller reduction in resource_rate, i.e. more food available) and see whether a less starved juvenile stage produces a more moderate jam, one that still oscillates and still bottlenecks, but lets enough biomass through to large sizes to make the fisheries question meaningful. The way I tested this was by running both versions side by side, today’s extreme parameterisation and the eased one and checking which actually produces a better outcome, not just assuming softer is better.

title: Day 9: Confirming the Jam, Then Easing It
section: Easing the Jam With Fishing Alone
text:
Easing the Jam With Fishing Alone
Even without touching the ecology, two changes to the fishing strategy on the bottleneck gear eased the congestion substantially within today’s (still extreme) model:


Code
bottleneck_sel <- function(w, w_low, w_high, ...) {
  as.numeric(w >= w_low & w <= w_high)
}

params_fished <- sim_300@params

gp <- params_fished@gear_params
gp$sel_func     <- "bottleneck_sel"
gp$w_low        <- 0.01
gp$w_high       <- p$w_mat
gp$catchability <- 1
gear_params(params_fished) <- gp   # proper setter: direct `@gear_params$x <-` assignment
                                    # skips setFishing() and leaves the cached
                                    # @selectivity array stale, silently ignoring the edit

sim_300_fished        <- sim_300
sim_300_fished@params <- params_fished

sim_fished <- project(sim_300_fished, t_max = 300, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                      effort = 0.3, progress_bar = FALSE,
                      method = "predictor-corrector")

all_times <- as.numeric(dimnames(sim_600@n)[[1]])
keep      <- all_times >= 300
t_p       <- all_times[keep]
time_lbls <- dimnames(sim_600@n)[[1]][keep]

bm   <- getBiomass(sim_600)[, "Anchovy"]
bm_p <- bm[time_lbls]

n_p <- length(bm_p)
is_peak <- logical(n_p)
is_peak[2:(n_p - 1)] <- bm_p[2:(n_p - 1)] > bm_p[1:(n_p - 2)] &
                        bm_p[2:(n_p - 1)] > bm_p[3:n_p]
peak_times <- t_p[is_peak]

window     <- 2.6     # widened from 1 year
fish_level <- 0.3

effort_vec <- rep(0, length(t_p))
for (pt in peak_times) {
  effort_vec[t_p >= pt - window / 2 & t_p <= pt + window / 2] <- fish_level
}

gear_name  <- params_fished@gear_params$gear[1]
effort_arr <- matrix(effort_vec, ncol = 1, dimnames = list(time_lbls, gear_name))

sim_peaks_only <- project(sim_300_fished, t_max = 300, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                          effort = effort_arr, progress_bar = FALSE,
                          method = "predictor-corrector")

plotYield(sim_peaks_only, sim_fished, tlim = c(550, 600))


Code
plotHover(getBiomass(sim_600), tlim = c(550, 600))
plotHover(getBiomass(sim_peaks_only), tlim = c(550, 600))
plotHover(getFlux(sim_600, power = 2), tlim = c(550, 600))
plotHover(getFlux(sim_peaks_only, power = 2), tlim = c(550, 600))


Two changes were made to the fishing strategy on the bottleneck gear:

Fishing constantly (effort applied at all times, not just near peaks), instead of not fishing at all.
Widening the fishing window around each peak (2.6 years either side, up from 1).

Eyeballing the plotHover panels for flux and biomass between sim_600 and sim_peaks_only, the dynamics clearly responded a lot to fishing pressure applied at this size and timing which is exactly what the “ramp metering” framing predicted back at the top of the day. Whether that response counts as “relief,” though, turned out to depend heavily on which size class you look at, and only became clear once plotRelative put an actual number on it rather than comparing two plots by eye.

title: Day 9: Confirming the Jam, Then Easing It
section: Quantifying the Relief: plotRelative on Flux
text:
Quantifying the Relief: plotRelative on Flux
Eyeballing two plotHover panels side by side is suggestive but not a number. mizer’s plotRelative() gives the relative difference directly, applied to flux rather than biomass since flux is the more direct signature of the bottleneck itself:


Code
plotRelative(getFlux(sim_600, power = 2), getFlux(sim_peaks_only, power = 2), tlim = c(550, 600))









The resulting curve is not the broad, mostly-positive shape I’d expected going in. Reading it left to right: at the very smallest sizes (near w_min) the relative difference starts out mildly positive, around +0.3, but immediately turns negative and dives to a sharp trough of roughly −1.0 around 0.05–0.1g which is right in the middle of the juvenile range the flux diagnostic identified as the bottleneck earlier today. It climbs back through zero around 1g, then turns positive through the sub-adult/adult range: a first peak of about +0.4 near w_mat (10g), a small dip to about +0.25 around 20g, and a second, sharper peak of about +0.55 around 30–40g. Then it crashes again, crossing zero around 50–60g and ending around −0.6 at the very top of the spectrum, near w_max.
So the honest read is close to the opposite of what I expected: peaks-only fishing on the bottleneck gear makes the juvenile congestion worse, not better, across almost the entire juvenile range ,from just above w_min out to roughly 1g , which is exactly where flux was shown to be stalling in the first place. The relief only shows up for sub-adults and adults (1g up to ~40g), and then reverses again at the largest sizes.
The small-number-artefact caution from earlier in the project still matters at the right-hand tail: abundance near w_max is small in both runs, so the −0.6 endpoint is probably exaggerated rather than fully real, and worth checking against the absolute flux values directly before trusting its exact size. The juvenile-range trough is a different story as that part of the spectrum is densely populated in both runs, so dividing two small numbers isn’t the issue there; that dip looks like a real effect, not a plotRelative artefact.
Net result, corrected: peaks-only fishing does not relieve the bottleneck where it matters most. It relieves congestion for sub-adults and fish approaching/just past maturity, but it measurably worsens the food-limited queue at juvenile sizes, the opposite of what eyeballing the plotHover panels suggested. That’s the real value of putting a number on it rather than comparing two plots by eye.

title: Day 9: Confirming the Jam, Then Easing It
section: Open Question: Why the Juvenile Phase, Specifically?
text:
Open Question: Why the Juvenile Phase, Specifically?
Confirming that the bottleneck sits at juvenile sizes isn’t the same as explaining why it has to be there. Day 8’s growth-scaling argument (juvenile growth rate ~ w^0.8 under this search-rate exponent, giving the w_mat^0.2 period law) explains how long juveniles take to grow through, but not why the food-limitation itself concentrates so heavily on that stage rather than being spread more evenly across the spectrum. Is it simply that juveniles sit at the steepest part of the encounter-rate-vs-requirement curve, or is there something more structural such as competition with adults for the same plankton pool, the shape of the plankton spectrum itself, the specific value of lambda?

title: Day 9: Confirming the Jam, Then Easing It
section: A Quiet Evening With the Textbook
text:
A Quiet Evening With the Textbook
Had a bit more breathing room in the evening, so instead of running more simulations I sat down with the nonlinear dynamics textbook for a while. It was a nice change of pace , going back to first principles on limit cycles, bifurcations, and phase portraits while everything I’d seen that day (the standing wave, the sensitivity to lambda near 2, the way fishing pressure reshaped the attractor) was still fresh made the abstract material land much more concretely than usual. It’s reassuring that the formal language for what’s happening in sim_600 already exists and is well worked out which gives me some confidence that the open questions above (especially the “why juveniles” one) are tractable with the right framing, not just empirical observations with no theory behind them.

title: Day 9: Confirming the Jam, Then Easing It
text:
What’s Next

Change the fishing selectivity to avoid fishing at juvenile age
Quantify how much of the easing came from effort vs. window, since both were changed together today. A small sweep over each independently would clarify which lever matters more.
The juvenile-bottleneck-gets-worse-under-fishing finding wasn’t just an artefact of the old severe parameterisation or the selectivity bug as it shows up directly in today’s plotRelative result, with both fixes in place. Worth understanding why peaks-only fishing on this gear worsens congestion for juveniles while relieving it for sub-adults/adults, rather than just confirming that it does.

title: Day 7: What’s Driving the Oscillation?
text:
Day 6 ended with a confirmed limit cycle and a rough period estimate of 7–9 years, close to three generation times. The natural next question: what’s actually driving it? Two candidate mechanisms were on the table:

Food-limitation cycle: The resource oscillates, fish growth rates follow, maturation is delayed and advanced on alternating half-cycles, and the period is set by that delay.
Cohort wave: A pulse of recruits moves through the size spectrum together, grazing the resource as it passes through small sizes, but individual growth rates barely change. The oscillation is in population structure, not food intake.

The way to distinguish them is to check whether growth rates actually change during the cycle.

title: Day 7: What’s Driving the Oscillation?
text:
Day 6 ended with a confirmed limit cycle and a rough period estimate of 7–9 years, close to three generation times. The natural next question: what’s actually driving it? Two candidate mechanisms were on the table:

Food-limitation cycle: The resource oscillates, fish growth rates follow, maturation is delayed and advanced on alternating half-cycles, and the period is set by that delay.
Cohort wave: A pulse of recruits moves through the size spectrum together, grazing the resource as it passes through small sizes, but individual growth rates barely change. The oscillation is in population structure, not food intake.

The way to distinguish them is to check whether growth rates actually change during the cycle.

title: Day 7: What’s Driving the Oscillation?
text:
Setup
Parameters, model construction, and the initial perturbation that starts the limit-cycle transient:

library(mizer)
library(patchwork)
library(reshape2)
library(plotly)
library(dplyr)
library(mizerExperimental)
library(tidyverse) 
library(glue)
library(ggplot2)

p <- list(
  dt     = 0.001,
  dx     = 0.1,
  w_min  = 0.0003,
  w_max  = 66.5,
  w_mat  = 10,
  alpha  = 0.1,
  gamma  = 750,
  lambda = 2,
  a0     = 100
)

kappa <- p$a0 * exp(-6.9 * (p$lambda - 1))
no_w  <- round(log(p$w_max / p$w_min) / p$dx)

params <- newSingleSpeciesParams(
  species_name = "Anchovy",
  w_min  = p$w_min,  w_max  = p$w_max,  w_mat  = p$w_mat,
  no_w   = no_w,     lambda = p$lambda,  kappa  = kappa,
  alpha  = p$alpha,  gamma  = p$gamma,   ks     = 0
)

r <- resource_rate(params) * 0.001
params <- setResource(params, resource_rate = r,
                      resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat")
params@initial_n_pp[] <- params@cc_pp * 0.1

# Spin up, then crash the large size class (10–100 g) by 10^3
sim <- project(params, t_max = 10, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
               progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")

rng  <- c(10, 100)
idx  <- params@w >= rng[1] & params@w <= rng[2]
last <- dim(sim@n)[1]
sim@n[last, , idx] <- sim@n[last, , idx] / 10^3

sim <- project(sim, t_max = 90, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
               progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")

sim_300 <- project(sim, t_max = 200, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                   progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")#can use tr_bdf2,but needs much finer dt

sim_600 <-  project(sim_300, t_max = 300, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                    progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")#can use tr_bdf2,but needs much finer dt

title: Day 7: What’s Driving the Oscillation?
text:
Animating EGrowth
The first attempt was to animate getEGrowth() across the oscillation — if growth rates are cycling, the curve should visibly rise and fall with the plankton. The mizer animate() function handles this directly once you have a long-enough simulation object:

t_trough <- 507.2
t_peak   <- 570.2
animate(getEGrowth(sim_600, time_range = c(t_trough - 1, t_peak + 1)), log = "xy")





The animation ran but the curve barely moved. Comparing two specific time points confirmed it. The EGrowth curves at t = 557 and t = 559 were essentially identical on a log-log scale, with only a hairline split visible at the very smallest sizes.

title: Day 7: What’s Driving the Oscillation?
text:
A Cleaner Comparison
The time points chosen (557 and 559, two years apart) were too close together to be meaningful for a 7–9 year cycle. Peak and trough of the plankton are roughly 3.5–4.5 years apart, so both points were likely at similar phases of the oscillation.
The right comparison is between the actual biomass peak and trough. plotHover() on the settled portion of the biomass time series makes it easy to read off the exact times interactively:

plotHover(getBiomass(sim_600), tlim = c(500, 580))




t_trough <- 507.2
t_peak   <- 570.2

Then overlaying EGrowth, the size spectrum, and individual spectra at those two times:

plot2(getEGrowth(sim_600, t = t_peak),
      getEGrowth(sim_600, t = t_trough),
      log = "xy")








The plot2 result is instructive. Across the bulk of the size range, from roughly 0.01 g up to the matur ation size at 10 g and beyond, the two curves sit exactly on top of each other. There is no detectable difference in EGrowth for medium or large fish between peak and trough. The only split appears at the very s mallest sizes, below about 0.01 g, where the trough curve (dashed, Second) drops below the peak curve (sol id, First). Even there the gap is modest in absolute terms, though clearly visible on the log-log scale.
This is meaningful in two ways. First, it confirms that the oscillation in growth rate is entirely a juven ile phenomenon — fish above roughly 0.01 g are not food-limited at any phase of the cycle. Second, it expl ains why the initial animation showed almost nothing: the signal is real but confined to a very narrow, ve ry low-biomass part of the size spectrum where the log-log axis compresses it. EGrowth is not the wrong di agnostic, it is just insufficiently sensitive at these size scales — the feeding level comparison, which i s dimensionless and directly measures the fraction of maximum intake achieved, is better suited to detecti ng this kind of subtle, size-localised food limitation.

title: Day 7: What’s Driving the Oscillation?
text:
Feeding Level: The Right Diagnostic
getEGrowth tells you energy available for growth, but it folds in the maturity and metabolic costs. A cleaner measure of whether fish are food-limited is the feeding level \(f(w)\) , the fraction of maximum intake rate actually achieved, running from 0 (no food) to 1 (fully saturated).

getFeedingLevel(getParams(sim_600, t_peak))

Feeding level (1 species x 123 sizes) 
  Anchovy: min=0.896 mean=0.949 max=0.995

# Feeding level (1 species x 123 sizes)
#   Anchovy: min=0.896 mean=0.949 max=0.995

getFeedingLevel(getParams(sim_600, t_trough))

Feeding level (1 species x 123 sizes) 
  Anchovy: min=0.244 mean=0.776 max=0.923

# Feeding level (1 species x 123 sizes)
#   Anchovy: min=0.244 mean=0.776 max=0.923

This is a large difference. At the plankton peak, fish are feeding at 90–100% of their maximum rate across all size classes meaning they are effectively saturated, and there is no food limitation. At the plankton trough, the smallest fish drop to a feeding level of 0.244 so eating at roughly a quarter of their maximum rate. That’s a substantial slowdown in growth for juveniles.
The earlier EGrowth animation showed no difference because the effect is concentrated in the smallest size classes, where the log-log scale compresses things visually. The feeding level comparison makes it explicit.

title: Day 7: What’s Driving the Oscillation?
text:
Animating the Feeding Level
With the static peak/trough comparison confirming food limitation, the next step was to animate getFeedingLevel() which allows us to watch the feeding level evolve at each size class over time rather than just seeing summary statistics:

animate(getFeedingLevel(sim_600, time_range = c(550, 600)))





The result was striking, and raises more questions than it answers.
The oscillation in feeding level is clearly periodic, which confirms the food-limitation cycle. But the pattern across size classes is uneven in a way that wasn’t expected:

Only the smaller size classes oscillate meaningfully. Larger fish maintain a near-constant, high feeding level throughout the cycle. Their food supply, larger prey, barely fluctuates.
The temporal shape is asymmetric. The smallest juveniles spend the majority of the cycle at a high feeding level, with only a brief, sharp crash before recovering. It is not a smooth sine-wave oscillation but instead looks more like the feeding level sustains near-saturation for an extended period, then collapses rapidly, then climbs back up again. The crash is fast; the recovery and plateau are slow.

This asymmetry is unexpected. In a simple predator-prey model you would expect roughly equal time above and below the mean. The fact that small fish are food-saturated for far longer than they are food-limited suggests the resource recovery is relatively fast compared to the grazing pressure that drives the depletion. Once a grazing cohort passes through the juvenile size range, the plankton bounces back quickly but the crash, while brief, is sharp enough to leave a lasting imprint on cohort growth.
This pattern needs more investigation. It may be that the plankton has a fast intrinsic recovery rate relative to the consumption rate, meaning depletions are short-lived but intense. Alternatively, the size-specificity of the crash could reflect something about how the cohort moves through the size spectrum.

title: Day 7: What’s Driving the Oscillation?
section: What This Means for the Mechanism
text:
What This Means for the Mechanism
The oscillation is food-limitation driven, concentrated in the juvenile size range:

A cohort of juveniles grazes the plankton hard as it passes through small sizes, driving plankton to its trough.
The next wave of recruits enters a depleted food environment, feeding level drops to ~0.24 at the smallest sizes and grows more slowly.
Slower growth means the cohort takes longer to reach maturity, delaying the next grazing pulse.
With fewer juveniles competing for it, the plankton recovers.
The following cohort grows fast on the recovered resource, matures quickly, grazes hard.
The cycle repeats.

The three-generation period from Day 6 is consistent with this: it takes roughly one generation for the depleted-food cohort to reach maturity, one for the recovery to propagate back into reproduction, and one more for that effect to produce a new grazing pulse.

title: Day 7: What’s Driving the Oscillation?
text:
Extending the Perturbation
With the mechanism clearer, the perturbation code was extended to also crash the plankton in the prey size range of the large fish, the part of the resource spectrum they feed on most heavily:

beta <- params@species_params$beta

prey_rng <- c(10, 100) / beta
pp_idx   <- params@w_full >= prey_rng[1] & params@w_full <= prey_rng[2]

sim@n_pp[last, pp_idx] <- sim@n_pp[last, pp_idx] / 10^3

The result is that the overall perturbation shape is essentially the same. The one visible difference is in the growth rate comparison plot: with the plankton also crashed, the second curve sits slightly above the first, whereas without the plankton crash it is the other way round. This makes sense: crashing the plankton directly depresses the feeding level of the remaining small fish immediately after the perturbation, so the first time point reflects a more food-limited state than the second, flipping the relative ordering of the curves. The system still converges to the same limit cycle; only the phase of the transient shifts slightly.
One surprising finding here: changing the magnitude of the initial large fish crash, whether you reduce abundance by 10,10^3,10^7 or another factor makes essentially no difference to the subsequent growth rate or the trajectory back toward the limit cycle. The system converges at the same rate regardless. This is strange. Naively, crashing large fish harder should produce a larger transient, and a larger transient might take a different path through the phase space. The fact that it doesn’t suggests the system is being pulled very strongly toward the same attractor along the same trajectory, and the initial condition is largely irrelevant once you are far enough from the limit cycle. It may also reflect that the large fish abundance is not the limiting factor in the dynamics. The plankton and the juvenile feeding level are doing most of the work, and varying the large fish crash magnitude just changes how quickly the large fish return to a non-rate-limiting level, not the dynamics that actually drive the cycle.

title: Day 7: What’s Driving the Oscillation?
text:
Extended Projection: Testing the Attractor
To properly test whether the fixed point (or more accurately, the limit cycle) is a genuine attractor, meaning perturbations decay back to it rather than growing or drifting, the projection time was substantially extended. Running the simulation for much longer after the perturbation gives the system enough time to either converge back to the cycle, settle to a new state, or diverge:

sim_300 <- project(sim, t_max = 200, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                   progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")

sim_600 <- project(sim_300, t_max = 300, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                   progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")

It converged. The trajectory returns cleanly to the same limit cycle after the perturbation, confirming that the oscillation is a stable attractor, not a transient or a neutrally stable orbit. The longer run also makes it easier to measure the period accurately and to check whether there is any amplitude modulation or beating that might indicate more than one frequency is present in the signal which, given the asymmetric shape of the feeding level animation, is a real possibility.

title: Day 7: What’s Driving the Oscillation?
text:
What’s Next

FFT on the projection: The feeding level animation and the biomass time series both show a signal that is more complicated than a simple sine wave. The asymmetric shape, long plateau, sharp crash, fast recovery, suggests the oscillation may be composed of multiple frequencies rather than a single dominant mode. A fast Fourier transform on the settled biomass (or feeding level) time series will decompose the signal and reveal whether there is one period, or several harmonics, or two incommensurate frequencies beating against each other. The answer matters: a single clean frequency implies one mechanism, while multiple frequencies would suggest the fish dynamics and the resource dynamics are on slightly different timescales that interfere.

Today was slower than expected in terms of code produced, but there were many interesting results. The feeding level animation added a layer of complexity to that picture that the FFT will hopefully help untangle.

title: Day 5: Visualising the Flux
text:
Yesterday’s phase diagram gave a map of where the system oscillates. Today’s question was more concrete: when it does oscillate, where is the biomass actually moving? The answer required shifting from plotting biomass directly to plotting flux, the rate at which biomass flows through each size class.
Mizer provides getFlux() for exactly this, and most of the morning was spent getting to grips with what it returns and how best to display it.

title: Day 5: Visualising the Flux
text:
Setting Up
The same single-species setup as previous days: \(\lambda = 2.05\), \(\beta = 30\), \(\sigma = 0.5\), with a resource rate scaled down by a factor of 1000 and a fivefold perturbation applied to the large size class (10–100 g) in the initial condition.

library(mizer)

varying_beta_sigma_test <- function(beta_new = 100, sigma_new = 1.3) {
  test_sizes <- list(
    "small"  = c(0.1, 1),
    "medium" = c(1, 10),
    "large"  = c(10, 100)
  )
  p <- newSingleSpeciesParams(lambda = 2.05, beta = beta_new, sigma = sigma_new)

  r <- resource_rate(p)
  r <- r * 0.001
  p <- setResource(p, resource_rate = r, resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat")
  rng <- test_sizes[["large"]]
  idx <- p@w >= rng[1] & p@w <= rng[2]
  initialN(p)[, idx] <- initialN(p)[, idx] * 5

  project(p, t_max = 100, t_save = 0.5)
}

sim <- varying_beta_sigma_test(30, 0.5)

title: Day 5: Visualising the Flux
text:
Exploring the Plots
The first plot was the energy growth rate across size classes over time:

plotHover(getEGrowth(sim))





This gives a sense of which sizes are gaining energy and how that changes over the simulation. But what was really of interest was the flux itself.

flux <- getFlux(sim)
plotHover(flux)





Raw flux is dominated by the smallest size classes, where numbers are enormous. To get a clearer picture of where the biomass is flowing rather than just the individuals, the flux can be weighted by body mass:

biomass_flux <- flux
biomass_flux[] <- sweep(flux, 3, w(getParams(sim)), "*")
plotHover(biomass_flux)





Finally, plotting both flux and biomass flux together on log-log axes lets you see the relationship between the two across the full size range:

plot2(biomass_flux, flux, log = "xy")

title: Day 5: Visualising the Flux
text:
What the Flux Plot Shows
The picture that emerged was stark. Flux is very high at the smallest sizes, around \(10^{-3}\) g, and drops sharply across several orders of magnitude, reaching essentially zero by 0.1 g. Very little biomass is successfully transiting into the larger size classes.
This is almost certainly a consequence of the extremely low resource rate. With so little food available, the growth rates at intermediate and large sizes are negligible, and the perturbation applied to the large size class has almost no pathway through which it can be replenished. The oscillations seen in previous days are playing out almost entirely in the small-to-medium size range.
It raises a question for later: what does the flux look like under a more realistic resource rate? Is the sharp cutoff a property of the model or an artefact of the deliberately depleted resource?

title: Day 5: Visualising the Flux
text:
Afternoon: Strogatz Chapter 5
The afternoon shifted to theory. Chapter 5 of Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos by Strogatz moves from one-dimensional flows to nonlinear flows in two dimensions, and the step up in richness is immediate.
In one dimension, a trajectory has nowhere to go but left or right. In two dimensions, the phase plane opens up and fixed points acquire character: stable and unstable nodes, saddle points, spirals, centres. Trajectories can approach a fixed point along a preferred direction, orbit around it indefinitely, or be repelled.
The analytical core of the chapter is linearisation. Near a fixed point, a nonlinear system can be approximated by a linear one, and the Jacobian evaluated at that point tells you everything about local behaviour. The eigenvalues of the Jacobian determine whether trajectories spiral in or out, approach along a curve, or diverge and a clean diagram classifying fixed points by the trace and determinant of the Jacobian puts the whole picture in one place.
What resonates most clearly with the simulation work is the limit of linearisation. It is precise and useful near a fixed point, but says nothing about the global structure of the phase plane: whether distant trajectories eventually converge, whether limit cycles exist, or whether the system can be pushed from one basin of attraction into another. That gap between local and global is exactly what made the flux plots this morning interesting. The model’s local behaviour near steady state is one thing, but following where the biomass actually goes is another.
The next chapter will presumably start closing that gap. For now, the foundations are solid.

title: Day 5: Visualising the Flux
text:
What’s Next
Two threads to follow up. On the simulation side: rerun the flux analysis under a less extreme resource rate and check whether the cutoff at 0.1 g shifts or disappears. On the theory side: continue with Strogatz and work through the tools for global analysis which are likely to be directly relevant to understanding why the oscillatory regime exists where it does in parameter space.

title: Day 3: Contents Pages, Oscillations & the Power Law Realisation
text:
Afternoon: Hunting for Oscillations
With the blog in better shape, I got back to the main task: trying to produce interesting dynamics in the single species mizer model.
The question from Day 2 had been nagging at me. The previous attempts at perturbing the size spectrum, bumping up abundance in different size ranges, kept converging back to steady state without producing anything that looked like a genuine oscillation or instability. The spectrum would wobble briefly and then flatten out again. Convincing yourself you’ve found something when you’ve just produced a slightly delayed equilibrium is a trap worth avoiding.
Today it finally clicked and the fix was conceptually simple once I saw it.

The Key Insight: Resource Rate Is a Power Law
When I’d been “reducing the resource rate” in earlier experiments, I’d been setting it to a constant. That’s not a small reduction but changing the shape of the function, not just its magnitude. You end up with a resource that replenishes at the same rate regardless of size, which is biologically wrong and dynamically different.
The correct way to reduce the resource rate while keeping the physics intact is to scale the existing power law by multiplying the whole curve by a small scalar. This preserves the size-dependence while genuinely suppressing replenishment across the board:
p <- newSingleSpeciesParams(lambda = 2.05)

r <- resource_rate(p)       # extract the power law
r <- r * 0.0001             # scale it down uniformly
p <- setResource(p,
  resource_rate = r,
  resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat"
)
That single change, extracting the rate, scaling it, and putting it back, made all the difference.


Adding the Initial Perturbation
With the resource replenishment suppressed, I then bumped the initial fish abundance in the large size range (10–100 g) by a factor of 5:
rng <- c(10, 100)
idx <- p@w >= rng[1] & p@w <= rng[2]
initialN(p)[, idx] <- initialN(p)[, idx] * 5
This seeds a localised excess of fish at large body sizes which is exactly the kind of perturbation that should reveal whether the system has an oscillatory or damped response.


The Full Experiment

library(mizer)
library(patchwork)
library(reshape2)
library(plotly)
library(dplyr)
library(mizerExperimental)
library(tidyverse)
library(glue)
# Build params
p <- newSingleSpeciesParams(lambda = 2.05)
# Deviation from power law
deviation_plot <- function(sim, title) {
  spec <- finalNResource(sim)
  expected <- p@w_full^(-2.05)
  deviation <- spec / expected
  plot(p@w_full, deviation, type = "l", log = "x",
       main = title, xlab = "Size (g)", ylab = "Deviation from power law")
  abline(h = 1, lty = 2)
}

# Scale down resource rate as a power law (not a constant)
r <- resource_rate(p)
r <- r * 0.0001
p <- setResource(p,
                 resource_rate = r,
                 resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat"
)

# Perturb the large size range
rng <- c(10, 100)
idx <- p@w >= rng[1] & p@w <= rng[2]
initialN(p)[, idx] <- initialN(p)[, idx] * 5

# Run simulation
sim <- project(p, t_max = 20, t_save = 0.5)







Note



Deviation Plot:
The reason why the deviation plot looks so small is due to the fact that this is being run when the population as almost gone back to the steady state.

# Deviation from power law
deviation_plot(sim, "Deviation — bump at large range")











animateSpectra(sim, resource = FALSE, log_x = FALSE, log_y = FALSE, power = 2)







The Result
Something genuinely interesting showed up. In the early part of the simulation, the spectrum doesn’t just relax but oscillates, with the abundance overshooting and undershooting before eventually settling. The fine time resolution (t_save = 0.5) was important here; a coarser save interval would have smoothed straight over it.
That said, the oscillation is transient. By the end of the run the system does converge back to steady state so this isn’t a self-sustaining instability, at least not under these parameters. What it is is a clear sign that the dynamics are richer than a pure monotonic decay: the system has enough inertia to ring before it settles.
That’s worth understanding better before drawing conclusions.

title: Day 3: Contents Pages, Oscillations & the Power Law Realisation
text:
What This Means
The Day 2 experiments weren’t wrong, they were just missing a critical detail. A resource rate reduced to a constant rather than scaled as a power law is a different model, not a lower-resource version of the same model. That distinction matters because mizer’s steady-state dynamics are calibrated around the power law structure: changing the shape breaks assumptions that the rest of the model depends on.
The lesson generalises: when you want to weaken a power law, multiply it but don’t replace it.
As for the transient oscillation, the next step is to understand what’s governing its decay. Is the system genuinely stable under these parameters, just with a slow ring-down? Or are there parameters we can change where the oscillation stops decaying and becomes self-sustaining? That’s the boundary worth finding.

title: Day 3: Contents Pages, Oscillations & the Power Law Realisation
text:
What’s Next
Read the mizer documentation: There’s more going on in these simulations than a single animated spectrum reveals. Mizer has a range of built-in diagnostics covering growth rates, feeding levels, mortality, and spectra over time. Getting familiar with what’s available and what each plot actually shows is the right foundation before pushing further into parameter space.
Vary \(\beta\) and \(\sigma\) : Once the diagnostic toolkit is better understood, explore how the predator-to-prey size ratio and diet breadth affect the transient dynamics, using whichever plots make those effects most legible.Today felt like a genuine step forward.
The power law insight unlocked dynamics that weren’t visible before, and the questions are now much sharper than they were this morning.Today felt like a step forward. The mechanism is clearer, the dynamics are more interesting than before, and the right questions are now in focus.

title: Day One: Setting the Stage
text:
The meeting this morning was a lot to take in. The idea that fishing could actually improve ecosystem productivity rather than harm it feels almost counterintuitive at first. But once the traffic analogy clicked, it made complete sense. Fish biomass flowing through size space behaves mathematically like cars on a motorway. When conditions are right, you get a phantom traffic jam, a pile-up at one size class that starves the fish above and below it. And just as motorway agencies can use speed limits to prevent jams, targeted fishing could in theory relieve them.
That’s the project. It’s a genuinely novel idea and it’s exciting to be working on it from day one.
