Second, the existence and uniqueness theorem which is the result that guarantees a unique solution through every initial condition, given the function f is continuously differentiable . This matters for simulations more than it might seem: if you’re running a numerical integrator and getting different trajectories depending on step size, it’s worth knowing whether that’s a numerical error or a sign that the theorem’s conditions actually break down somewhere in parameter space.

title: Day 6: Real Oscillations (Eventually)
text:
The Uncomfortable Check
My supervisor pointed out something I’d missed: the oscillations from Day 5 could be integration artefacts. The obvious test is to switch to a more accurate integration method and see if the feature survives.
Mizer supports a predictor-corrector integration method alongside the default. The predictor-corrector is second-order and has better error properties than the default scheme, if oscillations are real dynamics rather than integration artefacts, they should persist regardless of which method you use. Swapping in method = "predictor-corrector" is a one-line change:
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| output: false

sim <- project(params, t_max = 100, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
               progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
The oscillations disappeared, the biomass converged smoothly to equilibrium instead. That’s a clear sign: what I’d been looking at was a discretisation error, not a genuine feature of the model’s dynamics. The default integrator was producing numerical ringing that mimicked real oscillations.
Not a great feeling, but better to find out now. The dynamics aren’t as interesting as I thought, or at least, not under these parameter settings.

title: Day 6: Real Oscillations (Eventually)
text:
A Pointer from the Literature
With the original oscillations ruled out, the question became: is there a parameter regime where mizer does produce genuine cycles? I was almost certain the answer should be yes, the biological mechanisms for a Hopf bifurcation are clearly present in a size-structured consumer-resource model but I didn’t know where in parameter space to look.
At this point I was reminded of a piece of code I’d come across earlier in the project: a worked example on RPubs showing plankton-anchovy oscillations in mizer.
https://rpubs.com/gustav/plankton-anchovy
Reading through it, the setup was different from what I’d been doing, a two-species model (anchovy feeding on plankton) with specific parameter choices that had been tuned to produce interesting dynamics. The code was written for an older version of mizer, so several of the functions had changed names or signatures.
I worked through it and translated the setup to current mizer, newSingleSpeciesParams() in place of the old direct constructor, setResource() for the resource dynamics, and resource_semichemostat as the dynamics type. The key parameters from the original that produced oscillations were a low resource replenishment rate combined with a large predator-prey size ratio exactly the instability regime from Datta, Delius & Law (2011).

library(mizer)
library(reshape2)
library(plotly)
library(dplyr)
p <- list(
  dt     = 0.001,
  dx     = 0.1,
  w_min  = 0.0003,
  w_max  = 66.5,
  w_mat  = 10,
  alpha  = 0.1,      # assimilation efficiency
  gamma  = 750,
  lambda = 2,
  a0     = 100
)

kappa <- p$a0 * exp(-6.9 * (p$lambda - 1))
no_w  <- round(log(p$w_max / p$w_min) / p$dx)

params <- newSingleSpeciesParams(
  species_name = "Anchovy",
  w_min  = p$w_min,
  w_max  = p$w_max,
  w_mat  = p$w_mat,
  no_w   = no_w,
  lambda = p$lambda,
  kappa  = kappa,
  alpha  = p$alpha,
  gamma  = p$gamma,
  ks     = 0
)

r <- resource_rate(params)
r <- r * 0.001
params <- setResource(params, resource_rate = r,
                      resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat")

The r * 0.001 scaling is the critical detail, suppressing plankton replenishment to roughly a thousandth of its default value is what puts the system in the oscillatory regime.

title: Day 6: Real Oscillations (Eventually)
text:
The Oscillations That Survive
Running the adapted model with the predictor-corrector method, and introducing a perturbation mid-run by crashing the large size class to a thousandth of its current abundance:

test_sizes <- list(
  "small"  = c(0.1, 1),
  "medium" = c(1, 10),
  "large"  = c(10, 100)
)

params@initial_n_pp[] <- params@cc_pp * 0.1
T1 <- 10

sim <- project(params, t_max = T1, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
               progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")

rng <- test_sizes[["large"]]
idx <- params@w >= rng[1] & params@w <= rng[2]
last <- dim(sim@n)[1]
sim@n[last, , idx] <- sim@n[last, , idx] / 10^3

sim <- project(sim, t_max = 90, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
               progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
# can also use tr_bdf2, but needs much finer dt

The animated size spectrum gives the first read on whether anything interesting is happening:

nf        <- melt(sim@n)
names(nf) <- c("time", "sp", "w", "value")

n_ppf        <- melt(sim@n_pp)
names(n_ppf) <- c("time", "w", "value")
n_ppf$sp     <- "Plankton"

nf <- rbind(nf, n_ppf)

nf_plot <- nf %>%
  filter(w > 10^-5, time >= 50) %>%
  mutate(b = value * w^2)

plot_ly(nf_plot) %>%
  add_lines(
    x = ~w, y = ~b,
    color = ~sp,
    frame = ~time,
    line = list(simplify = FALSE)
  ) %>%
  layout(
    xaxis = list(type = "log", exponentformat = "power",
                 title_text = "body mass (g)"),
    yaxis = list(type = "log", exponentformat = "power",
                 title_text = "biomass (g/m^3)",
                 range = c(-8, 0))
  )

Warning in registerFrames(p, frameMapping = frameMapping): NaNs produced






The oscillations were still there. Switching to a more accurate method didn’t make them disappear, the exact opposite of what happened with the old parameter set. If the oscillations survive a change in integration method, they’re real. These are genuine limit cycle dynamics, not the numerical noise previously.

title: Day 6: Real Oscillations (Eventually)
text:
What Period?
With a credible oscillation in hand, the next question was what sets its period. The first tool was a biomass time series broken down by component, total Anchovy, “small Anchovy” (0.01–0.4 g), and Plankton, which makes the phase relationships visible:

abm  <- melt(getBiomass(sim))
abmr <- melt(getBiomass(sim, min_w = 0.01, max_w = 0.4))
abmr$sp <- "small Anchovy"

pbm <- sim@n_pp %*% (params@w_full * params@dw_full)
pbm <- melt(pbm)
names(pbm)[names(pbm) == "Var1"] <- "time"
pbm$Var2 <- NULL
pbm$sp <- "Plankton"

bm <- rbind(pbm, abm, abmr)

bm_plot <- bm %>% filter(time >= 10)

plot_ly(bm_plot) %>%
  add_lines(x = ~time, y = ~value, color = ~sp) %>%
  layout(
    yaxis = list(type = "log", exponentformat = "power",
                 title_text = "biomass (g/m^3)",
                 range = c(-7, 2)),
    xaxis = list(title_text = "time (year)")
  )





The three-component plot is more informative than total Anchovy alone, “small Anchovy” tracks the recruitment pulse, which leads the adult biomass signal by part of a generation. Eyeballing the period from this plot, the oscillations looked to be somewhere in the range of 7–9 years.
Settling on that range, the natural question is: what in the biology sets this timescale?

Three Generations
The obvious candidate is generation time, the time for a recruit to grow from minimum size to maturity. If the consumer-resource feedback loop runs on a delay set by how long fish take to grow up and start reproducing, the oscillation period should be some multiple of that delay.

gc <- getGrowthCurves(sim, species = "Anchovy", max_age = 20)
age <- as.numeric(colnames(gc))
w_of_age <- gc["Anchovy", ]

age_at_mat <- approx(x = w_of_age, y = age, xout = p$w_mat, rule = 2)$y
age_at_mat

[1] 2.636306

# [1] ~2.636306

A single generation is around 2.64 years. Three generations is roughly 7.9 years, right in the middle of the observed 7–9 year range.
This makes biological sense as a mechanism, though the three-generation lag rather than two is worth sitting with. A pulse of recruits grows up and reaches maturity; that’s one generation. They exert grazing pressure on the resource, which dips in response, slowing growth for the next cohort that’s a second generation passing. By the time that cohort reaches maturity and starts reproducing in earnest, the resource has recovered and a new pulse of fast-growing juveniles is produced and it’s the maturation of this third generation that closes the loop and restarts the cycle. Three transits, not two.
It’s not a precise derivation, but it’s the right order of magnitude and points at the right mechanism.

title: Day 6: Real Oscillations (Eventually)
text:
What’s Next

Verify the period more carefully: The peak-finding approach is sensitive to how much of the transient you include. Worth repeating with just the settled part of the time series (say, t > 100) and comparing to the ACF result.
Link the period to parameters explicitly: If the period is set by maturation time, varying w_mat or growth rate parameters should shift the period predictably. This is a testable prediction and would make the mechanism much more concrete.
Animate getEGrowth(): Plotting the energy available for somatic growth at each size class as a frame-by-frame animation over the oscillation cycle should make the feedback mechanism visible directly: resource depletion should s how up as a suppression of growth rates in the small size classes, propagating upward through the spectrum as the affected cohort matures. If the mechanism is what we think it is, the pattern in EGrowth should lag the Plankton dip by roughly one generation.

Today involved more backtracking than I’d have liked, but ruling out the discretisation artefacts was necessary work. The oscillations in the RPubs example are the real thing, and they’re now a concrete starting point rather than a vague hope.

title: Day 8: FFT, Scaling Laws, and Hunting the Traffic Jam
text:
Day 7 confirmed the oscillation mechanism: a food-limitation cycle concentrated in juvenile size classes, with feeding level at the smallest fish dropping to 0.244 at the plankton trough. The feeding level animation revealed an asymmetric waveform - long plateau, sharp crash, fast recovery - and raised the question of whether the signal was composed of multiple frequencies or a single nonlinear oscillation.
Three analyses were queued: FFT on the projection, a w_mat sweep to test whether the period scales with generation time, and cohort tracking to distinguish a standing wave from a travelling cohort wave. Today covered all three, and then opened a new thread on the traffic jam.

title: Day 8: FFT, Scaling Laws, and Hunting the Traffic Jam
text:
FFT: Decomposing the Signal
The power spectrum was computed for both the Anchovy biomass time series and the feeding level at the smallest size class, using the settled portion of sim_600 (t > 300):


Code
library(mizer)
library(patchwork)
library(reshape2)
library(plotly)
library(dplyr)
library(mizerExperimental)
library(tidyverse) 
library(glue)
library(ggplot2)
p <- list(
  dt     = 0.001,
  dx     = 0.1,
  w_min  = 0.0003,
  w_max  = 66.5,
  w_mat  = 10,
  alpha  = 0.1,
  gamma  = 750,
  lambda = 2,
  a0     = 100
)

kappa <- p$a0 * exp(-6.9 * (p$lambda - 1))
no_w  <- round(log(p$w_max / p$w_min) / p$dx)

params <- newSingleSpeciesParams(
  species_name = "Anchovy",
  w_min  = p$w_min,  w_max  = p$w_max,  w_mat  = p$w_mat,
  no_w   = no_w,     lambda = p$lambda,  kappa  = kappa,
  alpha  = p$alpha,  gamma  = p$gamma,   ks     = 0
)

r <- resource_rate(params) * 0.001
params <- setResource(params, resource_rate = r,
                      resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat")
params@initial_n_pp[] <- params@cc_pp * 0.1

# Spin up, then crash the large size class (10–100 g) by 10^3
sim <- project(params, t_max = 10, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
               progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")

rng  <- c(10, 100)
idx  <- params@w >= rng[1] & params@w <= rng[2]
last <- dim(sim@n)[1]
sim@n[last, , idx] <- sim@n[last, , idx] / 10^3

sim <- project(sim, t_max = 90, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
               progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")

sim_300 <- project(sim, t_max = 200, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                   progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")#can use tr_bdf2,but needs much finer dt

sim_600 <-  project(sim_300, t_max = 300, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                    progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")#can use tr_bdf2,but needs much finer dt




Code
power_spectrum <- function(signal, dt) {
  signal <- signal - mean(signal)
  n      <- length(signal)
  freqs  <- (1:(n - 1)) / (n * dt)
  power  <- Mod(fft(signal))^2
  half   <- seq_len(floor((n - 1) / 2))
  data.frame(freq = freqs[half], period = 1 / freqs[half], power = power[half + 1])
}

dt    <- 0.2
bm    <- getBiomass(sim_600)[, "Anchovy"]
times <- as.numeric(names(bm))

ps_bm <- power_spectrum(bm[times > 300], dt)

plot_ly(ps_bm |> filter(period > 1, period < 50)) |>
  add_lines(x = ~period, y = ~power) |>
  layout(xaxis = list(title = "Period (years)"),
         yaxis = list(title = "Power", type = "log"),
         title = "Power spectrum — Anchovy biomass")






Code
fl       <- getFeedingLevel(sim_600)
fl_times <- as.numeric(dimnames(fl)[[1]])
fl_small <- fl[, "Anchovy", 1]

ps_fl <- power_spectrum(fl_small[fl_times > 300], dt)

plot_ly(ps_fl |> filter(period > 1, period < 50)) |>
  add_lines(x = ~period, y = ~power) |>
  layout(xaxis = list(title = "Period (years)"),
         yaxis = list(title = "Power", type = "log"),
         title = "Power spectrum — feeding level (smallest size class)")






Code
period_dom <- ps_bm$period[which.max(ps_bm$power)]


Both spectra show the same structure: one sharp dominant peak at ~8–9 years, a cluster of smaller peaks at shorter periods (~2–5 years), and a broad red-noise background at long periods.
The secondary peaks are harmonics - they sit at approximately 1/2, 1/3 of the dominant period. This is the frequency-domain signature of a periodic but non-sinusoidal waveform: energy leaks into integer multiples of the fundamental. The sharp crash / long plateau shape seen in the feeding level animation is exactly what produces this harmonic series ; fast depletion generates high-frequency components, while the sustained recovery plateau suppresses them.
The feeding level spectrum has much stronger relative harmonic content than the biomass spectrum, which makes sense: the feeding level at the smallest size class is where the nonlinearity is sharpest (a near-instantaneous switch from saturation to ~0.24), so its waveform is more distorted. The biomass integrates over all sizes and smooths the signal.
The key result: one fundamental frequency, not two. If the oscillation were quasiperiodic (two incommensurate timescales interfering), the spectrum would show two sharp peaks at non-harmonically-related periods. That is not present. The complexity seen in the feeding level animation is the waveform shape of a single nonlinear feedback loop, not multiple mechanisms competing.
The y-axis (power) is the squared amplitude of the sinusoidal component at each period as it measures how much each frequency contributes to the total variance in the signal. The absolute power values are not comparable between the two plots (feeding level is dimensionless, biomass is g/m³), but the shapes are.

title: Day 8: FFT, Scaling Laws, and Hunting the Traffic Jam
section: Period vs w_mat: The Scaling Law
text:
Period vs w_mat: The Scaling Law
If the ~8–9 year period is set by maturation time, it should scale predictably with w_mat. Twelve simulations were run across a range of maturation sizes (roughly 3–50 g), each perturbed and run for 600 years. The dominant period was extracted from the FFT of the settled biomass:


Code
find_period <- function(bm, times, t_min = 300, dt = 0.2) {
  post <- times > t_min
  ps   <- power_spectrum(bm[post], dt)
  ps$period[which.max(ps$power)]
}

w_mat_vals <- 10^seq(0.5, 1.7, length.out = 12)

results_wmat <- lapply(w_mat_vals, function(wm) {
  params_wm <- newSingleSpeciesParams(
    species_name = "Anchovy",
    w_min = p$w_min, w_max = p$w_max, w_mat = wm,
    no_w  = no_w,    lambda = p$lambda, kappa = kappa,
    alpha = p$alpha, gamma  = p$gamma,  ks    = 0
  )
  r_wm      <- resource_rate(params_wm) * 0.001
  params_wm <- setResource(params_wm, resource_rate = r_wm,
                           resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat")
  params_wm@initial_n_pp[] <- params_wm@cc_pp * 0.1

  sim_wm  <- project(params_wm, t_max = 10, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                     progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
  idx_wm  <- params_wm@w >= wm & params_wm@w <= p$w_max
  last_wm <- dim(sim_wm@n)[1]
  sim_wm@n[last_wm, , idx_wm] <- sim_wm@n[last_wm, , idx_wm] / 10^3
  sim_wm  <- project(sim_wm, t_max = 590, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                     progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")

  bm_wm    <- getBiomass(sim_wm)[, "Anchovy"]
  times_wm <- as.numeric(names(bm_wm))
  settled  <- bm_wm[times_wm > 300]
  cv       <- sd(settled) / mean(settled)

  data.frame(
    w_mat  = wm,
    period = if (cv > 0.01) find_period(bm_wm, times_wm) else NA,
    cv     = cv
  )
})

df_wmat <- do.call(rbind, results_wmat)

plot_ly(df_wmat[!is.na(df_wmat$period), ]) |>
  add_markers(x = ~w_mat, y = ~period) |>
  layout(xaxis = list(type = "log", title = "w_mat (g)"),
         yaxis = list(type = "log", title = "Period (years)"),
         title = "Period vs maturation size")

fit <- lm(log10(period) ~ log10(w_mat), data = df_wmat[!is.na(df_wmat$period), ])
summary(fit)


The result was a clean power law: Period ~ w_mat^0.2, with R² = 0.9974. There is essentially no scatter - the period is determined entirely by maturation size across the full range tested.
The exponent 0.2 has a direct metabolic interpretation. Juvenile growth rate in this model scales as w^n where n ≈ 0.8 (set by the search rate exponent). The time to grow from w_min to w_mat then scales as:

T_mat ~ w_mat^(1 − n) = w_mat^0.2

The slight deviation from the classic quarter-power scaling (0.25, which would imply n = 3/4) reflects the specific parameterisation: with search rate exponent q = 0.8 and lambda = 2, juvenile growth is dominated by encounter rate rather than metabolic maintenance, giving a slightly steeper scaling.
The combination of the FFT result (one frequency) and the w_mat scaling (clean power law, metabolically grounded exponent) gives a complete mechanistic picture: one feedback loop, one timescale, set by how long it takes juveniles to reach maturation.

title: Day 8: FFT, Scaling Laws, and Hunting the Traffic Jam
text:
Cohort Tracking: Phase Analysis
With the mechanism confirmed, the question became whether the oscillation is a standing wave (all sizes pulsing in sync) or a travelling cohort wave (a pulse of fish moving through the size spectrum). The DFT coefficient at the dominant frequency was computed for each size class independently:


Code
omega  <- 2 * pi / period_dom
post   <- times > 300
t_post <- times[post]
t_vec  <- t_post - t_post[1]
n_post <- sim_600@n[post, "Anchovy", ]

coeffs <- apply(n_post, 2, function(x) {
  signal <- x - mean(x)
  sum(signal * exp(-1i * omega * t_vec))
})

df_phase <- data.frame(
  w         = params@w,
  amplitude = Mod(coeffs),
  phase     = Arg(coeffs)
)

p_amp <- ggplot(df_phase, aes(x = w, y = amplitude)) +
  geom_line() + scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Size (g)", y = "Amplitude", title = "Oscillation amplitude by size class")

p_phs <- ggplot(df_phase, aes(x = w, y = phase)) +
  geom_line() + scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Size (g)", y = "Phase (radians)", title = "Oscillation phase by size class")

p_amp + p_phs









The amplitude plot confirms what the feeding level already showed: the oscillation is overwhelmingly concentrated at juvenile sizes, with amplitude declining steeply across ~18 orders of magnitude from w_min to w_max. Large fish barely oscillate.
The phase plot is more informative. A pure cohort wave would show monotonically increasing phase (each larger size class lagging behind smaller ones). A pure standing wave would show flat phase. What appears is neither: the phase rises from ~0 at the smallest fish to a peak of ~2.5 radians around 0.01–0.05 g, then decreases continuously through sub-adults and adults, reaching ~−1.5 radians at 100 g.
Note on what “phase” means here: it’s Arg() of the DFT coefficient at the dominant frequency, computed a gainst t_vec <- t_post - t_post[1] - time measured from the first saved point after t = 300, an arbitrary cutoff with no biological meaning (not anchored to e.g. peak adult biomass or a spawning event). So the absolute phase values aren’t meaningful on their own; what matters is the relative phase across size classes, since every size class’s coefficient shares the same t_vec and omega. The lag/lead structure between sizes - not the literal radian values - is what supports the closed-loop interpretation below.
This non-monotonic pattern reveals a closed feedback loop. The causal chain is not a one-way wave travelling from small to large sizes - it circles back through reproduction:

Adults spawn → recruits appear at the smallest sizes
Recruits grow slowly through the food-limited juvenile bottleneck (accumulating phase lag)
Eventually mature into adults
Those adults spawn → new recruits

The reproductive connection between the large end of the spectrum and the small end is what produces the phase reversal. Adults and tiny recruits end up close in phase (adults peak, spawn, recruits appear shortly after), but the juvenile sizes in between carry the most lag because they spend extra time in the food-limited bottleneck. The delay that generates the ~8-year period lives in that bottleneck.

Space-time heatmap
The heatmap of the size spectrum over time confirms this directly:


Code
times  <- as.numeric(dimnames(sim_600@n)[[1]])
t_win  <- times > 300 & times < 380

bm_win  <- sweep(sim_600@n[t_win, "Anchovy", ], 2, params@w^2, "*")
df_heat <- melt(bm_win)
names(df_heat) <- c("time", "w", "bm")
df_heat$time   <- as.numeric(as.character(df_heat$time))
df_heat$w      <- as.numeric(as.character(df_heat$w))

ggplot(df_heat, aes(x = time, y = log10(w), fill = log10(pmax(bm, 1e-12)))) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "log10\nbiomass") +
  labs(x = "Time (years)", y = "log10(size [g])", title = "Size–time heatmap")









The heatmap shows vertical banding meaning all size classes brighten and dim together, in phase. A cohort wave would produce diagonal bands slanting from bottom-left to top-right. There are none. The oscillation is a synchronised food-limitation cycle.

title: Day 8: FFT, Scaling Laws, and Hunting the Traffic Jam
section: Lambda: What It Controls and Why 2.05 Is Interesting
text:
Lambda: What It Controls and Why 2.05 Is Interesting
Lambda (λ) is the slope of the plankton size spectrum: N_R(w) ~ κ · w^(−λ). It controls how quickly plankton abundance falls off with prey size, and therefore how food availability scales across fish sizes.
With the model’s search rate exponent q = 0.8, the food encounter rate for a fish of size w scales as w^(q + 2 − λ). At λ = 2 this gives w^0.8, which is approximately the balanced point ; food availability rises with fish size at the same rate as maximum consumption, so the feeding level is roughly uniform across sizes. No size class is systematically more food-limited than another.
Changing lambda from 2.0 to 2.05, a shift of just 0.05, produced a dramatically different phase structure:

At λ = 2: smooth, gradual non-monotonic phase variation across sizes (the closed-loop structure described above)
At λ = 2.05: near-discontinuous phase jumps at two specific size ranges (~0.003–0.01 g and ~1 g), with the phase traversing almost the full ±π range almost instantaneously at those sizes

The heatmap at λ = 2.05 still shows vertical stripes but the oscillation remains fundamentally synchronous, and no cohort wave appears. The phase analysis detects a real structural reorganisation of the internal dynamics, but it doesn’t manifest as a macroscopic change in the heatmap.
This extreme sensitivity to a 0.05 change in lambda suggests the system is near a bifurcation point at λ = 2. The balanced community condition may be a structurally degenerate special case where the neutral food environment simplifies the oscillation into a clean closed-loop structure. Moving even slightly above this value breaks the symmetry and reveals sharper, more localised food-limitation effects at specific size ranges.

title: Day 8: FFT, Scaling Laws, and Hunting the Traffic Jam
text:
What’s Next

Connecting the traffic jam to fisheries: If the bottleneck is a real congestion effect at the juvenile food ceiling, fishing pressure on the right size classes might relieve it rather than just removing biomass. Worth testing whether harvesting juveniles or sub-adults thinsthe queue enough to let the remaining cohort grow through the bottleneck faster, and whether that translates into a net gain in average yield rather than a loss.
Flux at fishery-relevant sizes: Rather than tracking flux across the full size spectrum, plot growth/flux specifically at the size classes fisheries actually target (the catch-relevant range), to see whether the bottleneck shows up there as a throughput constraint on what’s effectively landable.
Yield vs time: Plot total (or size-selective) yield over time under different fishing mortality scenarios, to check whether yield itself oscillates with the ~8–9 year cycle, and whether fishing at the bottleneck size shifts the average yield up or down relative to no fishing.

title: Day 10: Chasing the New Bottlenecks
text: Day 9 ended on an uncomfortable correction: once the gear_params<- selectivity bug was actually fixed and plotRelative was read properly instead of eyeballed, peaks-only fishing on the bottleneck gear didn’t relieve the jam where it mattered. It relieved congestion for sub-adults and fish approaching maturity, but it measurably worsened the food-limited queue at juvenile sizes. The open question going into today was why, and whether that was about selectivity (still catching too many juveniles), timing (fishing too rarely near each peak), or something else entirely.

text: Day 9 ended on an uncomfortable correction: once the gear_params<- selectivity bug was actually fixed and plotRelative was read properly instead of eyeballed, peaks-only fishing on the bottleneck gear didn’t relieve the jam where it mattered. It relieved congestion for sub-adults and fish approaching maturity, but it measurably worsened the food-limited queue at juvenile sizes. The open question going into today was why, and whether that was about selectivity (still catching too many juveniles), timing (fishing too rarely near each peak), or something else entirely.

title: Day 10: Chasing the New Bottlenecks
section: Closing Out Yesterday’s Bugs, For Real This Time
text:
Closing Out Yesterday’s Bugs, For Real This Time
First thing today: re-running yesterday’s fixed code in a fresh session immediately hit a new error.
Error in get(fun, mode = "function", envir = envir) :
  object 'box_selectivity_func' of mode 'function' was not found
The gear_params(params) <- gp fix from Day 9 was correct, but it calls setFishing() immediately, which looks up sel_func by name and calls it right away, not lazily later inside project(). The actual function definition had never made it into the saved script, only the string "box_selectivity_func" referencing it. Added it back in, with ... in the signature so it absorbs the species_params argument mizer’s calc_selectivity() always passes (the same fix bottleneck_sel needed in yesterday’s post):


Code
box_selectivity_func <- function(w, w_low, w_high, ...) {
  as.numeric(w >= w_low & w <= w_high)
}


With that in place, every comparison below is finally running on the gear that’s actually intended, not a silent default.

title: Day 10: Chasing the New Bottlenecks
section: Lambda Sets Where the Jam Sits
text:
Lambda Sets Where the Jam Sits
Before getting back to the fishing experiments, a side observation from poking at lambda again: it doesn’t just change whether there’s a bottleneck (Day 8 already showed that), it shifts where in time the bottleneck shows up in a settling simulation. Higher lambda pushes the bottleneck later; lower lambda brings it on earlier.
This is currently just an eyeballed observation from watching plotHover(getFlux(...)) across a couple of lambda values, not a quantified sweep and Day 9’s own lesson was “don’t trust an eyeballed read, put a number on it.” So this one goes straight into What’s Next rather than being treated as confirmed.

title: Day 10: Chasing the New Bottlenecks
section: Fishing Everywhere: Same Trade-off as Before
text:
Fishing Everywhere: Same Trade-off as Before
With the bug fixed, the gear now genuinely targets sub-adults only (w_low = 0.5 * w_mat to w_high = w_mat), not the unintended default:


Code
library(mizer)
library(patchwork)
library(reshape2)
library(plotly)
library(dplyr)
library(mizerExperimental)
library(tidyverse)
library(glue)
library(ggplot2)
#Useful Plots
nice_animation <- function(sim,t){
  nf <- melt(sim@n)
  n_ppf <- melt(sim@n_pp)
  n_ppf$sp <- "Plankton"
  nf <- rbind(nf, n_ppf)
  
  plot_ly(nf) %>%
    # show only part of plankton spectrum
    filter(w > 10^-5) %>%
    # start at time 50
    filter(time >= t) %>%
    # calculate biomass density with respect to log size
    mutate(b = value * w^2) %>%
    # Plot lines
    add_lines(
      x = ~w, y = ~b,
      color = ~sp,
      frame = ~time,
      line = list(simplify = FALSE)
    ) %>%
    # Use logarithmic axes
    layout(xaxis = list(type = "log", exponentformat = "power",
                        title_text = "body mass (g)"),
           yaxis = list(type = "log", exponentformat = "power",
                        title_text = "biomass (g/m^3)",
                        range = c(-8, 0)))
}

nice_biomass_plot <- function(sim,t){
  abm <- melt(getBiomass(sim))
  abmr <- melt(getBiomass(sim, min_w = 0.01, max_w = 0.4))
  abmr$sp <- "small Anchovy"
  pbm <- sim@n_pp %*% (params@w_full * params@dw_full)
  pbm <- melt(pbm)
  names(pbm)[names(pbm) == "Var1"] <- "time"
  pbm$Var2 <- NULL
  pbm$sp <- "Plankton"
  bm <- rbind(pbm, abm, abmr)
  plot_ly(bm) %>%
    filter(time >= t) %>%
    add_lines(x = ~time, y = ~value, color = ~sp) %>%
    # Use logarithmic axes
    layout(yaxis = list(type = "log", exponentformat = "power",
                        title_text = "biomass (g/m^3)",
                        range = c(-7, 2)),
           xaxis = list(title_text = "time (year)"))
}

################## Code from yesterday that I'll experiment on #################

p <- list(
  dt     = 0.001,
  dx     = 0.1,
  w_min  = 0.0003,
  w_max  = 66.5,     # was w_inf
  w_mat  = 10,
  alpha  = 0.1,      # assimilation efficiency (was p$K)
  gamma  = 750,
  lambda = 2.05,
  a0     = 100
)

kappa <- p$a0 * exp(-6.9 * (p$lambda - 1))
no_w  <- round(log(p$w_max / p$w_min) / p$dx)

params <- newSingleSpeciesParams(
  species_name = "Anchovy",
  w_min  = p$w_min,
  w_max  = p$w_max,
  w_mat  = p$w_mat,
  no_w   = no_w,
  lambda = p$lambda,
  kappa  = kappa,
  alpha  = p$alpha,
  gamma  = p$gamma,
  ks     = 0
)
r <- getResourceRate(params)
r <- r*0.001
params <- setResource(params, resource_rate = r, resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat")

params@initial_n_pp[] <- params@cc_pp * 0.1

test_sizes <- list(
  "small"  = c(0.1, 1),
  "medium" = c(1, 10),
  "large"  = c(10, 100)
)

# --- Shared phase: perturbation + settling, no fishing ---
sim <- project(params, t_max = 10, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
               effort = 0, progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")

# rng <- test_sizes[["large"]]
# idx <- params@w >= rng[1] & params@w <= rng[2]
# last <- dim(sim@n)[1]
# sim@n[last, , idx] <- sim@n[last, , idx] / 10^3

sim <- project(sim, t_max = 90, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
               effort = 0, progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")

sim_300 <- project(sim, t_max = 200, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                   effort = 0, progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")

# --- Branch 1: no fishing (this is your existing pipeline) ---
sim_600 <- project(sim_300, t_max = 300, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                   effort = 0, progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")

bottleneck_sel <- function(w, w_low, w_high) {
  as.numeric(w >= w_low & w <= w_high)
}

box_selectivity_func <- function(w, w_low, w_high, ...) {
  as.numeric(w >= w_low & w <= w_high)
}

params_fished <- sim_300@params

gp <- params_fished@gear_params
gp$sel_func        <- "box_selectivity_func"
gp$w_low           <- 0.5 * p$w_mat
gp$w_high          <- p$w_mat
gp$catchability    <- 1
gp$knife_edge_size <- NULL
gear_params(params_fished) <- gp

sim_300_fished        <- sim_300
sim_300_fished@params <- params_fished

sim_fished <- project(sim_300_fished, t_max = 300, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                      effort = 0.3, progress_bar = FALSE,
                      method = "predictor-corrector")

plotRelative(getFlux(sim_600, power = 2), getFlux(sim_fished, power = 2), tlim = c(550, 600))









Code
plotRelative(getBiomass(sim_600), getBiomass(sim_fished), tlim = c(550, 600))









Same qualitative result as before the bug was found: fishing the bottleneck gear constantly eases congestion at the worst point in the spectrum, but at the cost of introducing new bottlenecks elsewhere. Removing biomass continuously changes the whole flow pattern, not just the part you’re targeting so relief in one place seems to show up as a cost somewhere else in a closed system like this.

title: Day 10: Chasing the New Bottlenecks
section: Fishing Only the Peaks: A Worse Trade, At First
text:
Fishing Only the Peaks: A Worse Trade, At First
The peaks-only schedule from Day 9, rebuilt on the corrected gear:


Code
all_times <- as.numeric(dimnames(sim_600@n)[[1]])
keep      <- all_times >= 300
t_p       <- all_times[keep]
time_lbls <- dimnames(sim_600@n)[[1]][keep]

bm   <- getBiomass(sim_600)[, "Anchovy"]
bm_p <- bm[time_lbls]

n <- length(bm_p)
is_peak <- logical(n)
is_peak[2:(n-1)] <- bm_p[2:(n-1)] > bm_p[1:(n-2)] & bm_p[2:(n-1)] > bm_p[3:n]
peak_times <- t_p[is_peak]

window     <- 3    # years either side of peak to fish
fish_level <- 0.3

effort_vec <- rep(0, length(t_p))
for (pt in peak_times) {
  effort_vec[t_p >= pt - window / 2 & t_p <= pt + window / 2] <- fish_level
}

gear_name  <- params_fished@gear_params$gear[1]
effort_arr <- matrix(effort_vec, ncol = 1, dimnames = list(time_lbls, gear_name))

sim_peaks_only <- project(sim_300_fished, t_max = 300, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                          effort = effort_arr, progress_bar = FALSE,
                          method = "predictor-corrector")

plotRelative(getFlux(sim_600, power = 2), getFlux(sim_peaks_only, power = 2), tlim = c(550, 600))









Code
plotRelative(getFlux(sim_fished, power = 2), getFlux(sim_peaks_only, power = 2), tlim = c(550, 600))









Code
plotYield(sim_peaks_only, sim_fished, tlim = c(550, 600))









Code
y_fished <- getYield(sim_peaks_only)
y_base   <- getYield(sim_fished)
t_f      <- as.numeric(rownames(y_fished))
t_b      <- as.numeric(rownames(y_base))

mean(y_fished[t_f > 550, "Anchovy"])   # average yield, fishing the bottleneck (peaks-only)


[1] 1.597538e-05


Code
mean(y_base[t_b > 550, "Anchovy"])     # average yield, fishing constantly (sub-adults only)


[1] 2.095615e-05


The window shown above (3 years either side) is already the fixed value. The first pass today reused something close to Day 9’s narrower window, and it relieved the original bottleneck better than fishing everywhere did, exactly as hoped. But the new bottlenecks it introduced elsewhere in the spectrum were worse than the new bottlenecks fishing-everywhere had introduced. That’s a genuinely bad trade: better at the one thing it was supposed to fix, worse everywhere else. Worth digging into why before concluding peaks-only fishing was the better strategy after all.

title: Day 10: Chasing the New Bottlenecks
section: Ruling Out Selectivity As the Cause
text:
Ruling Out Selectivity As the Cause
First hypothesis: maybe the new, worse bottlenecks were because the gear was still catching too far down into the juvenile range. Built a juvenile-inclusive comparison variant, the original setup from before the sub-adults-only restriction, to test it directly:


Code
params_fished_juv <- sim_300@params
gp_juv <- params_fished_juv@gear_params
gp_juv$sel_func        <- "box_selectivity_func"
gp_juv$w_low           <- 0.01   # juveniles included
gp_juv$w_high          <- p$w_mat
gp_juv$catchability    <- 1
gp_juv$knife_edge_size <- NULL
gear_params(params_fished_juv) <- gp_juv

sim_300_fished_juv        <- sim_300
sim_300_fished_juv@params <- params_fished_juv

sim_fished_juv <- project(sim_300_fished_juv, t_max = 300, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                          effort = 0.3, progress_bar = FALSE,
                          method = "predictor-corrector")

sim_peaks_only_juv <- project(sim_300_fished_juv, t_max = 300, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                              effort = effort_arr, progress_bar = FALSE,
                              method = "predictor-corrector")

plotRelative(getFlux(sim_fished_juv, power = 2), getFlux(sim_fished, power = 2), tlim = c(550, 600))









Code
plotRelative(getBiomass(sim_fished_juv), getBiomass(sim_fished), tlim = c(550, 600))









Code
plotRelative(getFlux(sim_peaks_only_juv, power = 2), getFlux(sim_peaks_only, power = 2), tlim = c(550, 600))









Code
plotRelative(getBiomass(sim_peaks_only_juv), getBiomass(sim_peaks_only), tlim = c(550, 600))









This wasn’t it, or at least not the main driver ; juveniles-included vs. sub-adults-only produced broadly similar patterns of new bottlenecks under both fishing strategies. Excluding juveniles from the catch is still the right thing to do on biological grounds, but it isn’t what explains why peaks-only fishing was creating worse new congestion than fishing constantly.

title: Day 10: Chasing the New Bottlenecks
section: The Real Lever: Fishing Frequency, Not Selectivity
text:
The Real Lever: Fishing Frequency, Not Selectivity
Going back to basics: with a narrow window, the peaks-only schedule is only fishing for a small slice of each cycle as most of the time, effort is sitting at zero. That’s the entire appeal (avoid fishing during troughs), but it also means each fishing pulse has to do disproportionately more work whenever it is active, concentrating pressure into a short burst rather than spreading it out. That concentration looks like exactly the kind of thing that could create sharper, worse localised bottlenecks than constant low-level fishing does.
Widening the window from something close to Day 9’s ~2.6 years to 3 years either side of each peak (the window <- 3 already shown above) eased this substantially. The new-bottleneck problem that motivated the selectivity hypothesis mostly went away once fishing was active for a larger share of each cycle. It wasn’t about which sizes were being caught, it was about how often fishing was actually happening.

title: Day 10: Chasing the New Bottlenecks
text:
What’s Next

Quantify the lambda-vs-bottleneck-timing observation properly with an actual sweep and a plotRelative-style measurement, rather than eyeballing a couple of plotHover panels — same lesson Day 9 already learned the hard way, just applied to a new parameter.
Now that frequency looks like the dominant lever (not selectivity), run a proper window × effort grid sweep , the thing flagged as missing back on Day 9 , to map out where exactly the trade-off between “relieves the original bottleneck” and “introduces a worse one elsewhere” flips.
Re-run today’s plotRelative comparisons across the full size spectrum (not just eyeballing whether new bottlenecks look “worse”) to get an honest, quantified before/after picture now that window = 3 is in place as there may still be a smaller residual bottleneck hiding somewhere that hasn’t been checked for directly.
Connect the widened-window result back to the juvenile/sub-adult selectivity finding: now that frequency is fixed, is restricting the catch to sub-adults still worth doing on its own, or was most of its apparent benefit actually coming from changes in effective fishing frequency all along?

title: Day 12 and 13: Learning the Discrete Fourier Transform, Limit Cycles, and a Second Look at Generation Time
text:
Day 11 used fft() as a black box to get a dominant period and a phase argument out of the simulation, with a note left in “What’s Next” to actually learn what the transform is doing rather than keep treating it as a library call. Tuesday went looking for resources to do that properly, rather than diving straight back into mizer.


The most useful resources found were:

Julius O. Smith III’s Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT), the Stanford CCRMA page on the DFT, which derives the transform itself rather than just stating the formula and lists the standard properties (linearity, the shift and convolution theorems, Parseval’s relation) in one place.
YouTube explanations from 3Blue1Brown and Steve Brunton, for the geometric “winding the signal around a circle at different frequencies” intuition that’s harder to get from a written derivation alone.

The rest of Tuesday’s DFT time went into working through that material and starting a proper set of notes rather than anything that produces code or numbers worth showing here.



Alongside the DFT, Tuesday’s reading time also went into Strogatz’s Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos, picking up the limit-cycle chapter that had been queued since Day 11 (the system’s boom-bust oscillation is exactly the kind of self-sustained periodic attractor that chapter is about, and Day 11 had been reasoning about phase and feedback without that theory underneath it).



The other piece of Tuesday went back to Day 11’s generation-time calculation, re-running the same steady-state age-at-size integral to make sure the number being carried forward was right rather than half-remembered:


Code
library(mizer)
library(patchwork)
library(reshape2)
library(plotly)
library(dplyr)
library(mizerExperimental)
library(tidyverse)
library(glue)
library(ggplot2)

# Same single-species Anchovy setup as Day 8/11.
run_anchovy <- function(lambda) {
  p <- list(
    dt = 0.001, dx = 0.1, w_min = 0.0003, w_max = 66.5,
    w_mat = 10, alpha = 0.1, gamma = 750, lambda = lambda, a0 = 100
  )
  kappa <- p$a0 * exp(-6.9 * (p$lambda - 1))
  no_w  <- round(log(p$w_max / p$w_min) / p$dx)

  params <- newSingleSpeciesParams(
    species_name = "Anchovy",
    w_min = p$w_min, w_max = p$w_max, w_mat = p$w_mat,
    no_w  = no_w,    lambda = p$lambda, kappa = kappa,
    alpha = p$alpha, gamma  = p$gamma,  ks    = 0
  )
  r <- getResourceRate(params) * 0.001
  params <- setResource(params, resource_rate = r,
                        resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat")
  params@initial_n_pp[] <- params@cc_pp * 0.1

  sim <- project(params, t_max = 10, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                 progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
  idx  <- params@w >= 10 & params@w <= 100
  last <- dim(sim@n)[1]
  sim@n[last, , idx] <- sim@n[last, , idx] / 10^3

  sim     <- project(sim, t_max = 90, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                     progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
  sim_300 <- project(sim, t_max = 200, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                     progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
  sim_600 <- project(sim_300, t_max = 300, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                     progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
  list(params = params, sim_600 = sim_600)
}

# Reused from Day 8/11: power spectrum of a (mean-subtracted) signal.
power_spectrum <- function(signal, dt) {
  signal <- signal - mean(signal)
  n      <- length(signal)
  freqs  <- (1:(n - 1)) / (n * dt)
  power  <- Mod(fft(signal))^2
  half   <- seq_len(floor((n - 1) / 2))
  data.frame(freq = freqs[half], period = 1 / freqs[half], power = power[half + 1])
}

run_2   <- run_anchovy(2)
params  <- run_2$params
sim_600 <- run_2$sim_600
times   <- as.numeric(dimnames(sim_600@n)[[1]])
bm      <- getBiomass(sim_600)[, "Anchovy"]
ps      <- power_spectrum(bm[times > 300], 0.2)
period_dom <- ps$period[which.max(ps$power)]

# age(w) = integral_{w_min}^{w} 1/g(w') dw' under the steady-state growth
# rate, i.e. how long a fish takes to grow from w_min up to w.
g  <- getEGrowth(params)["Anchovy", ]
w  <- params@w
dw <- params@dw
integrand  <- 1 / g
age        <- c(0, cumsum((integrand[-1] + integrand[-length(integrand)]) / 2 * dw[-length(dw)]))
age_at_mat <- approx(x = w, y = age, xout = params@species_params$w_mat)$y




Code
round(c(period_dom = period_dom, age_at_mat = age_at_mat,
       ratio = period_dom / age_at_mat), 3)


period_dom age_at_mat      ratio 
     8.333      3.497      2.383 


The dominant oscillation period comes out at 8.33 years, age-at-maturity at 3.50 years, giving a period-to-generation-time ratio of 2.38. The earlier working assumption had been “about 3 generations” per period; the actual calculated number sits a bit below that, closer to “two and a bit” generations than three. Worth flagging honestly: this uses the same fixed, steady-state growth rate as Day 11, not a growth rate that varies with the cycle, so the number is a snapshot to build on rather than a final answer.



Day 11 derived a clean prediction for how phase should depend on growth rate, then checked it against the actual data and found it failed: the measured phase curve didn’t fall steadily the way the proof predicted, and the relative phase drop from \(w_{min}\) to \(w_{mat}\) had the wrong sign and was far too small in magnitude. An assumption behind that proof were flagged as suspect: that growth rate is fixed at its steady-state value when the food supply driving it actually oscillates along with everything else. The generation-time number just calculated rests on that same fixed-growth-rate assumption (getEGrowth(params), evaluated at the steady state), so before moving on to the DFT and limit-cycle reading, it was worth checking directly how much that assumption was costing.


The steady-state version of the age calculation rests on separating variables in \(dw/dt = g(w)\):
\[\frac{dw}{g(w)} = dt \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a(w) = \int_{w_{min}}^{w} \frac{dw'}{g(w')}\]
This works because \(g(w)\) depends only on \(w\), so all the \(w\)-stuff can be put on one side and all the \(t\)-stuff on the other before integrating each side independently. The moment growth rate also depends on time, \(g(w,t)\), that move stops being valid:
\[\frac{dw}{g(w,t)} = dt\]
looks the same, but the left side still has a \(t\) buried inside it, and that \(t\) isn’t free to integrate away on its own, because \(w\) and \(t\) are linked along the very trajectory being solved for. Writing \(\int dw/g(w,t)\) in isolation doesn’t mean anything yet: you’d need to already know \(w(t)\) to know what to plug into \(g\) at each step, which is circular.
There’s one case where separation still rescues you: if the time-dependence factors out multiplicatively, \(g(w,t) = g_0(w)\,h(t)\) (e.g. food availability scaling every size class’s growth by the same relative amount), then
\[\frac{dw}{g_0(w)} = h(t)\,dt \quad\Longrightarrow\quad A(w) = H(t) - H(t_{\text{birth}})\]
where \(A(w) = \int_{w_{min}}^w dw'/g_0(w')\) and \(H\) is an antiderivative of \(h\). This still gives a closed form, but a cohort-dependent one: \(t_{\text{peak}}(w) = H^{-1}(A(w) + H(t_{\text{birth}}))\) now depends on \(t_{\text{birth}}\) in a nonlinear way, unlike the steady-state case where every cohort shares the same offset \(a(w)\). There was no good reason to expect mizer’s actual \(g(w,t)\) to factor this cleanly, though, so rather than gamble on that assumption, the honest route is the fully general one: solve \(dw/dt = g(w,t)\) as the coupled equation it is, numerically, for each cohort separately. That’s what project() is already doing internally; the next step just pulls a labelled cohort’s trajectory back out of it after the fact.



getEGrowth() doesn’t have to be evaluated at the steady state. It recomputes growth from whatever population state n and resource state n_pp you hand it, so feeding each saved time step’s actual state back in gives the real, time-varying growth field instead of a single fixed snapshot:


Code
# Recompute growth at every saved time step in the settled window, using
# that time step's actual (n, n_pp), not the unperturbed steady state.
post     <- times > 300
idx_post <- which(post)
G <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = length(idx_post), ncol = length(w))
for (k in seq_along(idx_post)) {
  i      <- idx_post[k]
  n_t    <- array(sim_600@n[i, , , drop = FALSE], dim = dim(sim_600@n)[2:3],
                  dimnames = dimnames(sim_600@n)[2:3])
  n_pp_t <- sim_600@n_pp[i, ]
  G[k, ] <- getEGrowth(params, n = n_t, n_pp = n_pp_t)["Anchovy", ]
}
times_post <- times[idx_post]
t_save     <- times_post[2] - times_post[1]   # 0.2, matches the project() calls above


This shows that getEGrowth(params, n = n_t, n_pp = n_pp_t) for a single time step gives a growth profile very close to, but not identical to, the steady-state getEGrowth(params) used above. At \(t=19.8\) (an early, still-settling point), the smallest-size growth rate was 0.00683 vs. 0.00673 from the steady state, a small difference at that particular moment. The whole point of building G across every saved time step is that this difference isn’t constant, it swings with the cycle, and the steady-state calculation used only the time-averaged-looking (but actually unperturbed-equilibrium) snapshot.



With G built, a cohort’s trajectory is found by integrating \(dw/dt = g(w,t)\) forward from \(w_{min}\), looking up the growth rate at the cohort’s current size and time at every step rather than assuming a fixed function of size alone:


Code
# Bilinear-style lookup: blend the two bracketing saved time snapshots, then
# interpolate across size, to get g(w,t) at an arbitrary (t, w).
g_lookup <- function(t, w_now) {
  idx   <- floor((t - times_post[1]) / t_save) + 1
  idx   <- min(max(idx, 1), nrow(G) - 1)
  frac  <- (t - times_post[idx]) / t_save
  g_vec <- (1 - frac) * G[idx, ] + frac * G[idx + 1, ]
  approx(x = w, y = g_vec, xout = w_now, rule = 2)$y
}

# Forward-integrate a single fish born at t_birth through the real,
# time-varying growth field (simple Euler stepping; dt_step is fine enough
# relative to the ~8 year period that finer stepping doesn't change the result).
track_cohort <- function(t_birth, w_min = min(params@w), w_max = max(params@w),
                         dt_step = 0.02) {
  t_now <- t_birth; w_now <- w_min
  t_vec <- t_now;   w_vec <- w_now
  while (w_now < w_max && t_now < max(times_post) - 1) {
    g_now <- g_lookup(t_now, w_now)
    if (is.na(g_now) || g_now <= 0) break
    w_now <- w_now + g_now * dt_step
    t_now <- t_now + dt_step
    t_vec <- c(t_vec, t_now); w_vec <- c(w_vec, w_now)
  }
  data.frame(t = t_vec, w = w_vec, age = t_vec - t_birth)
}

# Track cohorts born at five phases spread across one full cycle, to see how
# much age-at-size depends on when a cohort happens to be born.
period_dom_check <- period_dom   # 8.333333, the dominant FFT period from above
birth_times <- seq(305, 305 + period_dom_check, length.out = 6)[-6]
cohorts     <- lapply(birth_times, track_cohort)
names(cohorts) <- paste0("t_birth=", round(birth_times, 2))

df_cohorts <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(cohorts), function(nm) {
  d <- cohorts[[nm]]; d$cohort <- nm; d
}))

ggplot(df_cohorts, aes(x = w, y = age, colour = cohort)) +
  geom_line() + scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "body mass (g)", y = "age since birth (years)",
       title = "Age-at-size for cohorts born at different phases", colour = "birth time")











Code
ages_at_mat <- sapply(cohorts, function(co)
  approx(x = co$w, y = co$age, xout = params@species_params$w_mat)$y)
round(ages_at_mat, 3)


   t_birth=305 t_birth=306.67 t_birth=308.33    t_birth=310 t_birth=311.67 
         2.464          2.512          2.808          2.490          2.467 


The five cohort curves sit almost exactly on top of each other across the entire size range, the plot doesn’t visually distinguish them. Age-at-maturity across the five birth phases comes out as 2.464, 2.512, 2.808, 2.490, and 2.467 years. There is a real spread (the 308.33 cohort takes noticeably longer), but it’s modest compared to the gap between any of these and the steady-state estimate of 3.50 years above. The dominant effect of switching to a real, time-varying growth rate isn’t that different cohorts now disagree with each other, it’s that all of them mature faster than the steady-state calculation predicted.



The calculation earlier today reproduced Day 11’s period-to-generation-time ratio of 8.33 / 3.50 \(\approx\) 2.38, and treated the original ballpark guess of “about 3 generations” as having been a slight overestimate once actually calculated. That conclusion needs to be walked back. Using the cohort-tracked ages instead of the steady-state one:


Code
ratios <- period_dom / ages_at_mat
round(ratios, 3)


   t_birth=305 t_birth=306.67 t_birth=308.33    t_birth=310 t_birth=311.67 
         3.382          3.317          2.968          3.347          3.378 


Code
round(mean(ratios), 3)


[1] 3.278


The ratio per cohort ranges from about 2.97 to 3.38, averaging 3.27. That’s much closer to the original “about 3 generations” intuition than the 2.38 figure calculated above, not further from it. The steady-state growth rate was underestimating how fast fish actually grow in this system by roughly 30%, which was dragging the calculated ratio down with it. Once the real, time-varying growth field is used, the rough guess holds up better than the more careful-looking calculation that initially seemed to correct it.



There’s a cleaner way to describe what went wrong with the steady-state estimate and what the cohort-tracking above actually fixed, borrowed from how dispersive waves are normally described.
For a wave built from a single frequency, points of constant phase move through space at the phase velocity, \(v_{\text{phase}} = k/\kappa\), where \(k\) is the (temporal) frequency and \(\kappa\) is the (spatial) wavenumber. A wave packet, a localised pulse built from a narrow spread of frequencies, instead moves at the group velocity, \(v_g = dk/d\kappa\). In a non-dispersive medium these are the same number. In a dispersive one, they aren’t, and the difference is exactly the gap between “where the ripples appear to be” and “where the actual energy is going.”
This system has a direct translation: size \(w\) plays the role of space, real time \(t\) plays the role of time, and Day 11’s \(\kappa(w) = d\varphi/dw = -k/g(w)\) is a wavenumber computed from a single frequency, the dominant FFT peak. That makes the whole Day 11 derivation a phase-velocity calculation: how fast a surface of constant phase, for one Fourier component, moves through size-space. track_cohort() above does something different: it forward-integrates the actual nonlinear \(g(w,t)\) that real fish experience, with no decomposition into frequencies at all. That’s a direct measurement of how fast the real pulse of fish moves through size-space, which is exactly what group velocity means once “wave packet” is replaced with “cohort.”
These two only have to agree if the underlying signal is a clean single sinusoid riding a linear, non-dispersive medium. Neither is true here. Day 8 already found the oscillation is a relaxation-oscillator shape (sharp crash, long plateau) loaded with harmonics, not a pure sine wave, and the growth field \(g(w,t)\) is itself nonlinear, depending on the very population state being transported through it, which is exactly what makes a medium dispersive rather than uniform. The mismatch between Day 11’s phase-velocity calculation and today’s cohort-tracked group velocity isn’t a separate failure from Day 8’s harmonic finding; it’s the same fact, met again in a different calculation.
It also gives a tidier reading of today’s cohort-to-cohort spread. If there were one well-defined phase velocity for this system, every cohort would share exactly the same generation time. Instead the five tracked cohorts came out at 2.46 to 2.81 years, and the period-to-generation-time ratio ranged from 2.97 to 3.38 rather than landing on one fixed number. That spread is the sign of their being dispersion. A single “the” generation time was never quite the right concept for a system like this; there’s a distribution of them, the same way a dispersive pulse doesn’t have one well-defined speed once you look closely enough.

title: Day 12 and 13: Learning the Discrete Fourier Transform, Limit Cycles, and a Second Look at Generation Time
text:
Day 11 used fft() as a black box to get a dominant period and a phase argument out of the simulation, with a note left in “What’s Next” to actually learn what the transform is doing rather than keep treating it as a library call. Tuesday went looking for resources to do that properly, rather than diving straight back into mizer.


The most useful resources found were:

Julius O. Smith III’s Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT), the Stanford CCRMA page on the DFT, which derives the transform itself rather than just stating the formula and lists the standard properties (linearity, the shift and convolution theorems, Parseval’s relation) in one place.
YouTube explanations from 3Blue1Brown and Steve Brunton, for the geometric “winding the signal around a circle at different frequencies” intuition that’s harder to get from a written derivation alone.

The rest of Tuesday’s DFT time went into working through that material and starting a proper set of notes rather than anything that produces code or numbers worth showing here.



Alongside the DFT, Tuesday’s reading time also went into Strogatz’s Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos, picking up the limit-cycle chapter that had been queued since Day 11 (the system’s boom-bust oscillation is exactly the kind of self-sustained periodic attractor that chapter is about, and Day 11 had been reasoning about phase and feedback without that theory underneath it).



The other piece of Tuesday went back to Day 11’s generation-time calculation, re-running the same steady-state age-at-size integral to make sure the number being carried forward was right rather than half-remembered:


Code
library(mizer)
library(patchwork)
library(reshape2)
library(plotly)
library(dplyr)
library(mizerExperimental)
library(tidyverse)
library(glue)
library(ggplot2)

# Same single-species Anchovy setup as Day 8/11.
run_anchovy <- function(lambda) {
  p <- list(
    dt = 0.001, dx = 0.1, w_min = 0.0003, w_max = 66.5,
    w_mat = 10, alpha = 0.1, gamma = 750, lambda = lambda, a0 = 100
  )
  kappa <- p$a0 * exp(-6.9 * (p$lambda - 1))
  no_w  <- round(log(p$w_max / p$w_min) / p$dx)

  params <- newSingleSpeciesParams(
    species_name = "Anchovy",
    w_min = p$w_min, w_max = p$w_max, w_mat = p$w_mat,
    no_w  = no_w,    lambda = p$lambda, kappa = kappa,
    alpha = p$alpha, gamma  = p$gamma,  ks    = 0
  )
  r <- getResourceRate(params) * 0.001
  params <- setResource(params, resource_rate = r,
                        resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat")
  params@initial_n_pp[] <- params@cc_pp * 0.1

  sim <- project(params, t_max = 10, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                 progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
  idx  <- params@w >= 10 & params@w <= 100
  last <- dim(sim@n)[1]
  sim@n[last, , idx] <- sim@n[last, , idx] / 10^3

  sim     <- project(sim, t_max = 90, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                     progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
  sim_300 <- project(sim, t_max = 200, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                     progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
  sim_600 <- project(sim_300, t_max = 300, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                     progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
  list(params = params, sim_600 = sim_600)
}

# Reused from Day 8/11: power spectrum of a (mean-subtracted) signal.
power_spectrum <- function(signal, dt) {
  signal <- signal - mean(signal)
  n      <- length(signal)
  freqs  <- (1:(n - 1)) / (n * dt)
  power  <- Mod(fft(signal))^2
  half   <- seq_len(floor((n - 1) / 2))
  data.frame(freq = freqs[half], period = 1 / freqs[half], power = power[half + 1])
}

run_2   <- run_anchovy(2)
params  <- run_2$params
sim_600 <- run_2$sim_600
times   <- as.numeric(dimnames(sim_600@n)[[1]])
bm      <- getBiomass(sim_600)[, "Anchovy"]
ps      <- power_spectrum(bm[times > 300], 0.2)
period_dom <- ps$period[which.max(ps$power)]

# age(w) = integral_{w_min}^{w} 1/g(w') dw' under the steady-state growth
# rate, i.e. how long a fish takes to grow from w_min up to w.
g  <- getEGrowth(params)["Anchovy", ]
w  <- params@w
dw <- params@dw
integrand  <- 1 / g
age        <- c(0, cumsum((integrand[-1] + integrand[-length(integrand)]) / 2 * dw[-length(dw)]))
age_at_mat <- approx(x = w, y = age, xout = params@species_params$w_mat)$y




Code
round(c(period_dom = period_dom, age_at_mat = age_at_mat,
       ratio = period_dom / age_at_mat), 3)


period_dom age_at_mat      ratio 
     8.333      3.497      2.383 


The dominant oscillation period comes out at 8.33 years, age-at-maturity at 3.50 years, giving a period-to-generation-time ratio of 2.38. The earlier working assumption had been “about 3 generations” per period; the actual calculated number sits a bit below that, closer to “two and a bit” generations than three. Worth flagging honestly: this uses the same fixed, steady-state growth rate as Day 11, not a growth rate that varies with the cycle, so the number is a snapshot to build on rather than a final answer.



Day 11 derived a clean prediction for how phase should depend on growth rate, then checked it against the actual data and found it failed: the measured phase curve didn’t fall steadily the way the proof predicted, and the relative phase drop from \(w_{min}\) to \(w_{mat}\) had the wrong sign and was far too small in magnitude. An assumption behind that proof were flagged as suspect: that growth rate is fixed at its steady-state value when the food supply driving it actually oscillates along with everything else. The generation-time number just calculated rests on that same fixed-growth-rate assumption (getEGrowth(params), evaluated at the steady state), so before moving on to the DFT and limit-cycle reading, it was worth checking directly how much that assumption was costing.


The steady-state version of the age calculation rests on separating variables in \(dw/dt = g(w)\):
\[\frac{dw}{g(w)} = dt \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a(w) = \int_{w_{min}}^{w} \frac{dw'}{g(w')}\]
This works because \(g(w)\) depends only on \(w\), so all the \(w\)-stuff can be put on one side and all the \(t\)-stuff on the other before integrating each side independently. The moment growth rate also depends on time, \(g(w,t)\), that move stops being valid:
\[\frac{dw}{g(w,t)} = dt\]
looks the same, but the left side still has a \(t\) buried inside it, and that \(t\) isn’t free to integrate away on its own, because \(w\) and \(t\) are linked along the very trajectory being solved for. Writing \(\int dw/g(w,t)\) in isolation doesn’t mean anything yet: you’d need to already know \(w(t)\) to know what to plug into \(g\) at each step, which is circular.
There’s one case where separation still rescues you: if the time-dependence factors out multiplicatively, \(g(w,t) = g_0(w)\,h(t)\) (e.g. food availability scaling every size class’s growth by the same relative amount), then
\[\frac{dw}{g_0(w)} = h(t)\,dt \quad\Longrightarrow\quad A(w) = H(t) - H(t_{\text{birth}})\]
where \(A(w) = \int_{w_{min}}^w dw'/g_0(w')\) and \(H\) is an antiderivative of \(h\). This still gives a closed form, but a cohort-dependent one: \(t_{\text{peak}}(w) = H^{-1}(A(w) + H(t_{\text{birth}}))\) now depends on \(t_{\text{birth}}\) in a nonlinear way, unlike the steady-state case where every cohort shares the same offset \(a(w)\). There was no good reason to expect mizer’s actual \(g(w,t)\) to factor this cleanly, though, so rather than gamble on that assumption, the honest route is the fully general one: solve \(dw/dt = g(w,t)\) as the coupled equation it is, numerically, for each cohort separately. That’s what project() is already doing internally; the next step just pulls a labelled cohort’s trajectory back out of it after the fact.



getEGrowth() doesn’t have to be evaluated at the steady state. It recomputes growth from whatever population state n and resource state n_pp you hand it, so feeding each saved time step’s actual state back in gives the real, time-varying growth field instead of a single fixed snapshot:


Code
# Recompute growth at every saved time step in the settled window, using
# that time step's actual (n, n_pp), not the unperturbed steady state.
post     <- times > 300
idx_post <- which(post)
G <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = length(idx_post), ncol = length(w))
for (k in seq_along(idx_post)) {
  i      <- idx_post[k]
  n_t    <- array(sim_600@n[i, , , drop = FALSE], dim = dim(sim_600@n)[2:3],
                  dimnames = dimnames(sim_600@n)[2:3])
  n_pp_t <- sim_600@n_pp[i, ]
  G[k, ] <- getEGrowth(params, n = n_t, n_pp = n_pp_t)["Anchovy", ]
}
times_post <- times[idx_post]
t_save     <- times_post[2] - times_post[1]   # 0.2, matches the project() calls above


This shows that getEGrowth(params, n = n_t, n_pp = n_pp_t) for a single time step gives a growth profile very close to, but not identical to, the steady-state getEGrowth(params) used above. At \(t=19.8\) (an early, still-settling point), the smallest-size growth rate was 0.00683 vs. 0.00673 from the steady state, a small difference at that particular moment. The whole point of building G across every saved time step is that this difference isn’t constant, it swings with the cycle, and the steady-state calculation used only the time-averaged-looking (but actually unperturbed-equilibrium) snapshot.



With G built, a cohort’s trajectory is found by integrating \(dw/dt = g(w,t)\) forward from \(w_{min}\), looking up the growth rate at the cohort’s current size and time at every step rather than assuming a fixed function of size alone:


Code
# Bilinear-style lookup: blend the two bracketing saved time snapshots, then
# interpolate across size, to get g(w,t) at an arbitrary (t, w).
g_lookup <- function(t, w_now) {
  idx   <- floor((t - times_post[1]) / t_save) + 1
  idx   <- min(max(idx, 1), nrow(G) - 1)
  frac  <- (t - times_post[idx]) / t_save
  g_vec <- (1 - frac) * G[idx, ] + frac * G[idx + 1, ]
  approx(x = w, y = g_vec, xout = w_now, rule = 2)$y
}

# Forward-integrate a single fish born at t_birth through the real,
# time-varying growth field (simple Euler stepping; dt_step is fine enough
# relative to the ~8 year period that finer stepping doesn't change the result).
track_cohort <- function(t_birth, w_min = min(params@w), w_max = max(params@w),
                         dt_step = 0.02) {
  t_now <- t_birth; w_now <- w_min
  t_vec <- t_now;   w_vec <- w_now
  while (w_now < w_max && t_now < max(times_post) - 1) {
    g_now <- g_lookup(t_now, w_now)
    if (is.na(g_now) || g_now <= 0) break
    w_now <- w_now + g_now * dt_step
    t_now <- t_now + dt_step
    t_vec <- c(t_vec, t_now); w_vec <- c(w_vec, w_now)
  }
  data.frame(t = t_vec, w = w_vec, age = t_vec - t_birth)
}

# Track cohorts born at five phases spread across one full cycle, to see how
# much age-at-size depends on when a cohort happens to be born.
period_dom_check <- period_dom   # 8.333333, the dominant FFT period from above
birth_times <- seq(305, 305 + period_dom_check, length.out = 6)[-6]
cohorts     <- lapply(birth_times, track_cohort)
names(cohorts) <- paste0("t_birth=", round(birth_times, 2))

df_cohorts <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(cohorts), function(nm) {
  d <- cohorts[[nm]]; d$cohort <- nm; d
}))

ggplot(df_cohorts, aes(x = w, y = age, colour = cohort)) +
  geom_line() + scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "body mass (g)", y = "age since birth (years)",
       title = "Age-at-size for cohorts born at different phases", colour = "birth time")











Code
ages_at_mat <- sapply(cohorts, function(co)
  approx(x = co$w, y = co$age, xout = params@species_params$w_mat)$y)
round(ages_at_mat, 3)


   t_birth=305 t_birth=306.67 t_birth=308.33    t_birth=310 t_birth=311.67 
         2.464          2.512          2.808          2.490          2.467 


The five cohort curves sit almost exactly on top of each other across the entire size range, the plot doesn’t visually distinguish them. Age-at-maturity across the five birth phases comes out as 2.464, 2.512, 2.808, 2.490, and 2.467 years. There is a real spread (the 308.33 cohort takes noticeably longer), but it’s modest compared to the gap between any of these and the steady-state estimate of 3.50 years above. The dominant effect of switching to a real, time-varying growth rate isn’t that different cohorts now disagree with each other, it’s that all of them mature faster than the steady-state calculation predicted.



The calculation earlier today reproduced Day 11’s period-to-generation-time ratio of 8.33 / 3.50 \(\approx\) 2.38, and treated the original ballpark guess of “about 3 generations” as having been a slight overestimate once actually calculated. That conclusion needs to be walked back. Using the cohort-tracked ages instead of the steady-state one:


Code
ratios <- period_dom / ages_at_mat
round(ratios, 3)


   t_birth=305 t_birth=306.67 t_birth=308.33    t_birth=310 t_birth=311.67 
         3.382          3.317          2.968          3.347          3.378 


Code
round(mean(ratios), 3)


[1] 3.278

The steady-state growth rate was underestimating how fast fish actually grow in this system by roughly 30%, which was dragging the calculated ratio down with it.
