title: Day 26: Closing Day 25’s Loose Ends, and a Delay That Actually Causes a Hopf Bifurcation
text:
Setup


Code
library(mizer)
library(patchwork)
library(reshape2)
library(plotly)
library(dplyr)
library(mizerExperimental)
library(tidyverse)
library(glue)
library(ggplot2)
library(colorRamps)
library(future)
library(scales)
library(deSolve)


Same anchovy builder and the same catchable_fraction_at()/run_param_sweep() pair from Day 25, carried over unchanged so today’s refinements are directly comparable to the sweeps that found the transition and the dip in the first place:


Code
make_second_order_params_kr <- function(lambda = 2.05, resource_decrease = 0.001,
                                        capacity_mult = 1, second_order = TRUE,
                                        ext_diff = 0.00, alpha = 0.1, gamma = 750,
                                        ks = 0, kappa_override = NULL) {
  a0    <- 100
  kappa <- if (is.null(kappa_override)) a0 * exp(-6.9 * (lambda - 1)) else kappa_override
  no_w  <- round(log(66.5 / 0.0003) / 0.1)

  params <- newSingleSpeciesParams(
    species_name = "Anchovy",
    w_min = 0.0003, w_max = 66.5, w_mat = 10,
    no_w = no_w, lambda = lambda, kappa = kappa,
    alpha = alpha, gamma = gamma, ks = ks
  )

  given_species_params(params)$D_ext <- ext_diff
  params <- setBevertonHolt(params)

  default_capacity <- getResourceCapacity(params)
  r  <- getResourceRate(params) * resource_decrease
  cc <- default_capacity * capacity_mult

  params <- setResource(params, resource_rate = r, resource_capacity = cc,
                        resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat",
                        balance = FALSE)

  if (second_order) {
    second_order_w(params) <- c(flux = "centred", bin_average = TRUE)
  }

  params
}

catchable_fraction_at <- function(params, t_max = 600) {
  sim <- project(params, t_max = t_max, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.5,
                 progress_bar = FALSE, effort = 0, method = "tr_bdf2")
  last  <- dim(sim@n)[1]
  w_mat <- params@species_params$w_mat[1]
  w     <- sim@params@w
  dw    <- sim@params@dw

  bm_density   <- sim@n[last, 1, ] * w * dw
  total_bm     <- sum(bm_density)
  catchable_bm <- sum(bm_density[w >= w_mat])

  data.frame(catchable_fraction = catchable_bm / total_bm, error = NA_character_)
}

run_param_sweep <- function(param_name, param_seq, capacity_mult = 10,
                            resource_decrease = 0.001, t_max = 600) {
  bind_rows(lapply(param_seq, function(v) {
    args <- list(capacity_mult = capacity_mult, resource_decrease = resource_decrease)
    args[[param_name]] <- v
    result <- tryCatch({
      p <- do.call(make_second_order_params_kr, args)
      catchable_fraction_at(p, t_max = t_max)
    }, error = function(e) {
      data.frame(catchable_fraction = NA_real_, error = conditionMessage(e))
    })
    if (!is.na(result$error)) {
      warning(sprintf("%s = %.4g: %s", param_name, v, result$error))
    }
    data.frame(param = param_name, value = v,
               catchable_fraction = result$catchable_fraction,
               error = result$error)
  }))
}

title: Day 26: Closing Day 25’s Loose Ends, and a Delay That Actually Causes a Hopf Bifurcation
text:
Pinning Down Alpha’s Transition Window
Day 25’s 15-point \(\alpha\) sweep found the catchable fraction jumps roughly 8 orders of magnitude between \(\alpha=0.057\) and \(\alpha=0.28\), but the grid wasn’t dense enough to say where the steep part starts and ends. Same move as Day 24’s capacity_mult refinement: 25 log-spaced points zoomed into \([0.05, 0.3]\), at the same t_run = 600 for direct comparability.


Code
alpha_seq_refine <- exp(seq(log(0.05), log(0.3), length.out = 25))
alpha_refine_df  <- run_param_sweep("alpha", alpha_seq_refine)


Unlike capacity_mult’s collapse bifurcation, there’s no natural alive/dead split here. catchable_fraction rises smoothly from near-zero to a plateau, not a bistable jump. So the window is bracketed with two threshold crossings: where the climb clearly starts (under 0.1%) and where it’s clearly finished (over 10%):


Code
find_crossing <- function(df, threshold, value_col = "value",
                          metric_col = "catchable_fraction") {
  df    <- df %>% arrange(.data[[value_col]])
  below <- df %>% filter(.data[[metric_col]] < threshold)  %>% pull(.data[[value_col]])
  above <- df %>% filter(.data[[metric_col]] >= threshold) %>% pull(.data[[value_col]])
  data.frame(
    threshold   = threshold,
    below_last  = if (length(below) > 0) max(below) else NA_real_,
    above_first = if (length(above) > 0) min(above) else NA_real_
  )
}

LOW_THRESHOLD  <- 1e-3
HIGH_THRESHOLD <- 0.10

alpha_crossings <- bind_rows(
  find_crossing(alpha_refine_df %>% filter(is.na(error)), LOW_THRESHOLD)  %>% mutate(edge = "climb starts"),
  find_crossing(alpha_refine_df %>% filter(is.na(error)), HIGH_THRESHOLD) %>% mutate(edge = "climb ends")
)




Code
ggplot(alpha_refine_df %>% filter(is.na(error)), aes(x = value, y = catchable_fraction)) +
  geom_line(color = "#4C72B0", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "#4C72B0", size = 1.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(LOW_THRESHOLD, HIGH_THRESHOLD), linetype = "dotted", color = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_scientific()) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "alpha (assimilation efficiency)", y = "Catchable fraction (biomass at or above w_mat)",
       title = "Refined alpha sweep: pinning down the transition window",
       subtitle = "25 points over [0.05, 0.3] -- dotted = threshold crossings; dashed = anchovy's own alpha = 0.1") +
  theme_minimal()









The steep part of the climb is compressed into a narrow window, \(\alpha \approx 0.105\text{–}0.178\) which is much tighter than Day 25’s coarse “0.057 to 0.28.” The anchovy’s own \(\alpha = 0.1\) sits at \(0.0237\%\) catchable fraction, just below the 0.1% “climb starts” threshold. This confirms Day 25’s “foot of the climb” read with an actual number.

title: Day 26: Closing Day 25’s Loose Ends, and a Delay That Actually Causes a Hopf Bifurcation
section: Is the Gamma = 305.8 Dip Real, or an Under-Settled Transient?
text:
Is the Gamma = 305.8 Dip Real, or an Under-Settled Transient?
Day 25’s 15-point \(\gamma\) sweep found one point breaking monotonicity. This code block reruns that point and its neighbours (located dynamically off the original grid) at increasingly long t_run.


Code
gamma_full_seq   <- exp(seq(log(100), log(5000), length.out = 15))
dip_idx          <- which.min(abs(gamma_full_seq - 305.8))
neighbour_idx    <- unique(pmax(1, pmin(length(gamma_full_seq), c(dip_idx - 1, dip_idx, dip_idx + 1))))
gamma_check_vals <- gamma_full_seq[neighbour_idx]

t_run_check_seq <- c(600, 1200, 2400, 4800)

gamma_dip_check_df <- bind_rows(lapply(t_run_check_seq, function(tr) {
  bind_rows(lapply(gamma_check_vals, function(g) {
    p   <- make_second_order_params_kr(gamma = g, capacity_mult = 10, resource_decrease = 0.001)
    res <- catchable_fraction_at(p, t_max = tr)
    data.frame(gamma = g, t_run = tr, catchable_fraction = res$catchable_fraction)
  }))
}))

dip_persistence <- gamma_dip_check_df %>%
  group_by(t_run) %>%
  arrange(gamma, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  summarise(
    dip_still_present = catchable_fraction[2] < catchable_fraction[1] &
                        catchable_fraction[2] < catchable_fraction[3],
    .groups = "drop"
  )




Code
ggplot(gamma_dip_check_df, aes(x = t_run, y = catchable_fraction, color = factor(round(gamma, 1)))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_scientific()) +
  labs(x = "t_run", y = "Catchable fraction",
       title = "Is the gamma = 305.8 dip real or an under-settled transient?",
       subtitle = "Same point and its two neighbours, rerun at increasing t_run", color = "gamma") +
  theme_minimal()









This isn’t “the dip shrinks and disappears” (critical slowing down) or “the dip holds steady” (a real feature) - it flips non-monotonically, and at t_run = 2400 the ordering of all three points scrambles, not just the middle one. That’s not what a converging transient looks like.
The likely explanation: catchable_fraction_at() reads a single snapshot at the last saved timestep, not an average over a settled window. If the system at this operating point (capacity_mult = 10, resource_decrease = 0.001, the fixed baseline every juvenile-pileup sweep since Day 24 has used) is still gently oscillating rather than sitting at a true fixed point, varying t_max just samples different phases, not different amounts of settling time, which is consistent with Day 23’s refined \([3,10]\) grid finding a reversal from fixed-point to oscillating right around capacity_mult = 10. That noise floor (values bouncing 2–3x between reruns) is negligible next to \(\alpha\)’s 27.5-order-of-magnitude range, but comparable to or larger than \(\gamma\)’s and \(\kappa\)’s entire reported ranges, so those “flat”/“modest effect” Day 25 conclusions may be sampling noise rather than a real parameter effect. Checking directly whether this operating point is actually oscillating is the natural follow-up.

title: Day 26: Closing Day 25’s Loose Ends, and a Delay That Actually Causes a Hopf Bifurcation
section: Confirming the Amplitude Decay for the Conversion-Delay Model
text:
Confirming the Amplitude Decay for the Conversion-Delay Model
Day 25’s time-delay model (delay on the predator’s conversion of intake into biomass) was proven analytically to never support a Hopf bifurcation, but rel_amplitude_P was still climbing with \(\tau\) across the tested range (up to 0.25 at \(\tau=40\)), which the algebra says must eventually decay rather than plateau. Reproducing Day 25’s model first to confirm the base case, then extending t_max well past the original 300:


Code
predator_prey_params_delay <- list(D = 1, a = 1, e = 0.5, m = 0.3, K = 1)

check_hopf_feasibility <- function(parms = predator_prey_params_delay) {
  D <- parms$D; a <- parms$a; e <- parms$e; m <- parms$m; K <- parms$K
  N_star <- m / (e * a)
  P_star <- D * (K - N_star) / (a * N_star)
  alpha  <- D + a * P_star
  beta   <- a * N_star
  gamma  <- e * a * P_star
  data.frame(N_star = N_star, P_star = P_star, alpha = alpha, beta = beta,
             gamma = gamma, beta_gamma = beta * gamma, two_m_alpha = 2 * m * alpha,
             hopf_possible = (beta * gamma) > (2 * m * alpha))
}
hopf_check <- check_hopf_feasibility()

predator_prey_rhs_delay <- function(t, state, parms) {
  N <- max(state[1], 0); P <- max(state[2], 0)
  D <- parms[["D"]]; a <- parms[["a"]]; e <- parms[["e"]]
  m <- parms[["m"]]; K <- parms[["K"]]; tau <- parms[["tau"]]
  N0 <- parms[["N0"]]; P0 <- parms[["P0"]]
  if (t <= tau) { lag_N <- N0; lag_P <- P0
  } else { lag <- lagvalue(t - tau); lag_N <- max(lag[1], 0); lag_P <- max(lag[2], 0) }
  dN <- D * (K - N) - a * N * P
  dP <- e * a * lag_N * lag_P - m * P
  list(c(dN, dP))
}

run_predator_prey_delay_long <- function(tau, t_max_long, state0 = c(N = 1, P = 0.1),
                                         parms = predator_prey_params_delay) {
  parms$tau <- tau; parms$N0 <- state0[["N"]]; parms$P0 <- state0[["P"]]
  as.data.frame(dede(y = state0, times = seq(0, t_max_long, by = 0.1),
                     func = predator_prey_rhs_delay, parms = parms))
}

amplitude_at_cutoff <- function(ts_df, t_max_effective) {
  late <- ts_df[ts_df$time > t_max_effective * 0.6 & ts_df$time <= t_max_effective, ]
  data.frame(t_max = t_max_effective, rel_amplitude_P = (max(late$P) - min(late$P)) / mean(late$P))
}

tau_check_seq   <- c(40, 80)
t_max_check_seq <- c(300, 600, 1200, 2400, 4800, 9600)

ts_long_by_tau <- setNames(
  lapply(tau_check_seq, function(tau) run_predator_prey_delay_long(tau, max(t_max_check_seq))),
  tau_check_seq
)

decay_check_df <- bind_rows(lapply(tau_check_seq, function(tau) {
  ts_long <- ts_long_by_tau[[as.character(tau)]]
  bind_rows(lapply(t_max_check_seq, function(tm) amplitude_at_cutoff(ts_long, tm) %>% mutate(tau = tau)))
}))




Code
ggplot(decay_check_df, aes(x = t_max, y = rel_amplitude_P, color = factor(tau))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_scientific()) +
  labs(x = "t_max", y = "Relative amplitude of P, late window",
       title = "Does rel_amplitude_P decay to ~0 given enough time, or plateau?",
       subtitle = "tau = 40 and 80, re-windowed at longer cutoffs -- analytic prediction: decays to 0",
       color = "tau") +
  theme_minimal()









Both \(\tau\) values decay across 15 orders of magnitude to machine-precision zero, which is clearly not a plateau. An endpoint check (distance from the trajectory’s final \(N,P\) to the analytic equilibrium) confirms it directly: both land within \(3.7\times10^{-15}\) of \((N^*,P^*)\) by t_max=9600. That closes Day 25’s third loose end: the climbing amplitude was an unfinished monotonic relaxation, not a real or growing oscillation, exactly as predicted.

title: Day 26: Closing Day 25’s Loose Ends, and a Delay That Actually Causes a Hopf Bifurcation
section: Why Couldn’t Delay Cause an Instability Here?
text:
Why Couldn’t Delay Cause an Instability Here?
Day 25’s model delays the predator’s conversion of intake into biomass, but leaves the prey’s own self-limitation instantaneous:
\[\begin{aligned}
\frac{dN}{dt} &= D(K - N(t)) - aN(t)P(t) \\
\frac{dP}{dt} &= eaN(t-\tau)P(t-\tau) - mP(t)
\end{aligned}\]
Step 1: Linearise. Substituting \(n,p\sim e^{\lambda t}\) around equilibrium gives the characteristic equation, with \(\alpha=D+aP^*\), \(\beta=aN^*\), \(\gamma=eaP^*\):
\[(\lambda+\alpha)\left(\lambda+m-me^{-\lambda\tau}\right) + \beta\gamma e^{-\lambda\tau} = 0\]
Step 2: Find the Hopf condition. Setting \(\lambda=i\omega\) and matching \(|P(i\omega)|=|Q(i\omega)|\) reduces this to a quadratic in \(u=\omega^2\):
\[u^2 + \alpha^2 u + \beta\gamma\left(2m\alpha - \beta\gamma\right) = 0\]
By Vieta’s formulas, the sum of the roots is \(-\alpha^2\) (always negative), so a positive root exists only if the product, \(\beta\gamma(2m\alpha-\beta\gamma)\), is negative, i.e. \(\beta\gamma>2m\alpha\).
Step 3: Check whether that can ever hold. Substituting and simplifying (using \(eaN^*=m\)):
\[\beta\gamma - 2m\alpha = -amP^* - 2mD\]
Factoring out \(-mD\) (after substituting \(P^*=D(K-N^*)/(aN^*)\)) gives a clean closed form:
\[\beta\gamma - 2m\alpha = -\frac{mD(K+N^*)}{N^*}\]
Every quantity in that bracket is positive, so this can never be positive for any positive \(D,a,e,m,K\). The undelayed prey renewal term \(D\) is a restoring force acting at full strength regardless of \(\tau\), strong enough here to prevent any Hopf bifurcation.
That raised an obvious question: what if the delay sat somewhere else?

title: Day 26: Closing Day 25’s Loose Ends, and a Delay That Actually Causes a Hopf Bifurcation
section: A Model That Does Support a Hopf Bifurcation: Delay the Prey’s Self-Limitation Instead
text:
A Model That Does Support a Hopf Bifurcation: Delay the Prey’s Self-Limitation Instead
Moving the delay onto the prey’s own self-limitation term instead \(\frac{dN}{dt} = D(K - N(t-\tau)) - aN(t)P(t)\) ,predation and conversion now instantaneous, is the classical route to delay-induced instability, the two-species analogue of Hutchinson’s single-species delayed logistic equation.

Working Out the Maths
Step 1: The equilibrium is unchanged: at a constant solution the delayed term equals its instantaneous value, so \(N^*=m/(ea)\), \(P^*=D(K-N^*)/(aN^*)\).
Step 2: Linearise. Writing \(N=N^*+n\), \(P=P^*+p\) and dropping second-order terms:
\[\begin{aligned}
\frac{dn}{dt} &= -\alpha n(t) - \beta p(t) - D n(t-\tau) \\
\frac{dp}{dt} &= \gamma n(t)
\end{aligned}\]
where now \(\alpha=aP^*\) (not \(D+aP^*\), \(D\) now sits on its own as the coefficient of the delayed term), and \(\gamma=eaP^*\) carries no delay.
Step 3: Characteristic equation:
\[\lambda^2 + \alpha\lambda + \beta\gamma + D\lambda e^{-\lambda\tau} = 0\]
At \(\tau=0\) this becomes \(\lambda^2+(\alpha+D)\lambda+\beta\gamma=0\), and \(\alpha+D=aP^*+D\) is exactly the old \(\alpha\) from the conversion-delay model, matching Day 24’s non-delayed result as it must.
Step 4: Matching moduli. Setting \(\lambda=i\omega\) gives a quadratic in \(u=\omega^2\):
\[u^2 + \left(\alpha^2 - D^2 - 2\beta\gamma\right) u + (\beta\gamma)^2 = 0\]
Step 5: Sign test. The product of roots is \((\beta\gamma)^2\), always non-negative as both roots share a sign, and the sum decides which. Requiring both real (discriminant \(\geq0\)) and positive (sum \(>0\)) collapses to one condition:
\[\text{Hopf possible} \iff \alpha < D \iff aP^* < D\]
At this project’s reference parameters (\(D=1,a=1,e=0.5,m=0.3,K=1\to P^*=0.667\)): \(aP^*=0.667<D=1\) the condition holds.


Confirming It Numerically


Code
predator_prey_rhs_selflim <- function(t, state, parms) {
  N <- max(state[1], 0); P <- max(state[2], 0)
  D <- parms[["D"]]; a <- parms[["a"]]; e <- parms[["e"]]
  m <- parms[["m"]]; K <- parms[["K"]]; tau <- parms[["tau"]]; N0 <- parms[["N0"]]
  lag_N <- if (t <= tau) N0 else max(lagvalue(t - tau, 1), 0)
  dN <- D * (K - lag_N) - a * N * P
  dP <- e * a * N * P - m * P
  list(c(dN, dP))
}

check_hopf_feasibility_selflim <- function(parms = predator_prey_params_delay) {
  D <- parms$D; a <- parms$a; e <- parms$e; m <- parms$m; K <- parms$K
  N_star  <- m / (e * a)
  P_star  <- D * (K - N_star) / (a * N_star)
  data.frame(N_star = N_star, P_star = P_star, alpha_s = a * P_star, D = D,
             hopf_possible = (a * P_star) < D)
}

hopf_check_selflim <- check_hopf_feasibility_selflim()
print(hopf_check_selflim)
cat(sprintf(
  paste0(
    "Self-limitation-delay Hopf check: a*P* = %.4f vs D = %.4f -- %s\n",
    "(derived condition: Hopf possible iff a*P* < D; contrast with the conversion-\n",
    "delay model, where the analogous condition could never hold for any parameters)\n"
  ),
  hopf_check_selflim$alpha_s, hopf_check_selflim$D,
  ifelse(hopf_check_selflim$hopf_possible, "HOPF POSSIBLE", "not possible")
))

run_predator_prey_selflim <- function(tau, state0 = c(N = 1, P = 0.1), t_max = 300,
                                      parms = predator_prey_params_delay) {
  parms$tau <- tau
  parms$N0  <- state0[["N"]]
  out  <- as.data.frame(dede(y = state0, times = seq(0, t_max, by = 0.1),
                             func = predator_prey_rhs_selflim, parms = parms))
  late <- out[out$time > t_max * 0.6, ]
  data.frame(tau = tau, max_N = max(late$N), min_N = min(late$N),
             max_P = max(late$P), min_P = min(late$P),
             rel_amplitude_P = (max(late$P) - min(late$P)) / mean(late$P))
}

tau_seq_selflim  <- c(0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.2, 2.4, 2.6, 2.8, 3, 4, 5, 7, 10, 15, 20)
selflim_sweep_df <- bind_rows(lapply(tau_seq_selflim, run_predator_prey_selflim))




Code
ggplot(selflim_sweep_df, aes(x = tau, y = rel_amplitude_P)) +
  geom_line(color = "#C44E52", linewidth = 1) + geom_point(color = "#C44E52", size = 1.5) +
  labs(x = "tau (delay in prey self-limitation)", y = "Relative amplitude of P (settled)",
       title = "Delaying the prey's self-limitation: a genuine Hopf bifurcation appears",
       subtitle = "Same D=1,a=1,e=0.5,m=0.3,K=1 -- analytic condition a*P*=0.667 < D=1 predicts yes") +
  theme_minimal()









The onset is sharp, between \(\tau=2.2\) (amplitude still \(0.02\)) and \(\tau=2.4\) (amplitude jumps to \(0.66\)), landing almost exactly on the \(\tau\approx2.4\) hand estimate. A persistence check at \(\tau=10\) across t_max = 300, 1500, 3000 gives rel_amplitude_P = 3.06, 2.95, 2.92, which is steady, confirming a sustained limit cycle rather than an unsettled transient.
But there’s a real problem. The min_N column shows \(N\) going negative right at onset and dramatically more negative as \(\tau\) grows, down to \(-15.5\) by \(\tau=20\). This toy model has no saturating mechanism to cap the oscillation, so past the bifurcation the “population” swings through biologically nonsensical negative values. The Hopf bifurcation itself is real but the model can’t be trusted as a faithful biological picture much beyond its onset.

title: Day 26: Closing Day 25’s Loose Ends, and a Delay That Actually Causes a Hopf Bifurcation
section: A Third Variant: Delay Only the Predator’s Intake, Not Its Own Growth
text:
A Third Variant: Delay Only the Predator’s Intake, Not Its Own Growth
A natural intermediate case: what if only \(P(t-\tau)\) is delayed inside the predator’s growth term, while \(N(t)\) there stays instantaneous?
\[\begin{aligned}
\frac{dN}{dt} &= D(K - N(t)) - aN(t)P(t) \\
\frac{dP}{dt} &= eaN(t)P(t-\tau) - mP(t)
\end{aligned}\]

The Maths
Step 1: Linearise. \(\frac{dp}{dt}=\gamma n(t)+mp(t-\tau)-mp(t)\): the \(n\) term loses its delay, but \(mp(t-\tau)\) survives (it comes from \(N^*\), a constant, multiplying the still-delayed \(P(t-\tau)\)).
Step 2: Characteristic equation, with \(\alpha=D+aP^*\) as in the original model, but now \(\beta\gamma\) carries no \(e^{-\lambda\tau}\) factor:
\[(\lambda+\alpha)\left(\lambda+m-me^{-\lambda\tau}\right) + \beta\gamma = 0\]
Step 3: Match moduli:
\[u^2 + \left(\alpha^2 - 2\beta\gamma\right) u + \beta\gamma\left(2\alpha m + \beta\gamma\right) = 0\]
The product of roots, \(\beta\gamma(2\alpha m+\beta\gamma)\), is always positive ; same situation as the self-limitation model, so both roots share a sign and the sum decides which:
\[\text{Hopf possible} \iff 2\beta\gamma > \alpha^2\]
Step 4: Reduce to a threshold on D. Writing \(P^*=DC\) (\(C=(K-N^*)/(aN^*)\), independent of \(D\)) reduces this to a genuine threshold on \(D\), unlike the original model’s absolute impossibility or the self-limitation model’s condition (which held outright at the reference parameters):
\[D < \frac{2amC}{(1+aC)^2}\]
At the reference parameters (\(N^*=0.6, C=0.667\)), that threshold works out to \(\sim0.144\). \(D=1\) is far above it, so no Hopf is predicted there. This is tested below alongside \(D=0.1\), comfortably under the threshold.


Confirming It Numerically


Code
predator_prey_rhs_pdelay <- function(t, state, parms) {
  N <- max(state[1], 0); P <- max(state[2], 0)
  D <- parms[["D"]]; a <- parms[["a"]]; e <- parms[["e"]]
  m <- parms[["m"]]; K <- parms[["K"]]; tau <- parms[["tau"]]; P0 <- parms[["P0"]]
  lag_P <- if (t <= tau) P0 else max(lagvalue(t - tau, 2), 0)
  dN <- D * (K - N) - a * N * P
  dP <- e * a * N * lag_P - m * P
  list(c(dN, dP))
}

run_predator_prey_pdelay <- function(tau, state0 = c(N = 1, P = 0.1), t_max = 300,
                                     parms = predator_prey_params_delay) {
  parms$tau <- tau; parms$P0 <- state0[["P"]]
  out  <- as.data.frame(dede(y = state0, times = seq(0, t_max, by = 0.1),
                             func = predator_prey_rhs_pdelay, parms = parms))
  late <- out[out$time > t_max * 0.6, ]
  data.frame(tau = tau, max_N = max(late$N), min_N = min(late$N),
             max_P = max(late$P), min_P = min(late$P),
             rel_amplitude_P = (max(late$P) - min(late$P)) / mean(late$P))
}

params_small_D  <- modifyList(predator_prey_params_delay, list(D = 0.1))
tau_seq_pdelay  <- c(0, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 15, 20)

pdelay_sweep_refD   <- bind_rows(lapply(tau_seq_pdelay, run_predator_prey_pdelay)) %>%
  mutate(D_label = "D = 1 (above threshold)")
pdelay_sweep_smallD <- bind_rows(lapply(tau_seq_pdelay, run_predator_prey_pdelay,
                                        parms = params_small_D)) %>%
  mutate(D_label = "D = 0.1 (below threshold)")
pdelay_sweep_df <- bind_rows(pdelay_sweep_refD, pdelay_sweep_smallD)




Code
ggplot(pdelay_sweep_df, aes(x = tau, y = rel_amplitude_P, color = D_label)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  labs(x = "tau (delay in P(t-tau) term only, N instantaneous)", y = "Relative amplitude of P",
       title = "Delaying only P inside the intake term: a threshold on D, not an absolute block",
       subtitle = "Derived threshold D < 0.144 -- tested on both sides", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()









At \(D=1\) (above threshold), rel_amplitude_P climbs smoothly from \(1.8\times10^{-10}\) to \(0.145\) by \(\tau=20\), the same non-Hopf shape as the original conversion-delay model. At \(D=0.1\) (below threshold, Hopf predicted), the climb is smaller and equally gradual, reaching only \(0.033\) by \(\tau=20\), with no sharp transition visible.
A persistence check at \(D=0.1,\tau=10\) settles it: rel_amplitude_P at t_max = 300, 1500, 3000 is \(0.00164\to9.18\times10^{-14}\to1.04\times10^{-15}\) .This is collapsing toward machine-precision zero, the same “critical slowing down” signature as earlier, clearly not a sustained cycle. So even though \(D=0.1\) satisfies the derived existence condition, \(\tau=10\) isn’t past this variant’s real onset,so the true critical \(\tau\) sits beyond 20, not yet located. The threshold on \(D\) is correctly derived, but pinning down where the bifurcation occurs for a given \(D\) needs a wider sweep.

title: Day 26: Closing Day 25’s Loose Ends, and a Delay That Actually Causes a Hopf Bifurcation
section: What This All Adds Up To
text:
What This All Adds Up To
Three loose ends from Day 25 closed cleanly: \(\alpha\)’s transition window is now a precise \((0.105, 0.178)\) bracket, the \(\tau=40/80\) amplitude climb is confirmed to decay to machine-precision zero, and the \(\gamma=305.8\) dip turned out to be neither “real” nor “transient” - its non-monotonic flipping points at an unsettled oscillation at the sweep’s own operating point, casting doubt on \(\gamma\) and \(\kappa\)’s “modest”/“flat” Day 25 conclusions.
The deeper result is about where a delay sits, not whether delay can destabilise a system in general. Delaying the predator’s conversion (Day 25’s model) can never produce a Hopf bifurcation, proven by factoring the destabilising quantity into \(-mD(K+N^*)/N^*\), a bare positive \(D\) multiplying an unconditionally negative bracket. Delaying the prey’s self-limitation instead does produce one, confirmed both analytically (\(aP^*<D\)) and by simulation landing the onset almost exactly where predicted. Though the limit cycle’s amplitude grows unboundedly past onset, driving prey biomass negative, a limitation of this toy model rather than the underlying mechanism. A third, intermediate variant (delay only the predator’s intake) derives a genuine threshold on \(D\) rather than an absolute block, but the tested \(\tau\) wasn’t far enough to actually see it.

title: Day 26: Closing Day 25’s Loose Ends, and a Delay That Actually Causes a Hopf Bifurcation
text:
What’s Next

Find the actual critical tau for the P-only-delay variant at D=0.1: Extend tau_seq_pdelay well past 20 (e.g. up to 40–60) and rerun the persistence check at each candidate onset to locate where rel_amplitude_P stops decaying and starts holding steady.
Characterise how far past onset the self-limitation model’s amplitude stays biologically sensible: min_N is already negative at \(\tau=2.4\) (barely past onset) and reaches \(-15.5\) by \(\tau=20\). It’s worth finding the \(\tau\) range where \(N\) stays non-negative, and considering whether a saturating term (a proper functional response, rather than mass-action) would cap the amplitude the way it should.
Check directly whether capacity_mult=10, resource_decrease=0.001 is actually oscillating: Rather than reading single-timestep snapshots at different t_max. A real time series at this exact operating point would settle whether the gamma/kappa sweep’s noise floor is genuine unsettled oscillation or something else.
Rerun gamma and kappa’s isolation sweeps: Do this with a windowed-average read (the same “late window” convention used throughout the delay-model work) instead of a single final-timestep snapshot, to check whether their “modest”/“flat” Day 25 conclusions survive averaging out whatever phase-sampling noise today’s gamma recheck exposed.
Carry these toy-model findings back over to the actual size-spectrum (mizer) model: Everything above was worked out on the abstract two-species predator-prey system, not on the anchovy model itself - the natural next step is checking which of these delay mechanisms, if any, has a real biological analogue in the size-spectrum setting, and whether it could plausibly help explain the juvenile-pileup dynamics this project has been tracking since Day 6.

title: Day 28: Carrying the Hopf Hunt to the Real Cod Model - Stable Everywhere Tested, and Adults Out-Eat Juveniles
section: A New Tool: getStability() from mizer PR #452
text:
A New Tool: getStability() from mizer PR #452
Everything in Days 25-27 relied on writing down a characteristic equation by hand and finding where its roots cross the imaginary axis. That doesn’t scale to the real cod model - there’s no closed form for a discretised size-spectrum PDE. getStability() (installed via pak::pkg_install("sizespectrum/mizer#452")) does the equivalent numerically: it linearises mizer’s actual one-step-ahead map \(G(N) = A(N)^{-1}S(N)\) at a steady state by direct numerical differentiation, and returns the eigenvalues of that linearisation. The steady state is stable iff the spectral radius (largest eigenvalue modulus) is below 1 and critically, a Hopf bifurcation specifically requires the destabilising eigenvalue to be complex, not real. A real eigenvalue crossing 1 is a different, non-oscillatory kind of instability (collapse/extinction-type), so spectral_radius >= 1 alone can’t tell the two apart – exactly the same “sum condition isn’t sufficient, check the discriminant” lesson from Day 27’s P-delay correction, just with eigenvalue type standing in for the discriminant this time.
Two checks against results already known to work, before trusting this on cod_params: a sanity check against mizer’s own built-in NS_params (matching the PR’s own test suite claim that it comes back stable), and a reduced-vs-full agreement check (include_resource = FALSE, the quasi-static approximation, vs TRUE, perturbing the resource explicitly too) on cod_params itself. Both passed before any of the results below were trusted.


Code
library(mizer)
library(mizerExperimental)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(future)
library(future.apply)
plan(multisession)

# Read-only: cod_params.rds is never written back to. Every perturbation
# below goes through resource_limitation(), which returns a NEW params
# object -- this binding itself is never reassigned.
cod_params <- readRDS("../cod_params.rds")

# balance=FALSE is required, not just stylistic: setResource() errors
# outright if resource_rate is given while balance resolves to TRUE (its
# default for resource_semichemostat dynamics), since with balance=TRUE the
# other resource parameter is always computed FOR you to preserve the
# current production=consumption steady state -- exactly the perturbation
# this sweep is trying to introduce.
resource_limitation <- function(params, resource_decrease) {
  new_rate <- getResourceRate(params) * resource_decrease
  setResource(params, resource_rate = new_rate, balance = FALSE)
}

title: Day 28: Carrying the Hopf Hunt to the Real Cod Model - Stable Everywhere Tested, and Adults Out-Eat Juveniles
section: Does Slowing the Resource’s Renewal Destabilise Cod? A Direct Simulation Says No
text:
Does Slowing the Resource’s Renewal Destabilise Cod? A Direct Simulation Says No
Same “windowed read after a settling period” convention as every sweep since Day 20, but read as a genuine bifurcation diagram: every local max/min of biomass in the late window of a simulation becomes its own point, so a fixed point shows as a single dot and a limit cycle would show as two branches.


Code
make_limit_cycle_sim <- function(params, t_total = 600, effort = 0) {
  params@initial_n_pp[] <- params@cc_pp * 0.1
  sim_init <- project(params, t_max = 10, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                      progress_bar = FALSE, effort = 0, method = "predictor-corrector")
  idx  <- params@w >= 10 & params@w <= 100
  last <- dim(sim_init@n)[1]
  sim_init@n[last, , idx] <- sim_init@n[last, , idx] / 1e3
  project(sim_init, t_max = t_total - 10, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
          progress_bar = FALSE, effort = effort, method = "predictor-corrector")
}

resource_decrease_seq <- exp(seq(log(0.001), log(1), length.out = 12))
# ... resource_bifurcation_point() perturbs the resource rate, runs the
# above, and returns every late-window local extremum -- full definition in
# 28_experiments.R.


All twelve tested points, spanning resource_decrease from 0.001 to 1, came back "settled". Not one point produced a min/max branch split. Biomass scales up smoothly by three orders of magnitude as the resource renews faster (more food, more standing biomass, no surprise there), but nothing about that relationship destabilises the fixed point anywhere in the tested range.

title: Day 28: Carrying the Hopf Hunt to the Real Cod Model - Stable Everywhere Tested, and Adults Out-Eat Juveniles
section: Predicted vs Simulated: They Agree, But the Prediction Is Suspiciously Flat
text:
Predicted vs Simulated: They Agree, But the Prediction Is Suspiciously Flat
Rerunning the same resource_decrease grid through steadyNewton(..., stability = TRUE) instead of a full simulation:


Code
stability_sweep_point <- function(resource_decrease, params = cod_params) {
  p        <- resource_limitation(params, resource_decrease)
  p_steady <- steadyNewton(p, stability = TRUE)
  attr(p_steady, "stability")
}


stable = TRUE at all twelve points, matching the simulation exactly. But look at spectral_radius: it’s 0.508413331747... at every single point, agreeing to eleven decimal places regardless of whether the resource renews at 0.1% or 100% of its default rate. That’s not “stable across a wide range” so much as “completely insensitive to this parameter” - under the quasi-static resource approximation (include_resource = FALSE, the default), the fish dynamics’ own linearisation apparently doesn’t see resource_decrease moving at all. hopf_period bounces around unpredictably (64 to 186, no visible pattern) while spectral_radius stays frozen - consistent with it tracking whatever complex eigenvalue happens to sit nearest the unit circle (per its definition) rather than the actual dominant, real-valued eigenvalue setting spectral_radius i.e. noise from a non-dominant pair, not a real signal. Worth checking the include_resource = TRUE mode across this same sweep (only checked at a single point so far) before trusting that this parameter is genuinely irrelevant to cod’s stability rather than an artifact of the reduced approximation.

title: Day 28: Carrying the Hopf Hunt to the Real Cod Model - Stable Everywhere Tested, and Adults Out-Eat Juveniles
section: Widening the Search: A 2D Grid Over Resource Rate and Capacity
text:
Widening the Search: A 2D Grid Over Resource Rate and Capacity
Days 22-24 found that raising capacity_mult (the resource’s carrying capacity) past a threshold around 7 destabilised the anchovy model into oscillation - a paradox-of-enrichment signature, though never confirmed there as specifically Hopf (Day 27 only later showed the operating point at capacity_mult=10 was in fact flat, not oscillating, muddying that finding further). Worth checking directly whether cod shows anything similar over the same kind of range, and whether it’s actually Hopf-type if it does.


Code
resource_limitation_2d <- function(params, resource_decrease, capacity_mult) {
  new_rate     <- getResourceRate(params) * resource_decrease
  new_capacity <- getResourceCapacity(params) * capacity_mult
  setResource(params, resource_rate = new_rate, resource_capacity = new_capacity, balance = FALSE)
}

check_hopf_grid_point <- function(resource_decrease, capacity_mult, params = cod_params, effort = 0) {
  p        <- resource_limitation_2d(params, resource_decrease, capacity_mult)
  p_steady <- steadyNewton(p, effort = effort, stability = TRUE)
  stab     <- attr(p_steady, "stability")
  dominant <- stab$eigenvalues[1]
  is_complex <- abs(Im(dominant)) > 1e-8
  data.frame(spectral_radius = stab$spectral_radius, stable = stab$stable,
             bifurcation_type = if (stab$stable) "stable" else if (is_complex) "hopf" else "non-oscillatory")
}

capacity_mult_seq <- exp(seq(log(1), log(20), length.out = 10))


resource_decrease (12 points, 0.001-1) crossed with capacity_mult (10 points, 1-20, the same direction Days 22-24 found destabilisation in) gives 120 grid points. All 120 came back "stable". spectral_radius ranges from 0.761250163324095 to 0.7612501633240114 across the entire grid - again essentially frozen, this time under both parameters simultaneously, not just one. Extending capacity_mult up to 20 - comfortably past where the anchovy model destabilised - didn’t move cod off its fixed point at all. Whatever mechanism drove the anchovy paradox-of-enrichment finding, cod doesn’t reproduce it over this range, at least not through this pair of levers.
Each grid point costs a steadyNewton() convergence plus a full numerical-differentiation Jacobian (n_active = 200 confirmed from the sweep above, so getStability() runs on the order of 400 extra full solver evaluations per point, centred differences). Flattened to one job of 120 independent points and dispatched across future_lapply() workers (plan(multisession)) rather than run sequentially, once this turned out to be the actual bottleneck rather than the Newton solve itself.

title: Day 28: Carrying the Hopf Hunt to the Real Cod Model - Stable Everywhere Tested, and Adults Out-Eat Juveniles
section: Checking the Juvenile-vs-Adult Mechanism (de Roos & Persson)
text:
Checking the Juvenile-vs-Adult Mechanism (de Roos & Persson)
Both the direct simulation and getStability() agreeing on “stable everywhere tested” raises the obvious next question: is the resource-rate/capacity axis even the right place to be looking? de Roos & Persson (2003), added to Further_Reading.md this session alongside several delayed-chemostat Hopf papers. This should help give a concrete, checkable criterion for a completely different candidate mechanism: whichever life stage has the higher mass-specific (per body mass) feeding rate determines whether a population shows juvenile-driven or adult-driven cycles. This is directly testable on cod_params via mizer’s own encounter/feeding-level machinery:


Code
E <- getEncounter(cod_params)      # encounter rate, g/year
f <- getFeedingLevel(cod_params)   # feeding level (satiation), 0-1

per_capita_rate    <- E * (1 - f)          # realised per-capita intake, g/year
mass_specific_rate <- per_capita_rate / cod_params@w

w     <- cod_params@w
w_mat <- cod_params@species_params$w_mat

juvenile_rate <- mass_specific_rate[1, w < w_mat]
adult_rate    <- mass_specific_rate[1, w >= w_mat]


The first attempt at the comparison, juvenile_rate - adult_rate, printed a long named vector with an obviously wrong shape: values climbing steadily more negative, then jumping back up near where they started, repeating that pattern several times, alongside an R warning about mismatched lengths. The cause: juvenile_rate and adult_rate are per-weight-bin vectors with different numbers of elements (the weight grid doesn’t split evenly at w_mat), so subtracting them directly doesn’t compare juveniles to adults at all - R silently recycles the shorter vector to match the longer one’s length, and the “resets” in the output are just where the recycled vector wraps back to its own start. Not a finding, a bug. Summarising each side to a single number before comparing fixes it:
mean(juvenile_rate) - mean(adult_rate)



params
mean(juvenile) - mean(adult)




Day 22’s (anchovy) params
-321.2177


cod_params
-14194.29



Both negative: in both parameter sets, adults have the higher mass-specific feeding rate, not juveniles - the signature de Roos & Persson associate with adult-driven cycles, not juvenile-driven ones. That’s a real caveat worth sitting with: the mechanism this whole project has informally called “juvenile pileup” since Day 6 doesn’t show the juvenile-driven signature this specific criterion checks for, in either species’ own calibrated parameters. It doesn’t rule out a juvenile-pileup-style bottleneck existing for some other reason (this is one specific mechanism from one specific paper, not an exhaustive test), but it’s evidence against this particular explanation for it.
The two numbers also aren’t remotely the same scale - cod’s imbalance is about 44x starker than anchovy’s, even after dividing by body weight to get a mass-specific rate. Worth being cautious about reading too much into that gap directly, since it could reflect a genuine biological difference between the species, or just a difference in how each parameter set’s intake-rate scaling was calibrated, but I have not yet checked which.

title: Day 28: Carrying the Hopf Hunt to the Real Cod Model - Stable Everywhere Tested, and Adults Out-Eat Juveniles
text:
What’s Next

Check whether the ~44x gap in imbalance between the two is a real biological difference or a calibration artifact.
Actually run the fishing-effort grid (effort = 0.5) and compare its 120-point classification against the unfished grid computed today.
Check include_resource = TRUE across the full resource_decrease sweep, not just at one point, to see whether spectral_radius’s near-total insensitivity to resource_decrease survives dropping the quasi-static resource assumption, or whether that’s an artifact of the reduced mode specifically.
Read the newly-added chemostat/Hopf papers (Further_Reading.md #21-26): with this session’s null result in mind - particularly Toth (2008), whose age-structured-predator-in-a-chemostat model found that age structure alone can trigger a Hopf bifurcation, but only in some dilution-rate regimes and not others. Worth checking whether cod’s parameters simply sit outside the regime where that mechanism would show up, rather than concluding the mechanism doesn’t apply at all.
Widen the grid itself: Both swept parameters topped out at values chosen to match the anchovy work’s own range (capacity_mult up to 20, mirroring Days 22-24). Cod’s own parameters may need a wider or differently-centred range before any instability shows up, if one exists at all.

title: Day 30: Cod Oscillates After All - Just Far Outside Every Grid Tested So Far.
text:
Day 29 closed with three open threads on cod: investigate the small, likely-transient hot spot in cod’s “bottom left” corner properly; introduce fishing mortality against yield; and sweep cod’s lambda, which every anchovy-template build in this project fixes at 2.05 by convention without ever checking whether cod’s own value matters. Today runs the lambda sweep, widens the corner investigation, adds a much coarser but much wider reconnaissance scan, starts a sweep of mizer’s own q parameter, and - along the way - finds a second bug in the metric Day 29 used to call cod and anchovy juvenile- vs adult-driven.

classify_perturbed_run <- function(sim, window_frac = 0.4) {
  bm    <- rowSums(getBiomass(sim))
  times <- as.numeric(names(bm))
  late  <- bm[times >= max(times) * (1 - window_frac)]
  rel_amplitude <- (max(late) - min(late)) / mean(late)
  data.frame(rel_amplitude = rel_amplitude,
             perturbed_verdict = if (rel_amplitude > 1e-6) "oscillating" else "settled",
             error = NA_character_)
}

Same self-contained convention as every script since Day 20: redefined here rather than sourced from 29_experiments.R.

title: Day 30: Cod Oscillates After All - Just Far Outside Every Grid Tested So Far.
section: Sweeping Cod’s lambda and the Wrong Mental Model Behind It
text:
Sweeping Cod’s lambda and the Wrong Mental Model Behind It
The starting idea for today was to reach de Roos & Persson’s oscillatory territory without touching mizer’s own q (the search-volume exponent) directly. mizer’s classic scaling framework ties together the growth-rate exponent, the resource spectrum’s slope, and the search-volume exponent through an identity of the rough shape n = 2 + lambda - q: change lambda, and , so the reasoning went, you’ve effectively moved along the same axis q would, without needing to touch q itself.
That was the wrong mentality. The identity only holds when the rest of the calibration is set up the way the classic scaling derivation assumes it - a single self-similar power-law spectrum, with every other exponent held at the value the identity expects. lambda doesn’t enter this project’s own code that way at all: every build in this project sets kappa from lambda through a completely separate, ad hoc empirical formula (kappa <- a0 * exp(-6.9 * (lambda - 1))), not through the scaling identity. Moving lambda here shifts the background resource spectrum’s overall scale and slope through that formula, which isn’t the same lever the n = 2 + lambda - q identity describes moving. The lambda sweep below still found something real, but it wasn’t a proxy for a q sweep, and the two shouldn’t be read as interchangeable evidence for the same mechanism, which is exactly why q gets swept directly and separately further down.


Code
cod_sp    <- cod_params@species_params
cod_gamma <- unname(cod_sp$gamma[1])
cod_alpha <- unname(cod_sp$alpha[1])
cod_ks    <- unname(cod_sp$ks[1])
cod_w_max <- unname(cod_sp$w_max[1])
cod_w_mat <- unname(cod_sp$w_mat[1])
cod_w_min <- unname(min(cod_params@w))

lambda_seq <- seq(1.95, 2.15, by = 0.05)

make_cod_with_lambda <- function(lambda, resource_decrease, capacity_mult,
                                 second_order = TRUE, ext_diff = 0.00) {
  a0    <- 100
  kappa <- a0 * exp(-6.9 * (lambda - 1))  # same formula every anchovy build uses
  no_w  <- round(log(cod_w_max / cod_w_min) / 0.1)

  params <- newSingleSpeciesParams(
    species_name = sprintf("cod_lambda_%.2f", lambda),
    w_min = cod_w_min, w_max = cod_w_max, w_mat = cod_w_mat,
    no_w = no_w, lambda = lambda, kappa = kappa,
    alpha = cod_alpha, gamma = cod_gamma, ks = cod_ks
  )
  given_species_params(params)$D_ext <- ext_diff
  params <- setBevertonHolt(params)

  default_capacity <- getResourceCapacity(params)
  r  <- getResourceRate(params) * resource_decrease
  cc <- default_capacity * capacity_mult
  params <- setResource(params, resource_rate = r, resource_capacity = cc,
                        resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat", balance = FALSE)
  if (second_order) second_order_w(params) <- c(flux = "centred", bin_average = TRUE)
  params
}

# Reproduces cod's OWN gamma/alpha/ks/w_max/w_mat, not cod_params' full
# calibration (mortality/erepro/R_max untouched) -- same caveat as Day 29
# Section 3's body=cod/rates=cod hybrid.
make_build_cod_lambda <- function(lambda) {
  function(resource_decrease, capacity_mult) make_cod_with_lambda(lambda, resource_decrease, capacity_mult)
}

resource_decrease_seq <- exp(seq(log(0.001), log(1), length.out = 12))
capacity_mult_seq     <- exp(seq(log(1), log(20), length.out = 10))
lambda_grid_params    <- expand.grid(resource_decrease = resource_decrease_seq, capacity_mult = capacity_mult_seq)

# ... perturbed_grid_point()/perturbed_grid_generic() at every
# (resource_decrease, capacity_mult) combo, once per lambda -- same
# pattern as Day 29 Section 9's perturbed_grid_generic(), just parameterised
# over lambda instead of species.



A sharp threshold sits between lambda=2.00 and lambda=2.05 - every prior test of cod-shaped traits in this project (native cod_params across the full grid, the body/rates factorial, capacity_mult extended to 500x, reproduction-level and selective-fishing sweeps) came back completely null, and this is the first lever that actually flips cod into oscillation. It isn’t scattered either: at lambda=1.95 and 2.00, the oscillating points form complete horizontal bands at capacity_mult >= ~10, independent of resource_decrease ,which is the same signature as anchovy’s paradox-of-enrichment collapse from Days 22-24, and max rel_amplitude decreases monotonically as lambda rises from 1.95 to 2.15, so this reads like a continuous approach to a bifurcation rather than a coincidence at one value.However, if you look at the scales, you can see that isn’t the case - the “oscillations” are too small to be something noteworthy, especially if you compare it against the mean biomass.

title: Day 30: Cod Oscillates After All - Just Far Outside Every Grid Tested So Far.
section: A Much Wider, Much Coarser Scan – and Cod Really Does Oscillate
text:
A Much Wider, Much Coarser Scan – and Cod Really Does Oscillate
Every grid this project has used since Day 24 stays inside resource_decrease 1e-3 to 1 and capacity_mult 1 to 20 (or 500 at the very widest). Before refining that window any further, today ran one deliberately coarse (8x6=48 point) reconnaissance pass on native cod_params, no lambda/q substitution, the real, fully-calibrated object, across resource_decrease from 1e-7 to 1 and capacity_mult from 1e-3 (an actively shrunk carrying capacity, never tested before) to 1e2.


Code
broad_resource_decrease_seq <- exp(seq(log(1e-7), log(1), length.out = 8))
broad_capacity_mult_seq     <- exp(seq(log(1e-3), log(1e2), length.out = 6))
broad_grid_params <- expand.grid(resource_decrease = broad_resource_decrease_seq,
                                 capacity_mult = broad_capacity_mult_seq)

# At resource_decrease=1e-7 the resource barely renews -- population
# collapse (biomass -> 0) is a real outcome, not just oscillation, and
# rel_amplitude = (max-min)/mean blows up to NaN/Inf under that condition
# (0/0). Each point checks final biomass against a collapse floor
# (1e-6x the run's own starting biomass) and reports "collapsed" as its
# own category rather than letting it masquerade as "oscillating".
broad_scan_point <- function(build_fn, resource_decrease, capacity_mult, t_total = 600) {
  p     <- build_fn(resource_decrease, capacity_mult)
  sim   <- make_limit_cycle_sim(p, t_total = t_total)
  bm    <- rowSums(getBiomass(sim))
  times <- as.numeric(names(bm))
  late  <- bm[times >= max(times) * 0.6]
  mean_late_biomass <- mean(late)
  collapsed <- mean_late_biomass < bm[1] * 1e-6
  rel_amplitude <- if (collapsed) NA_real_ else (max(late) - min(late)) / mean_late_biomass
  data.frame(resource_decrease = resource_decrease, capacity_mult = capacity_mult,
             rel_amplitude = rel_amplitude,
             perturbed_verdict = if (collapsed) "collapsed" else if (rel_amplitude > 1e-6) "oscillating" else "settled")
}




Of the 48 points: 24 collapsed, 17 settled, 7 oscillating. The pattern is clean and worth reading as three distinct regions rather than noise:

capacity_mult <= 0.1 (below cod’s native baseline): total collapse. All 24 points across every resource_decrease tested go extinct (mean late-window biomass under a millionth of the starting biomass) – every grid before today only ever multiplied capacity_mult up; nobody had checked what happens shrinking it.
capacity_mult=1 (cod’s own reference capacity), extreme resource starvation: real, substantial oscillation. At resource_decrease from 1e-7 to 1e-4, rel_amplitude runs 0.041, 0.004, 0.00047, 0.00004 – decaying smoothly across four orders of magnitude as starvation eases, settling only once resource_decrease >= 0.001. 0.041 is a genuinely large number by this project’s own scale: two orders of magnitude past the 1e-6 oscillating threshold, and far bigger than anything the fine 12x10 grids (max ~9e-7 for native cod) ever found – because none of them ever tested resource_decrease below 1e-3.
capacity_mult=10 and 100: oscillation retreats to only the very lowest resource_decrease tested, rel_amplitude up to 2.0e-6 and 2.3e-5 respectively at resource_decrease=1e-7, settled everywhere else.

The point specifically checked afterward, resource_decrease=1e-6, capacity_mult=100, lands exactly on this grid (it’s a clean decade point) at rel_amplitude=1.62e-6, just over the oscillating threshold.I ran it for a bit longer, using the final state to feed into a new sim and it ended up going to extinction.

title: Day 30: Cod Oscillates After All - Just Far Outside Every Grid Tested So Far.
text:
Sweeping Cod’s Native q
Section “Sweeping Cod’s lambda” above explains why a lambda sweep isn’t a substitute for actually moving mizer’s own q (the search-volume exponent, SearchVolume = gamma * w^q) – so today also sets up sweeping q directly. Unlike the lambda sweep, q is a genuine column on the real, fully-calibrated cod_params object, so this applies straight to it via given_species_params() – no newSingleSpeciesParams() reconstruction, no partial-calibration caveat.


Code
native_cod_q <- unname(cod_params@species_params$q[1])

# given_species_params() has been a silent no-op before in this exact
# project -- D_ext gets attached but never actually consumed without a
# follow-up setExtDiffusion() call (still unresolved since Day 20), and
# Day 29 separately found capacity_mult sitting unused in an early
# make_anchovy_params() draft. q feeds into SearchVolume, which mizer may
# cache at construction time rather than recompute live -- so before
# trusting a whole grid built on this, check directly whether
# search_vol/getEncounter() actually move when q changes.
q_probe_base <- cod_params
q_probe_low  <- cod_params
given_species_params(q_probe_low)$q <- native_cod_q - 0.3

search_vol_changed <- !isTRUE(all.equal(q_probe_base@search_vol, q_probe_low@search_vol))
encounter_changed  <- !isTRUE(all.equal(getEncounter(q_probe_base), getEncounter(q_probe_low)))

make_build_cod_q <- function(q_value) {
  function(resource_decrease, capacity_mult) {
    p <- cod_params
    given_species_params(p)$q <- q_value
    resource_limitation_2d_cod(p, resource_decrease, capacity_mult)
  }
}

# Centred on cod's own fitted q, +/- 0.3 in steps of 0.1 -- same
# "bracket the native value" convention as the lambda sweep, reusing the
# exact same resource_decrease x capacity_mult grid.
q_seq <- round(native_cod_q + seq(-0.3, 0.3, by = 0.1), 4)


This grid (7 q values x 120 points) hasn’t finished running yet, so there’s no heatmap to show today – the code and the propagation safety-check are written and queued, and results land in day30_cod_q_grid.csv/day30_cod_q_heatmap.png once it does.

title: Day 30: Cod Oscillates After All - Just Far Outside Every Grid Tested So Far.
section: What This All Adds Up To
text:
What This All Adds Up To
The headline isn’t the lambda sweep, even though it found a real threshold but it’s that cod can oscillate, just nowhere any grid before today had looked: resource_decrease down at 1e-7 to 1e-4, at cod’s own native capacity_mult. Every previous “cod is stable everywhere” verdict was true only within the window every grid since Day 24 happened to test, not true of cod’s model as a whole. That said, the oscillations themselves are real but small. rel_amplitude=0.041 at the largest is a genuine two-order-of-magnitude jump past the 1e-6 threshold this project uses to call something “oscillating” at all, but set against cod’s actual standing biomass it’s a ripple, not a swing: nowhere near the kind of boom-bust cycle that would threaten the population on its own. The more consequential finding sits right next to it. Shrinking capacity_mult below baseline doesn’t produce a milder version of the same story. Instead, it collapses the population outright, a qualitatively different failure mode neither getStability() nor the earlier perturbed-amplitude grids were built to distinguish from oscillation until today’s explicit collapse check. And underneath all of it, the metric this project has used since Day 28 to call cod and anchovy juvenile- or adult-driven had a second, independent bug the whole time. It was caught only because today went back and actually checked whether mean() was the right way to average across mizer’s own unequal-width bins.

title: Day 30: Cod Oscillates After All - Just Far Outside Every Grid Tested So Far.
text:
What’s Next

Try to find some other parameters that cause oscillations.
Finish the q sweep and the corrected competitiveness metric: Both are written and queued; today only has the methodology and the direction, not final numbers.
Understand the capacity_mult < 1 collapse boundary: Is 24/24 total collapse a real ecological result, or an artifact of the perturbation kick (resource to 10% of capacity, a size-class slice to 1/1000) being disproportionately large once capacity_mult itself has already shrunk the baseline it’s being measured against?
Fishing mortality against yield: carried over from Day 29, still not started.
Write up a summary document: So that all the interesting and longstanding results are located in one place.

title: Summary: What Thirty Days Actually Found
text: Thirty days in, with results scattered across dozens of individual posts, corrections layered on corrections, and dead ends that turned out to matter as much as the results they blocked, that’s worth doing properly rather than leaving as a TODO. This post is that document, read back over every day-by-day post from Day One through Day 30 and organised by the arc of the actual investigation rather than by date.

title: Summary: What Thirty Days Actually Found
text: Thirty days in, with results scattered across dozens of individual posts, corrections layered on corrections, and dead ends that turned out to matter as much as the results they blocked, that’s worth doing properly rather than leaving as a TODO. This post is that document, read back over every day-by-day post from Day One through Day 30 and organised by the arc of the actual investigation rather than by date.

title: Summary: What Thirty Days Actually Found
text:
The Starting Idea
The project began with a single analogy: fish biomass moving through size space behaves like traffic moving through a road network. A transport system with density-dependent flux, cars slowing down as the road gets crowded, fish growing more slowly as food per individual drops, can jam when the feedback between density and flow rate is strong enough. Just as metered on-ramps can relieve a motorway jam without adding capacity, targeted fishing might in principle relieve a size-spectrum “jam” rather than simply remove biomass from it. Days 1-2 were about getting mizer itself to move at all - the model initialises very close to its own steady state, so the very first technical hurdle was learning to perturb it hard enough to see any dynamics before there was anything to analyse.

title: Summary: What Thirty Days Actually Found
section: Act One: Finding a Real Oscillation, and What Drives It (Days 1-10)
text:
Act One: Finding a Real Oscillation, and What Drives It (Days 1-10)
Day 3’s real breakthrough was realising that “reducing the resource rate” has to mean scaling the existing power-law curve, not replacing it with a constant - the two are different models, not different strengths of the same one. That unlocked the first genuine transient oscillations, and Day 4 mapped a rough stability boundary in \((\beta,\sigma)\) space using relative amplitude (peak-to-peak over the mean), since absolute amplitude is confounded by how the steady-state biomass itself shifts with those parameters.
Day 6 delivered a necessary correction: the oscillations found so far turned out to be numerical ringing from the default integrator, not real dynamics - they vanished entirely under mizer’s more accurate predictor-corrector scheme. The real oscillation came from adapting a two-species anchovy/plankton model (from an RPubs example) with resource replenishment suppressed to ~0.1% of default, and it survived the switch to the accurate integrator, confirming it as a genuine limit cycle with a period of roughly 7-9 years.
Day 7 pinned down the mechanism: a food-limitation cycle concentrated almost entirely in juvenile size classes. Feeding level at the smallest fish crashes to around 0.24 (a quarter of maximum intake) at the resource trough while larger fish stay essentially saturated throughout. Day 8’s FFT analysis confirmed this was one fundamental frequency with harmonics (not two competing timescales), found a clean power-law scaling of period with maturation size (\(\text{period} \sim w_{mat}^{0.2}\), \(R^2=0.9974\)).
Days 9-10 turned to fishing as an intervention. The first attempts at “fish only near the biomass peaks” looked like they worsened the juvenile bottleneck rather than relieving it, and it took real debugging (a selectivity-function bug, then isolating the actual cause) to establish that fishing frequency, not size-selectivity, was the dominant lever - a peaks-only schedule fishing too rarely concentrates pressure into short, damaging bursts, and widening the fishing window fixed most of the problem.

title: Summary: What Thirty Days Actually Found
section: Act Two: Rigor - Wave Theory, Generation Time, and the Unstable Fixed Point (Days 11-18)
text:
Act Two: Rigor - Wave Theory, Generation Time, and the Unstable Fixed Point (Days 11-18)
Day 11 caught its own near-miss: an apparent “bifurcation” in the phase-vs-size-class plot at \(\lambda=2.05\) turned out to be nothing more than Arg() wrapping modulo \(2\pi\), not a real structural change - confirmed directly against the underlying heatmap, which showed no corresponding change in the raw dynamics. A from-scratch derivation of how phase should depend on growth rate then failed its own direct check against the data, pointing at the fixed, steady-state growth rate assumption as the culprit rather than the model itself.
Days 12-13 fixed exactly that: replacing the fixed growth-rate snapshot with the real, time-varying growth field and tracking actual cohorts through it pulled the generation-time estimate from 2.38 years (steady-state) back up to about 3.27 (cohort-tracked) - much closer to the original “about three generations” intuition than the more careful-looking calculation had first suggested. Days 14-15 were pure theory: working through the method of characteristics, gradient catastrophe, shock waves, and rarefaction waves as the formal PDE foundation underneath everything the project had been doing with cohort tracking and phase.
Day 16 introduced steadyNewton(), which can locate a steady state directly regardless of whether it’s stable - crucially, the unstable fixed point that the limit cycle actually orbits. Once the earlier (Euler-based) estimate was redone properly with the predictor-corrector integrator, the limit cycle’s time-averaged biomass exceeded the unstable fixed point by a real but modest 13-23% (not the ~94% the less accurate method had suggested), and a duty-cycle decomposition explained exactly where that gain comes from: an asymmetric relaxation-oscillator shape, not a symmetric wobble. The size-spectrum comparison showed this isn’t a uniform scaling either - it’s a genuine cohort wave, with juvenile sizes depleted on average and large adults elevated. Fishing at realistic effort (0-0.5) barely touched it: mean biomass dropped only 6%, and yield scaled roughly linearly with no sign of a maximum-sustainable-yield peak in that range.
Day 17 found where fishing does eventually kill the cycle - effort \(\approx 8\), an order of magnitude past anything realistic, via a gradual, damped-spiral transition rather than a sudden collapse (a supercritical Hopf signature). Day 18 confirmed the limit cycle is a genuine, wide-basin global attractor (five perturbations spanning three orders of magnitude all converged to the same orbit), but a first hysteresis test left the supercritical-vs-subcritical question wide open: the forward and backward sweeps disagreed by more than could be dismissed as an artefact of where the sweep happened to start.

title: Summary: What Thirty Days Actually Found
text:
Act Three: The Hysteresis Investigation (Days 19-24)
This stretch is the project’s longest sustained debugging arc, and it’s worth reading as one continuous story even though it spans six days and several dead ends.
Day 19 found that balance = FALSE appeared to kill the oscillation outright - until a controlled A/B comparison showed it was actually starving the population across the whole tested range, not stabilising it. Separately, feeding-kernel shape (beta/sigma) was shown to set oscillation amplitude directly, and an 8x yield gap between two kernels turned out to be a size-selectivity artefact: the higher-amplitude kernel’s extra biomass was almost entirely juveniles below the gear’s catchable-size cutoff, not extra mature stock.
Day 20 widened the sweep and found a much bigger hysteresis gap than Day 18’s - but the external diffusion array had been built as a flat constant rather than mizer’s intended allometric \(D_{ext}(w) = D_{ext,i}\cdot w^{n+1}\) shape, so the result needed reproducing properly. Day 21 fixed that and watched hysteresis play out directly in biomass time series rather than just settled max/min summaries, confirming a clear forward/backward disagreement at resource_decrease = 0.05.
Day 22 fixed a Beverton-Holt double-build bug and switched the resource setup to balance = FALSE, resource_level = 0.5 - which cleared the backwards (more-resource-goes-extinct) result, but also flattened the oscillation and hysteresis it was meant to preserve. Diffusion strength was ruled out as the cause; the actual issue was a missing perturbation-kick step that had silently disappeared from every sweep since Day 20. Switching from resource_level (not an independent capacity control, it turns out) to setting capacity_mult and resource_decrease directly recovered real oscillation, specifically a paradox-of-enrichment signature: raising carrying capacity past a threshold destabilised the fixed point, the opposite of the “lower the capacity” hypothesis the search had started from.
Day 23 confirmed, via a snake-sweep phase diagram checked three different ways (forward, reversed, transposed) plus scan-rate, perturbation, and resolution checks, a genuinely clean “no path dependence” result - but only for capacity_mult >= 3. Below that, a classic bifurcation sweep found a real hysteresis loop right at the collapse boundary, and two hypotheses for why capacity_mult = 1 collapses entirely (an over-strong perturbation kick; a rate/capacity mismatch) were both directly refuted. Day 24 refined that loop down to a precisely bracketed (1.30, 1.41) window - about 8% relative width, an order of magnitude tighter than Day 23’s rough bracket - and confirmed it survives two robustness checks: a faster-replenishing resource shifts and narrows it exactly as predicted, and swapping in a completely different (mizer default) species reproduces the same collapse-then-rise shape with a comparably narrow (~12%) window.
The sharpest result of this whole arc is a bare, non-size-structured two-ODE predator-prey toy model, built specifically to test whether size resolution is even necessary. It reproduces mizer’s collapse threshold exactly (a textbook Tilman \(R^*\)/transcritical bifurcation), but shows no hysteresis at all - chemostat-style prey growth structurally forbids it (Rosenzweig’s paradox-of-enrichment argument: the Jacobian’s trace stays negative no matter the predation term’s shape). So the collapse threshold itself doesn’t need size structure; the hysteresis around it apparently does. Separately, Day 24 also showed the severe juvenile-biomass pileup this project had been carrying since Day 6 (only ~0.03% of anchovy biomass “catchable” at maturity) is specific to this project’s own anchovy calibration, not a general mizer feature - mizer’s own default species shows a much milder version of the same skew (~7% catchable).

title: Summary: What Thirty Days Actually Found
section: Act Four: Alpha, and Delay Differential Equations (Days 25-27)
text:
Act Four: Alpha, and Delay Differential Equations (Days 25-27)
Day 25 ran the real parameter sweep the juvenile-pileup question had needed all along - not two guessed points but a proper range for \(\alpha\), \(\gamma\), and \(\kappa\) each. \(\alpha\) dominates by a huge margin (a 27.5-order-of-magnitude range in catchable fraction) ; it’s a viability threshold. The anchovy’s own calibrated \(\alpha=0.1\) sits right at the foot of that climb. \(\gamma\) and \(\kappa\) are real but minor by comparison.
The same day, a time-delay predator-prey model (delaying the predator’s conversion of intake into growth) was proven, both analytically and by simulation, to be structurally incapable of a Hopf bifurcation for any delay or parameter choice: the undelayed prey-renewal term acts as a restoring force strong enough to block it outright. That raised the natural question of whether a delay placed somewhere else in the same system would behave differently.
Day 26 answered it: delaying the prey’s own self-limitation term instead does produce a genuine Hopf bifurcation (confirmed analytically and by simulation, onset near \(\tau \approx 2.4\)), though the toy model’s lack of a saturating functional response lets the resulting cycle drive prey biomass unphysically negative past onset. A third variant, delaying only the predator’s intake term, was reported that day as conditionally possible, with “a genuine threshold \(D < 0.144\).”
Day 27 caught that claim as wrong: it had checked only that the characteristic quadratic’s roots sum to something positive, not that they’re real - the discriminant condition was never checked, and once it was, the two conditions turned out never to overlap for any parameter choice. That delay placement is structurally impossible, not conditional. A fourth, previously untried placement (delaying only the prey term inside the predator’s intake) was then derived and shown to be always possible for any parameters, with a closed-form critical delay after nondimensionalising the whole system down to two ratios. The final tally across all four ways a single delay can sit in this model: two absolute-impossible, two absolute-possible - a clean, even split.

title: Summary: What Thirty Days Actually Found
section: Act Five: Back to the Real Cod Model (Days 28-30)
text:
Act Five: Back to the Real Cod Model (Days 28-30)
Day 28 brought all of this theory to bear on the actual, calibrated cod model for the first time, using a new experimental mizer feature (getStability()/steadyNewton(stability = TRUE), from PR #452) that linearises mizer’s own numerical map directly rather than requiring a hand-derived characteristic equation. Both a direct simulated sweep and the analytic eigenvalue check agreed: cod stayed stable across every point tested (resource_decrease 0.001-1 crossed with capacity_mult 1-20, 120 points) - no sign of anchovy’s paradox-of-enrichment behaviour.
Four separate, deliberately different searches for a lever that would destabilise cod or anchovy (relaxing the reproduction cap, size-selective fishing, pushing capacity_mult to 500x, a body-size/intake-rate factorial) all came back null - and the real finding of the day was methodological, not parametric: getStability() only proves local stability. Perturbing the actual simulation directly, rather than trusting the linearisation, revealed anchovy oscillating across 80 of 120 grid points that getStability() had called uniformly stable (rel_amplitude up to 1.41) - cod, notably, agreed between both methods at every point checked.
Day 30 pushed further on cod specifically. A lambda sweep found a real oscillatory threshold between \(\lambda=2.00\) and \(2.05\) - but built on a flawed mental model of mizer’s own scaling identity (kappa is derived from lambda via a separate, ad hoc empirical formula in this project’s code, not through the classical scaling relation), and the resulting oscillations turned out to be too small to matter next to cod’s mean biomass anyway. The more consequential result came from a deliberately coarse but much wider reconnaissance scan - resource_decrease down to \(10^{-7}\) and capacity_mult down to \(10^{-3}\) (an actively shrunk capacity, never tested before) up to \(10^2\). Cod does oscillate, with rel_amplitude up to 0.041 at extreme resource starvation - territory no grid since Day 24 had ever reached - but that oscillation is real and small, a ripple against cod’s standing biomass rather than anything close to a boom-bust cycle. Sitting right next to it is a more important finding: shrinking capacity_mult below baseline doesn’t produce a milder version of the same story, instead, it collapses the population outright, a qualitatively different failure mode that neither getStability() nor any of the earlier perturbed-amplitude grids were built to distinguish from oscillation until Day 30’s explicit collapse check.

title: Summary: What Thirty Days Actually Found
text:
Recurring Methodological Lessons
A few lessons surfaced more than once, in different forms, across the thirty days:

Verify oscillations under a second, more accurate integration method before trusting them. Day 6’s entire premise rested on this - the original “oscillations” were pure numerical ringing from the default integrator.
Scaling a power law and replacing it with a constant are different models. Day 3’s key realisation, and the reason the first four days produced only transient, not sustained, dynamics.
Use relative amplitude, not absolute, when comparing across parameter values with different baseline scales. Established Day 4, reused in every amplitude-based sweep since.
mizer’s weight grid is logarithmically spaced - a plain mean()/sum() over it silently misweights small vs. large individuals. This specific bug recurred at least three times under different names: Day 19’s catchable_fraction (fixed by weighting with dw), and twice in the juvenile/adult competitiveness metric itself (Day 28’s difference-vs-ratio bug on Day 29, then the unweighted-mean bug caught fresh on Day 30).
Differences aren’t comparable across differently-calibrated systems - use ratios. The exact fix that flipped cod and anchovy’s classification between Day 28 and Day 29.
A coarse grid can only ever overestimate the width of a hysteresis or bistable region. Demonstrated repeatedly - Day 23’s [3,10] plateau, the capacity_mult hysteresis loop refined across Days 23-24, and the default-species hysteresis window refined within Day 24 itself.
A purely local (linearised) stability check can miss real, large-amplitude dynamics reachable from a large-enough perturbation. Day 29’s central finding, and the reason cod’s own “stable everywhere” verdict from Day 28 needed revisiting by Day 30.
State-carrying (“chained”) sweeps are essential for detecting hysteresis, but they actively break models with no immigration term and an absorbing zero state. Day 24’s toy predator-prey model needed fresh starts, not chained sweeps, once a single harsh early value could otherwise drag every later point down with it.
A quadratic’s roots summing to something positive isn’t enough to prove a Hopf crossing exists - the discriminant has to be checked too. Day 26’s error, caught and fixed on Day 27.
Critical slowing down near a bifurcation can look like either a shrinking-but-real effect or pure sampling noise. This recurred across Days 18, 23, 24, 25, and 26, and cost at least one clean conclusion (Day 25’s gamma/kappa sweep) a full day of re-verification before it could be trusted.

title: Day 35 Summary: The Project So Far, By Topic
text: A reference document, not a narrative: what we actually established, grouped by topic, with the mathematics stated once rather than re-derived. The Day 30 summary has the chronological story with its wrong turns intact; this is the condensed version for jogging our own memory and for feeding directly into the final report. \(w\) = body mass (g), \(t\) = time (yr).
